en: The Compendium of the Bodhisattva’s Training (Śikṣāsamuccaya), Fascicle One.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmakīrti;
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Minister of Silver Light and Rank of Honor.
I have heard that the hells are a great peril and terror, where endless, fierce suffering burns incessantly;
because I once lacked a mind of tranquility, I now delight in extensive learning and draw near to the Great Dharma.
Having heard this, I shall distance myself from all evils; I repent for all that I have previously done, leaving nothing behind.
Regarding the wholesome benefits I have never yet attained, how much of them have I already lost?
The sublime joy of the Bodhisattvas is supreme and inexhaustible; only a Buddha fully realizes the principle of equality.
Within this rare and inconceivable jewel of the Dharma, I pray that you will joyfully listen to my words for even a single moment.

The Lord who has attained mastery over the three realms of existence, together with his retinue of the eight classes of dragon deities and others, all give rise to yearning and compassion; with joy, they attentively receive these words of peace and security.
The Tathāgata’s True Dharma and his sons, who have skillfully entered the body born of the Buddha’s precepts—I now collect and explain the words of the Great Sage;
may all who delight in them offer their sincere devotion and reverent prostrations.
In the past, I possessed not the slightest understanding; I lacked instruction and speech, and was not skillful.
I brought no benefit or joy to sentient beings, but sought only my own single mind as a companion in the Dharma.
Yet my aspiration is for the pure Dharma; in order to nurture all roots of goodness, those like us who behold this text but have not yet practiced its meaning should explain it.
The Treatise says:
For one who seeks to accomplish the goal of a person (*puruṣārtha*), it is difficult to find [the necessary conditions] complete even within a single moment.
If one does not contemplate this state of security (*kṣema*), how could such right practice (*samyakpratipatti*) ever exist?
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Sudhana had this thought regarding the Brahmin Jvalanānta: 'It is difficult to obtain a human body; it is difficult to escape from all calamities;

it is difficult to attain a state free from calamities; it is difficult to possess complete purity in every moment; it is difficult to encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world; it is difficult for the sense faculties to be fully intact; it is difficult to hear the Buddha-dharma; it is difficult to meet virtuous people; it is difficult to encounter a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); it is difficult to receive correct instruction according to the principle; and it is difficult to attain a right livelihood.'"
The Commentary says:

Having understood these various kinds of right knowledge, if there is a Mahāsattva who observes in this way—"My intention is to liberate others from all suffering and fear; what excellence is there in delighting in one's own body? Rather, I shall protect the *śīla* (precepts) throughout the realm of sentient beings, uproot the source of all suffering, aspire to the practice of sublime bliss, establish the causes for Bodhi, and give rise to a firm resolve that does not destroy the faculty of faith."
As stated in the verse from the *Ratnaprabhāsa-dhāraṇī*:

"Faithfully following all Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma, as well as the path practiced by the sons of the Buddha, and faith in unsurpassed great bodhi—by these means, a bodhisattva first generates the mind [of enlightenment]."
Faith is the precursor and the mother of merit; it nurtures all supreme and wholesome dharmas. It severs the net of doubt and dries up the flow of craving.
Faith can manifest the practice of patience; faith is free from turbidity and defilement, purifying the mind. It abandons pride and serves as the foundation for reverence.
Faith is like a pure hand that grasps the causes; it is the supreme practice of the seven noble treasures.
Faith enables all joyful relinquishment, and through faith and joy, one enters the Buddha-dharma.
This faith gives birth to the merit of wisdom, penetrating everything taught by the Buddha.
The light and purity of the faculty of faith are exceedingly sharp; it truly and forever severs the root of afflictions.
The power of faith is firm and indestructible; with single-minded sincerity, one believes in the Buddha’s virtues.
Believing in both the associated and the non-associated, one is in an instant free from all defilements and attachments.
Faith can transcend all realms of Māra and reveal the supreme path to liberation.
Faith is the indestructible seed of merit, for it is able to cause the sprouts of Bodhi to grow.
Faith is the gateway for the arising of supreme wisdom; it manifests as all the Awakened Ones throughout the ten directions.

If one always places deep faith and respect in the Jewel of the Buddha, one will remain far removed from what is non-precept and non-training. If one can remain far removed from non-precepts and non-training, such a person deeply extols the virtues of the Buddha.

If one always places faith and honor in the Jewel of the Dharma, then one will never grow weary of hearing the Buddha's teachings; if one never grows weary of hearing the Buddha's teachings, one will attain inconceivable faith and understanding in the Dharma.

If one always places deep faith and respect in the Sangha Jewel, then one will never grow weary or retreat from the pure assembly; if one never grows weary or retreats from the pure assembly, then one's power of faith will remain unshakable.

If one is unshakable in the power of faith, then one attains the purity, clarity, and sharpness of the faculties; if one attains the purity, clarity, and sharpness of the faculties, that person remains far removed from evil companions.
If a person stays far away from all evil friends and is embraced by virtuous spiritual friends, once embraced by such virtuous spiritual friends, they will constantly cultivate vast goodness.
If one constantly cultivates vast goodness, one will accomplish the power of great causes; if one accomplishes the power of great causes, that person’s faith and understanding are most supreme.

If one attains the most supreme faith and understanding, one will be constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas; if one is constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas, then one will be able to give rise to the bodhicitta.

If one can give rise to the bodhicitta and diligently cultivate the qualities of a Buddha, and if one diligently cultivates the qualities of a Buddha, then one will be born into the family of the Tathāgata.

If one is born into the family of the Tathāgata, one is liberated from both attachment and non-attachment; having attained liberation from both attachment and non-attachment, one then achieves the purity of profound faith.

If one attains deep-seated faith that is pure, then one attains the most supreme and most excellent; having attained the most supreme and excellent, one constantly practices the profound and wondrous pāramitās.

If one practices the profound and sublime pāramitās, then one can awaken to and enter the Mahāyāna; if one can awaken to and enter the Mahāyāna, then one knows how to make offerings to the Buddha in accordance with the Dharma.

If one knows how to make offerings to the Buddha in accordance with the Dharma, then one will attain an unmoving mind of mindfulness of the Buddha; if one attains an unmoving mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, then one will constantly contemplate the inconceivable nature of the Buddha.

If one constantly contemplates the inconceivable Buddha, one finds that the Buddha is neither born nor abiding anywhere; if the Buddha is neither born nor abides anywhere, then one knows that this Dharma is eternally imperishable.
The Commentary states:
Among these, the merit of first giving rise to the faculty of faith is vast and immeasurable; it is here described briefly from within the totality.
Furthermore, for ordinary beings and those born as such, it is difficult to give rise to faith and understanding regarding such a Dharma.

If one plants the provisions of merit with a pure deep resolve, through the power of the cause of faith, one shall abide for as many eons as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, experiencing various sublime joys and the excellent rewards of virtuous merit.
One should give rise to faith and understanding toward such teachings.
As stated in a verse from the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra*:
"Faith is the supreme vehicle that carries one to the attainment of perfect enlightenment; therefore, the wise should cultivate matters such as faith."
"If a person lacks the faculty of faith, they will not give rise to any wholesome dharmas; they are like parched grain seeds, which likewise cannot produce sprouts or stalks.
Furthermore, the *Mahā-saṃgiti-sūtra* states:
"At that time, the Tathāgata commanded Ānanda, saying:"
"In the Dharma of faith, one should practice it exactly as it has been understood.
The Commentary states:
"One who practices this faith attains firmness in the faculty of faith within a single moment; thus, the bodhicitta becomes firm, enabling one to gather all meritorious rewards."
As stated in the *Sīharājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
“At that time, Prince Siṃhala addressed the Buddha, saying:
‘World-Honored One!...’”
"How can one cause all sentient beings, in whatever place they are born, to always find joy in and be gathered by the teachings?

The Buddha said, "Those who wish to liberate all sentient beings should constantly give rise to humility and respect and resolve for bodhicitta; this is what is called 'always finding joy in and being gathered by the teachings.'"
Furthermore, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Good son!
The bodhicitta is like a seed, for it can give birth to all the dharmas of the Buddhas."
The bodhicitta is like a fertile field, for it can cause the pure and white dharmas of sentient beings to grow;
it is like the great earth, for it is that upon which all worlds depend and are sustained.
The bodhicitta is like a compassionate father, for it instructs and protects all bodhisattvas;
it is like Vaiśravaṇa, for it can sever all suffering of poverty;
it is like a maṇi jewel, for it accomplishes all purposes and benefits.
The bodhicitta is like a precious vase, for it fulfills all virtuous aspirations;
it is like a single-pronged vajra, for it can ultimately crush the enemies of the afflictions;
it is like the True Dharma, for it can sever all mental engagements of the deep-seated mind.
It is like a sharp sword, for it can sever the heads of all afflictions.
The bodhicitta is like a sharp axe, for it can fell the trees of all sufferings;
it is like weaponry, for it can defend against all extreme hardships and calamities.
It is like a hook and rod, for it lifts sentient beings out of the ocean of saṃsāra;
it is like a great wind-circle, for it can swiftly blow away all obstructing clouds, mists, and grasses.
The bodhicitta is like a grove of trees, for it accumulates all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva;
it is like a Buddhist stūpa or temple, for it is revered by all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
"Good son! The bodhicitta accomplishes such immeasurable and sublime merits.
The Treatise says:
How, furthermore, is it known that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can resolve their minds toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*)?
Regarding this, authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) is cited, as clarified not in a single sūtra alone.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Even if one gives rise to the view of a self as vast as Mount Sumeru, one can still generate the mind of great bodhicitta and give birth to the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* explains this meaning of an ordinary person who is a bodhisattva, saying:
"The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:"
"Just as the chick of the kalaviṅka bird is already able to produce exquisite and beautiful sounds even before it has emerged from its egg,
Mañjuśrī, so too is this bodhisattva:

although they have not yet severed the view of self, have not yet exited the triple world, and remain within the shell of ignorance, they are already able to produce the sublime sounds of all Buddhas— namely, the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and liberation."
Furthermore, the *Sarvadharmānuśāsanī-sūtra* states:

"At that time, when the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya entered parinirvāṇa within his earthen cave, he took rebirth in a great city because he had cultivated the remedy through faith and understanding in emptiness."
Furthermore, the *Samādhy-asamādhi-mudrā-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
'What is meant by a bodhisattva who proceeds by means of a sheep-cart?'"

For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to travel across worlds as numerous as the atoms in five buddha-fields. This person boards a sheep-drawn carriage and proceeds along the road; after a vast period of time has passed while traveling a hundred *yojana*s, they encounter a great wind-circle, and by reason of this, they are driven back eighty thousand *yojana*s.
"Later, would that person, riding this sheep-cart in that world, be able to traverse even a single world-system throughout unspeakably unspeakable kalpas? Mañjuśrī replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“If one who belongs to the Mahāyāna has already resolved upon bodhicitta, they should not uphold, recite, or study the teachings of the Śrāvaka-yāna; nor should they dwell together with śrāvakas to practice the Śrāvaka-yāna, or, out of their own deep-seated mind, be instructed by others in such a vehicle as to attain understanding and the wisdom thereof. For these reasons, they will immediately fall away from the Unsurpassed Way.”
Such a bodhisattva utterly destroys the faculty of wisdom and the eye of wisdom obtained through the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Mañjuśrī,
I call such a person a "bodhisattva who travels by sheep-cart."
The Commentary says:

If a bodhisattva delights in the Mahāyāna and has faith-understanding (*adhimukti*) in emptiness, they attain perfection in the stage of practice through faith-understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*). This authoritative scriptural statement (*āptavacana*) is seen as such an event only by a bodhisattva on the stage of practice through faith-understanding.
As stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:

"By means of countless dhāraṇīs, gateways of samādhi, the playful mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the infinite collection of liberating wisdom and clarity, one equally transcends all the conduct and retributions of ordinary fools. Even unto the end of time, one does not act for the sake of gain or offerings; regarding the worldly requisites and enjoyments obtained throughout billions of eons, the mind is free from attachment and makes no conceptual distinctions, like a lotus in full bloom, complete with its adornments."

Furthermore, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, they abide securely in the Mahāyāna, clearly realizing the ultimate truth; their accumulations of merit and wisdom are never diminished, and they are fully endowed with the hundreds of thousands of doors of practice corresponding to the previously cultivated paths of renunciation.
The Commentary says:
What is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?

It refers to those who have first generated the bodhicitta being told that they abide on this stage. The non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*) consists of obtaining freedom from doubt through a few partial signs.

This is the meaning of the words produced by the practice of faith and understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) as expressed in this authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*); it should be understood through faith and understanding according to its medium, extensive, and concise versions.
Furthermore, the *Tathāgataguhyasūtra* states:
"At that time, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:"
“World-Honored One!
How should that bodhicitta be generated?
The Buddha said:
"Great King! It means that the profound mind does not regress. The King said:
“World-Honored One!
How does one’s profound resolve not regress?
The Buddha said:
“Great King! It is that which can give rise to great compassion. The king said:
“World-Honored One!
How can one bring forth the great vajra?
The Buddha said:
"Great King! It means not giving rise to a mind of aversion or abandonment toward sentient beings.
The King said:
“World-Honored One!
How does one attain freedom from weariness or abandonment regarding all sentient beings?
The Buddha said:
"O Great King!
It means that if one does not cling to one's own happiness, one attains insatiable relinquishment.
The Commentary says:
In this context, "bodhicitta" refers to the meaning of inspiring great compassion, joy, and reverent love.
If one does not rely on the corresponding teachings of the Tathāgata, such a person will have no liberation.
If this bodhicitta is seen as something to be censured and loathed, one is not called a person who has generated the mind of enlightenment.
As the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra* states:
"O son of good family!..."

If, when bodhisattvas manifest the essence of the arousal of the bodhicitta, they encounter Tathāgatas and the assembly of śrāvakas who teach and exhort them to arouse the mind for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called the first characteristic of joyfully arousing the bodhicitta.

If, upon hearing an exposition of bodhi and the bodhicitta, one immediately resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called the second characteristic of joyfully resolving to attain bodhicitta.

If those sentient beings have no refuge and no protector, and one perceives these two conditions and dwells in great compassion, even to the point of giving rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is called the third characteristic of joyfully giving rise to the bodhicitta.
"If one sees the Tathāgata’s various marks as perfectly complete, one immediately gives rise to reverence and affection; this is called the fourth characteristic of generating the bodhicitta.
The Commentary states:
"As for the bodhicitta, there are two kinds:"
The first is the bodhicitta of aspiration; the second is the bodhicitta of abiding.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"O son of good family!..."

Furthermore, there are sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings who aspire to realize the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is difficult to attain; and there are further sentient beings who abide in this mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is difficult to attain.
The Commentary says:
First is the vow to realize Buddhahood; second is the vow to abide in successive births.
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Having already generated the bodhicitta in the presence of a certain Buddha, why would one perform only minor roots of virtue?
As stated in the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*:
"In the past, when the Tathāgata Jyotiṣprabha first generated the bodhicitta in the presence of the Tathāgata Dānaśabda, he was a cowherd who offered *tandula* leaves to that Buddha."
When the Tathāgata Amitayaśas first resolved his mind upon bodhi in the presence of the Tathāgata Vidyutprabha, he was a cotton-weaver who offered that Buddha exquisite garments.
When the Tathāgata Arciṣmān first resolved his mind on awakening in the presence of the Tathāgata Amitābha, he was residing within a city and offered a grass lamp-torch to that Buddha.
When the Tathāgata Durjayo first resolved his mind upon bodhicitta in the presence of the Tathāgata Dṛḍhapada, he was a woodcutter who offered the Buddha a small piece of tooth-stick.
When the Tathāgata Guṇaketurāja first resolved his mind upon awakening in the presence of the Tathāgata Mañjuśrīkīrti, he was a physician who offered a single *āmra* fruit to that Buddha.
The Commentary says:
Although this initial generation of the bodhicitta is not yet the fulfillment of practice, even this act of renunciation can still liberate one from saṃsāra and attain immeasurable bliss.
As stated in the *Maitreya-vimokṣa-sūtra*:
"O son of noble family!
It is like a jewel named vajra, which is able to sever all suffering of poverty."
"Good son! This mind of omniscience is also like this, for it can sever all the sufferings of saṃsāra.
The Treatise says:
Only those who have generated this bodhicitta can draw near to that fruit; it should be understood in this way.
Furthermore, the *Suyodhana-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha said:..."

"Great King! If you think that among many types of actions one can perform many types of actions, it does not compare to my performing all types of practices within all practices, and benefiting all places within all places—namely, training in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), and so on, up to training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
"Great King!
Therefore, regarding your own attainment of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is likewise so:
you should joyfully give rise to pure faith and the aspiration to benefit others, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether dreaming or awake; or at the time of eating and drinking."
Constantly possessing the mental attention of recollection, one observes the bodies of all Buddhas,
Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings, as well as all roots of virtue accumulated in the past,
future, and present; having weighed them and brought them together, one should personally manifest sympathetic joy for that which is worthy of sympathetic joy.
Extending even to the entirety of the realm of empty space and the realm of nirvana, they likewise rejoice; furthermore,
they rejoice in all the acts of making offerings performed by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas,
dedicating them equally to all sentient beings, until all beings attain the wisdom of all-knowledge, universally and completely perfected.
Fulfilling all the wholesome dharmas of the Buddhas,
he daily and at the three times of the day dedicated [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Great King!
"Since you have attained the title of 'King' through such right practice, you shall also achieve perfection in seeking the conduct of Bodhi without abandoning your precious throne.
Having spoken these words of response, he said: "Great King!"

At that time, because you gave rise to the bodhicitta, through the karmic retribution of those roots of goodness, you were constantly born in the heavens for immeasurable eons; among the gods, you became Śakra, Lord of the Devas, or you were born in the human realm as a king among men.
"O Great King!
It is solely by the power of the root of goodness from having once resolved upon bodhicitta that they are either perfected or not yet perfected, with no other distinct karma involved;
this you should know. To state the essential point, the Buddha said:

“Great King! One who gives rise to the bodhicitta alone does so for the sake of rescuing and delivering all sentient beings, for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, for the sake of bringing peace and security to all sentient beings, for the sake of ultimately leading all sentient beings to nirvana, and for the sake of attaining immeasurable and innumerable roots of goodness.”
"Great King!
Furthermore, what is meant by saying that among the various types of actions, one can perform many kinds of actions?
The treatise says:
Regarding the characteristics of this bodhicitta practice, the sūtras explain it as the dependent origination of the past and present.
As for the bodhicitta of aspiration, at what stage of the bodhisattva path does one obtain the precepts?
Some say: nine stages.
The *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* states:
"Renown and material gain are the root of all transgressions.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:

"In the description of the first bhūmi, it says that one does not have even the slightest intimacy with or longing for such gain; rather, if sentient beings come to me, I shall provide them with everything they require, even in double measure."
The Commentary states:

According to what has been said, the Bodhisattva of the Stage of Utmost Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) attains firm abiding in accordance with immovability; furthermore, it is taught that they are born into the family of the Tathāgata and are destined to attain perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
Furthermore, the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* states:
"The Śrāvaka vehicle cannot attain such [realization], except for those who delight in the Mahāyāna.
As it is said in the *Paramārthaviniścaya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
"This dharma of stinginess and envy is precisely what is called 'bondage.

This teaching fully indicates that on the Stage of Supreme Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), one is far removed from the notion of "I" and the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) does not arise; how then could one again cling to all necessities, as when it is said that one should give away even one's head and eyes?
The Commentary states:
Such sūtras as these primarily manifest this training for those who have already entered the stages (bhūmi).

If one were to discuss the bodhisattva’s corresponding cultivation in its entirety, it might be necessary to exclude certain practices that should not be undertaken all at once, because the bodhisattva has not yet mastered them; thus, it should be understood that these two types [of training] pervade all the points of training (śikṣāpada).
Furthermore, because there is no training in the accomplishment of its function for this other type of training, there is no fault even if one does not cultivate it.
The *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:

"When practicing extensive giving, one does not abandon pure ethical discipline out of indolence; because it was not previously taught, one does not accumulate its practice, but approaches it according to one's capacity."
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"Even if one commits sexual misconduct, the defilement of the transgression against the precepts is slight because of the delight in the bodhicitta. O Śāriputra!"
It is said that a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the prātimokṣa precepts consists of four dharmas;
namely, that this bodhisattva attains truthful speech in the course of cultivation. Śāriputra!

If a son or daughter of good family, having resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is dedicated to diligence and zealously seeks the wholesome dharmas, practices various discourses, maintains the prohibitive precepts, and fully cultivates the training of a bodhisattva.

Due to associating with others, one may at times transgress such training in ethical discipline or slight and disparage one's venerable teacher; yet, out of extreme shame and remorse, one gives rise to great dread.
Furthermore, by receiving and utilizing what is respected and cherished, one brings this equalizing dharma of ethical discipline to full completion.

This bodhisattva, regarding the training in the precepts manifested by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, should generate a desire for practice and undergo formal instruction. If such a person lacks a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they should, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas currently residing in the ten directions, focus their mindfulness and cultivate visualization, weighing their capacity according to their strength. Having done so, they should firmly uphold these precepts, never again deceiving the assembly of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the ten directions, nor the gods and humans of the world.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"First having little intention to give, and later competing with others not to give, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts;
having spoken [of giving] but failing to give, one falls into the realm of hell-dwellers."
How much more so for unsurpassed enlightenment, which is granted as a complete gift to all sentient beings in the world without exception?
As the *Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra* says:
"O son of noble family!..."
A bodhisattva should revere the ultimate truth. Why is this?
O son of good family!
Because the collection of the true reality is called the "Dharma-collection. Good son!
What is meant by "true reality"?

If a bodhisattva resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, even at the cost of abandoning body and life, does not forsake this resolve because they do not abandon all sentient beings, this is called the bodhisattva’s ultimate truth (*bhūta-artha*).

If a bodhisattva, having already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, later abandons this resolve and forsakes all sentient beings, that bodhisattva commits a great falsehood and is truly to be censured and loathed.
Furthermore, the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-vimala-mudrā-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha said: 'Sāgaramati!'"

For example, if a king or his ministers wish to provide sustenance for all the people of the cities and towns, yet having gathered them together, they abandon them and fail to prepare either drink or food, they would be deceiving those people.
"However, they were unable to obtain even a small amount of food and drink; they rebuked [the attendants] with loud voices and departed in a fit of anger.
The Buddha said, "Sāgaramati!"

This bodhisattva is also like this: while they cause those among sentient beings who have not yet been delivered to cross over, they should not merely cultivate quick speech and sharp eloquence; rather, they must diligently cultivate extensive learning and accumulate all the wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). If such a bodhisattva does not do so, they would be deceiving the devas, humans, and worldlings.

As previously taught by the Buddhas, this is that which the noble ones censure and loathe; it is extremely difficult to obtain even for those possessing wisdom, great wisdom, and the unsurpassed, supreme wisdom.
Therefore, you should know that a bodhisattva ought not to deceive all devas, humans, and the world with mere words and falsehoods.
Furthermore, Sāgaramati!

When someone comes to request that he preach the Dharma and perform acts of benefit, that bodhisattva speaks in accordance with their words; even to the point of sacrificing his own body to cultivate the bodhisattva practices, he never again deceives any sentient being. It should be understood in this way.
The Compendium of Training for Bodhisattvas (Śikṣāsamuccaya), Fascicle One.
The Compendium of Training for Bodhisattvas, Fascicle Two.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmakīrti.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others—Śramaṇas of the Purple Robe and Subjects of the Emperor, including the Great Master of Indian Translation, Pu-ming Cizhao, who was granted the title of Silver Light Luoguo Dafu and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments—by Imperial Decree. Chapter One, Part Two: On the Training in Generosity. The Treatise states:
Therefore, one should know that what is accumulated through one's own effort must be guarded even within a single wholesome path, in accordance with its specific characteristics.
As stated in the *Daśabhūmikavibhāṣā-śāstra*:
"These ten paths of wholesome action are the fruits realized by the Buddha. If one does not truly guard even a single path of wholesome action, yet at the time of death proclaims of oneself:
'I am a true practitioner of the Mahāyāna; I seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"

"You should know that such a person is utterly deceitful and a great liar; before the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions, they delude the world by preaching views of emptiness and nihilism to entice and deceive the ignorant. When their body perishes and their life ends, they will fall into the various evil realms."
The Commentary states:
Even until the moment of death, one should continue to practice by gathering all categories of wholesome qualities, even if only for a brief moment.
As it is said in the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-sūtra*:

"If one sees a being of great resolve who, having heard of the bodhisattva’s difficult and painful practices as well as his wondrous and supreme wisdom, even to the point of entering into understanding, rousing great courage, and taking up the heavy burden to rescue and protect sentient beings by exhausting the root of all suffering; and who performs prostrations and offerings, confesses transgressions, rejoices in merit, and entreats the Buddhas to remain in the world to preach the Dharma, even up to dedicating [merit] toward enlightenment; or who, for the sake of a spiritual friend, requests them to preach the Dharma or delights in preaching it themselves—know that such a person is called 'one who shows the path.'"
As stated in the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-guṇavyūha-sūtra*:
"World-Honored One!
When this Mañjughoṣa was born in former lives, he generated the bodhicitta through the causal conditions of his original practices; he has likewise generated it now, just as was described therein."
Until the very limit of beginningless saṃsāra, I shall perform such deeds for the benefit of sentient beings.

Having generated the bodhicitta in the presence of the Honored One, I now entreat you to cause all worlds to be liberated from the retribution of poverty, anger, resentment, stinginess, greed, and jealousy; that when I attain bodhi, these shall never arise again, and that I may constantly practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) until I am freed from all sinful desires.

Following the Buddha in training in pure ethical discipline, I cherish and respect great enlightenment; I do not hasten to realize it, for I remain until the final limit of time, regarding all sentient beings as having a single, undifferentiated nature.

At that time, throughout the worlds of the ten directions—immeasurable and inconceivable lands where my name had not yet been heard—all were completely adorned and purified; because the actions of my body, speech, and mind were pure, all that I undertook was likewise pure.
Furthermore, at all times they firmly maintain pure precepts, remaining free from all faults and evils until the very end of saṃsāra.
Also, the *Akṣobhyatathāgatasya Pūrvapraṇidhāna-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states:
“When that Tathāgata Akṣobhya was formerly a bodhisattva, he spoke as follows:”
"If I were not to go forth as a renunciant in birth after birth throughout all my lives, I would be deceiving all the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas. Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva should likewise follow and learn from the example of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, whenever Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are born, they leave the home life; whether Tathāgatas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, they ultimately renounce their homes and go forth into homelessness, training in this very same way.
Why is this? Śāriputra,

if one says that for a bodhisattva to leave home and go forth is the most supreme, even to the point of not giving rise to attachment toward male or female relatives— just as when I was born, I was free from all faults.
The Commentary says:
Let us set aside for now what has been stated above.

If one were to claim that the characteristics of giving and the characteristics of transgression are identical, or that they correspond in their respective natures, one should abandon such a view oneself.

If individual modes of conduct are also not without fault—because although they may apply to specific modes of conduct, they do not encompass [the whole]—then for a bodhisattva to fail to exert diligent effort through body, speech, and mind to bring all future sufferings of sentient beings to liberation and to cause all sublime happiness to increase; to take no pleasure in exhorting and transforming others when conditions converge; to not seek out those in states of dispersal or destruction; to fail to give rise to remedies for either predominant or minor afflictions; and to neither benefit nor harm, but rather abandon instantaneously, matters of great significance, minor significance, or even what is not significant—this is said to be a transgression.
Briefly stated, there is no offense when one’s own power is entirely incapable of producing a result regarding the object and the matter;
or when one holds that such a thing constitutes an offense in terms of the nature of the training and its manifest characteristics.
If there is no locus of transgression corresponding to the sphere of one’s own power, then it is said that the equality of transgressions is identical to liberation from signs.
This Bodhisattva trains in the equality of the body, which is extensively and infinitely taught throughout the future limit of immeasurable eons.

Furthermore, to speak briefly, these two kinds of offenses of a bodhisattva consist in abandoning [the practice] without any discernment regarding whether they are accomplished or not, appropriate or not, and what may or may not be done. This is an offense because of such abandonment.
This refers to the fault of falsely interpreting the meaning by claiming that [the ultimate] completely transcends vitarka and vicāra, as is the case with those such as the outcaste slaves.
What does this mean? The *Gambhīrāśayaparivarta-sūtra* states:
“As for the four kinds of eloquence possessed by Maitreya during his stage of practice, these are the very words of all Buddhas.

What are the four? First, discerning that which is meaningful and beneficial while rejecting that which is not; second, discerning this True Dharma while rejecting what is not the Dharma; third, dispelling afflictions rather than increasing them; and fourth, delighting in seeing the merits of nirvāṇa rather than delighting in seeing the merits of saṃsāra. These are called the four kinds.”
To state it briefly: if that is so, why did Maitreya, while still in the stage of a bodhisattva, speak of these four kinds of eloquence?
It is because faithful sons and daughters of good family conceive the notion of the Buddhas and the notion of engaging in discourse when they hear the sublime Dharma.
Why is this so? It is because whatever virtuous teachings Maitreya possesses are the very words of the Buddhas.

If one slanders the eloquence of Maitreya, failing to respect it as the word of the Buddhas, such a person is an evil individual who slanders the eloquence spoken by the Buddhas. By disparaging the sublime Dharma, they will incur the retribution of sinful karma and fall into the miserable realms.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, one should cultivate skillfulness and give rise to joyful aspiration; within this gateway of practice, the most excellent function is the gathering of training, which one ought to study for the sake of aspiring to the great fruit.
As stated in the *Śāntiniyata-vikurvaṇa-sūtra*: "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,

if a bodhisattva were to take as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River belonging to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and were to fill them with sovereign king maṇi jewels and offer them as a gift for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River."
If bodhisattvas, having heard such characteristics of the Dharma, contemplate with single-minded intent, "I shall practice and learn this," Mañjuśrī,

compared to the merit and reward of those previously mentioned who have no more to learn (*aśaikṣa*), the merit of giving to a bodhisattva on the stage of aspiring to learn (*śikṣamāṇa-bhūmi*) is far greater.
The Commentary says:
Although this bodhisattva perceives these merits, he has not yet spoken of how they are to be cultivated and so forth.
Furthermore, it is as stated there:
"Mañjuśrī! Suppose one were to teach and transform as many sentient beings as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, and each of those sentient beings were to become a King of Jambudvīpa.

If one were to praise with all manner of sounds those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice according to the instructions this Mahāyāna sūtra, and were to cut and sever the flesh, fingers, and nails from their own bodies for a single day and night, continuing such devoted practice until the end of their life;

Mañjuśrī! Because of this, the bodhisattva’s mind of giving is free from timidity; he is not startled, not terrified, and has no fear. With ultimate single-mindedness, he gives rise to the thought of intimacy, being without regret, without doubt, and without discrimination. He accords with and embraces this supreme true Dharma, delighting in its recitation and study, and practicing according to what is taught.

Mañjuśrī! Because this bodhisattva’s mind is courageous, they are courageous in generosity, courageous in ethical discipline, courageous in diligence, courageous in meditative concentration, courageous in wisdom, and courageous in all samādhis.
Mañjuśrī! Even if such a bodhisattva encounters wicked people, they do not give rise to anger, aversion, or any other faults toward them. Mañjuśrī!
"This bodhisattva is as unmoving as Śakra, Brahmā, and the other kings.
The Commentary says:
Now is precisely the time; one should study with a single mind, aspiring for the great fruit of retribution.
A verse from the *Samādhirāja Sūtra* says:

"If for many billions of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one were to make offerings to hundreds of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, providing food and delicacies with pure faith, and also offering lamps, garlands, banners, and canopies."

If, during the degenerate age when the True Dharma is declining and such Buddha-dharma is about to perish, one practices these deeds for even a single day and night, this merit will surpass that of the former.
The Commentary says:
Therefore, one should practice with single-minded diligence according to the meaning of the bodhisattva’s training as taught in the Buddha’s sūtras.
As it is said in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:
“Good son! A bodhisattva who firmly maintains the pure precepts in the bodhisattva training reflects and investigates thus:
‘If I do not abide within the bodhisattva prātimokṣa vows, how could I possibly attain the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?’”
Furthermore, why not [apply myself] to the bodhisattva practices elucidated within the Mahāyāna sūtras of the Tathāgata, and to the bodhisattva training therein?
I shall cultivate these extensively in such a manner.
The Commentary says: We are ignorant;

regarding this extensive explanation that the Bodhisattva’s prohibitions might allow for the arising of unwholesome thoughts, why would this not be reasonable? For in the context of cultivation, there is absolutely no fault.
What is the place of cultivation?

It refers to when one practices pure relinquishment regarding all bodily enjoyments throughout the three periods of time, protecting all sentient beings so that they may increase in purity; having received these bodhisattva precepts, if this bodhisattva dwells in the place of cultivation, he speaks of the characteristics of these transgressions.
As stated in the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
"In the bodhisattva path, one gathers in all sentient beings so that they may exhaust the realms of suffering.
While dwelling in that bodhisattva path for more than a hundred million eons (*koṭi-kalpa*), one gives rise to only a single thought of peace and a thought of intimacy."
"A Bodhisattva who gives rise to this mind should know that they consistently embrace sentient beings in many ways of dwelling.
As it is said in the *Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-vinaya*:
"At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Devaputra Silent Sound (*Śāntasvara*):"
"If a bodhisattva is endowed with these five kinds of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), they will swiftly attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. What are the five?

When a bodhisattva applies profound and firm attention (*manasikāra*) in seeking the unsurpassed path, and resolves their mind so as not to fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is the first immediate succession of the resolve for enlightenment."
To renounce all that one possesses and not dwell with a mind of stinginess—this is the second immediate cause.
To resolve, "I shall deliver all sentient beings," and therein never give rise to a mind of indolence or retreat—this is the third immediate cause.
To realize that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent, neither arising nor ceasing, and therein not to fall into any views—this is the fourth immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

To unify the wisdom regarding all phenomena into a single characteristic, and thus to give rise to the mind of awakening without abiding anywhere, and by virtue of this non-abiding to find nothing at all within omniscience—this is the fifth immediate succession.
The Commentary states:
Regarding the uninterrupted continuity of the meritorious rewards experienced by the body, one should cause them to be purified and increased through the acts of relinquishing and guarding.
As it is said in the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya-vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*:

"Because one perceives the faults in grasping at the objects that have been relinquished, and gives rise to the perception of detachment within the gateway of visualization by contemplating the merit of relinquishment.
As it is said in a verse from the *Samādhirāja Sūtra*:
"Such an impermanent body is what the minds of fools delight in."
Within this transient life, every moment is like an illusion or a dream.
Because one creates various evil karmas, the retribution for those sins constantly pursues one.
Due to these causes of ignorance, at death one mostly falls into the evil realms.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*:
"How do sentient beings come to have the causes for strife and contention?
It is said that their attachment to wealth and profit constitutes the root."
"One should abandon [them]; if one is free from craving and attachment, one will immediately obtain this dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "Moreover, Śāriputra!"
A bodhisattva does not give rise to the notion of "other" regarding even the most subtle parts of all phenomena. Why is this?
Because they fear grasping and attachment.
The *Paramārthaviniścayasūtra* states:
"That is to say, if one who practices giving is free from all stinginess, yet one who clings to things constantly guards them."
Furthermore, one who practices giving brings an end to craving and attachment, whereas one who clings increases craving and attachment.
One who practices giving is free from all conceptual constructions, whereas one who clings possesses all conceptual constructions.
The one who practices giving has no fear; the one who clings is full of fear.
The one who practices giving dwells on the path to enlightenment; the one who clings dwells within the realm of Māra.
The giver conceives the thought of inexhaustibility, while the one who clings conceives the thought of exhaustion.
Furthermore, the giver attains all manner of sublime joys, whereas the one who clings is constantly oppressed.
The giver abandons afflictions, while the one who clings increases them.
Furthermore, the giver attains great wealth and abundance, whereas the one who clings suffers great poverty and lack.
Generosity is the virtuous undertaking of the noble; attachment is the calculating scheme of the wicked.
Generosity is praised by all Buddhas; attachment is praised by the foolish.

Even so, the donor does not give rise to attachment toward their own biological offspring, as they do not feel such [attachment] toward other sentient beings because they instead arouse compassion for them.
One should know that there are three types of one's own mind as explained here.
What are these three?
First, a bodhisattva is correctly and appropriately engaged with the path to enlightenment, not erroneously or perversely engaged.
Second, a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward the path to enlightenment, not a mind of superiority or inferiority.
"Third, the Bodhisattva has no manifold practices regarding the path to enlightenment; there are no manifold practices.
These are called the three kinds of what is spoken from one's own mind.
The Treatise says:
This means that regarding one's own biological son, one should conceive of him as not being a virtuous friend; since he is not a virtuous friend, he is not my [true] friend.

Because one trains to bear the heavy burden in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions for the sake of benefiting others, one does not give rise to attachment toward one's own biological son, unlike the compassion one feels toward other sentient beings.

One should know that once this mind has been generated, just as one gives rise to loving-kindness toward one's own child, so too does one accordingly give rise to loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Observing and realizing with such a profound mind, since my son is no different from all sentient beings, then all sentient beings are my sons.

Whether for oneself or others, including even lay bodhisattvas among the householders, one should not be attached to wealth and profit or to things that do not lead to the gathering of sentient beings, nor to those dharmas that lack the quality of renunciation.
Furthermore, one should not take pleasure in or conform to defiled desires.
Moreover, if a householder bodhisattva encounters someone coming to beg, they should, regardless of what is required, give with a courageous and resolute mind.
Furthermore, one reflects:
"Whether these wealth and gains of mine are relinquished or not, they will ultimately perish.
How, then, can one attain freedom from desire at the time of relinquishing them?

That is to say, having attained ultimate patience regarding "I" and "mine," one is free from the suffering of the womb with respect to the objects to be relinquished; the mind abides in right mindfulness, and joy and delight arise without further entanglement.
Furthermore, regarding such renunciation, one should understand that there are four types of perceptions concerning the objects to be given away and the beggars.
What are these four? They are:
[the perception arising from] being timid and weak, whereby one is unable to bring to maturity the roots of goodness and the karma previously performed;
In the Mahāyāna, one lacks mastery of mind because of the perception of acceptance and rejection.
Furthermore, if one abides in the power of patience regarding "self" and "what belongs to self," one will not give rise to regret or vexation when encountering virtuous people.
One should practice in this way, exult in this way, and exert diligence in this way, for the sake of fulfilling all that sentient beings desire.
Thus should a lay bodhisattva conceive such thoughts toward those who beg from him.
If a beggar should instead increase their faults, the bodhisattva should comfort them with kind words.
Furthermore, even if a beggar is ungrateful, the bodhisattva likewise does not give rise to stinginess or envy.
This is to be without fault.
Regarding this, for the sake of planting the seeds for bodhisattvas, the World-Honored One has spoken as it is said in the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa*: "Śāriputra!..."
A bodhisattva does not possess four things. What are these four?
First, a bodhisattva has no lack of faith.
Second, the bodhisattva is free from stinginess and greed;
third, the bodhisattva is free from double-tongued speech and jealousy;
fourth, the bodhisattva is free from a lazy mind, meaning they do not say, "I am unable to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Śāriputra! If I possess these four qualities, a wise person, understanding them, would say: "He maintains a wrong livelihood through deceitful seeking, practicing unrighteous and defiled dharmas for the sake of heavy worldly wealth and profit; this is the first way of stealing the offerings of the faithful."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the bodhisattva’s mind is thus courageous, he is able to relinquish everything, including his head, eyes, hands, feet, body, and limbs; his sons, daughters, and retinue; all things most cherished by the heart and sources of supreme delight; and his houses, cities, and kingdoms.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Nārāyaṇaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"If one gives rise to this mind of renunciation toward wealth and treasures, one should know that no attachment to profit or gain will arise."

However, because equanimity has not yet arisen through wisdom, if one does not give rise to a mind of equanimity regarding what is acquired, one will likewise remain constantly attached to what is not acquired.

But if, in accordance with the wishes of those who beg, one gives rise to wisdom regarding what is acquired, then one will have no attachment even toward one's kin, no attachment to the most exalted honors, and no attachment to the enjoyment of precious treasures.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of relinquishment regarding wealth and profit, even down to the most minute fraction, it should be known that they harbor attachment.
Moreover, son of good family!

Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to such a thought: "I am even able to relinquish these parts of my own body for the sake of all sentient beings, let alone all external wealth and possessions!"

Furthermore, if toward sentient beings one is able to give whatever they require—meaning that if there comes a beggar who needs a hand, one gives a hand; who needs a foot, one gives a foot; who needs an eye, one gives an eye; even down to fat, marrow, blood, flesh, and other parts of the body—one gives each according to their need.
What, furthermore, are called external material resources? They are:

whatever is stored in treasuries or consists of livestock; gold, silver, precious gems, and exquisite ornaments; elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles; kingdoms, palaces, cities, towns, and villages; officials, commoners, servants, and laborers; and male and female attendants and their retinues.

If there are sentient beings who require anything whatsoever, I shall give to each such being whatever they may need, without giving rise to regret or vexation, nor with any sense of withdrawal or discouragement, and without hoping for karmic rewards or any other form of deceitful flattery.

Furthermore, this giving of mine is for the sake of conforming to all sentient beings, out of compassion for all sentient beings, for the benefit of all sentient beings, and for the purpose of gathering in all sentient beings.
Just as I embrace sentient beings, knowing that by understanding such dharmas one attains bodhi.
To speak briefly, son of good family!

It is like a medicinal tree—its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, bark, and seeds—which, whether taken as a whole or in part, does not give rise to discrimination toward those who take them.
Furthermore, when liberating sentient beings from the suffering and hardships of illness, one does not discriminate between their superior, middling, or inferior natures.

Son of good family! A bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this; you should know that they conceive of the body composed of the four great elements as a medicinal tree. For the sake of benefiting those sentient beings, if they need a hand, they give a hand; if they need a foot, they give a foot. Just as the aforementioned medicinal tree, they do not give rise to discrimination regarding those who take what they require.
The Compendium of Training for Bodhisattvas (Śikṣāsamuccaya), Fascicle Two;
The Compendium of Training for Bodhisattvas, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Minister of Silver Light and Grandee.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Subject Fahu (Dharmarakṣa), a Grand Master of the Propagation of the *Brahma-language*, who was conferred the purple robe, together with the Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Puming and Cijue. Chapter One: Training in Generosity, Part Three. As it is said in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"A bodhisattva should contemplate his own person regarding what he ought to do for all sentient beings."

That is to say, the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—possess various gateways, various functions, various associations, various implements, and various enjoyments, which accord with the conduct of sentient beings, whether in their entirety or in part.

Yet this body of mine, a collection of the four great elements, is likewise thus: it has various gateways, various functions, various dependencies, various implements, and various enjoyments, serving as a great support for all sentient beings.
"Observing in this manner, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, even if one's body experiences suffering, one does not give rise to weariness.
The Commentary says:
"One relinquishes the merit of enjoyments."
As the *Vajradhvaja Sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva bestows various kinds of gifts upon the immeasurable poor, destitute, and suffering beings of the ten directions.
Those who receive these gifts, who have faith in the Bodhisattva’s conduct, who hear the Bodhisattva’s voice, and who are moved by the Bodhisattva’s words, all gather there."

However, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they first make a vow; having heard the words of the bodhisattva’s aspiration, they joyfully relinquish everything without weariness, causing those who beg to have their hearts’ desires fulfilled, and as each person arrives, they resolve to offer repentance and gratitude.
As it is said in that verse:
"I should go to him to give; you know he cannot be found.
Those who have come from afar—have they not been exhausted?"

Thus, he prostrated at the feet of the beggars, paid his respects, apologized, and comforted them; he bathed their bodies to remove impurities and provided them with bedding and requisites, granting them everything they required—namely, either a mani-jewel chariot, complete with all the necessary appurtenances of a gentle and virtuous woman-treasure from Jambudvīpa;
or a golden chariot, complete with pure female attendants and all the requisite appurtenances of a woman-treasure;
or a vaidūrya chariot, with the most excellent and delightful singing and music, all as previously described.
In the crystal chariot, four precious women appeared on the four sides, holding exquisite ornaments; their physical forms were incomparable and perfectly complete, just as previously described.
As for the mani-jewel chariot, it was draped with various jeweled nets covering its top, drawn by white elephants and guided by elephant drivers adorned with immeasurable finery.

The mark of its precious wheel was commensurate with the chariot; furthermore, upon it were placed various exquisite jeweled lion-thrones, and even canopies of many jewels were set up to cover it entirely. Jeweled curtains were draped as adornments all around, while exquisite banners and streamers were planted in the four directions, and various kinds of incense were burned. Exquisite, solid fragrances were used for anointing, and various wonderful flowers were scattered, covering and adorning the whole.

Furthermore, above it, hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens are bound together by jeweled cords; those skillful charioteers drive with perfect harmony and without error. Even when blended with various powdered incenses, though one hears this fragrance, it is of the highest quality, causing the sexual conduct of both men and women to become harmonious and balanced.

Furthermore, as it is said there, for the sake of all sentient beings one should sacrifice one’s own body to be sustained by the service of the Buddhas, or relinquish the position of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), including kingdoms, cities, palaces, and all superior ornaments.

In accordance with those who beg, he relinquishes all his kinsmen—sons, daughters, wives, and concubines—as well as his houses, people, and even his entire or partial possessions, giving them all away in charity.

Regarding such flavors of food and drink, the Bodhisattva fully relinquishes various pure and exquisite delicacies—bitter, pungent, salty, and bland, as well as all kinds of superior tastes—which thoroughly nourish the great elements with softness, smoothness, and luster, harmonizing body and mind and causing him to dwell securely in physical strength.
Furthermore, wherever he goes, he heals all diseases and brings peace and happiness to all.

In this way, the Bodhisattva provides lamps, powdered incense, ointments, flower garlands, clothing, beds, mats, tables, dwellings, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick, giving them according to their needs.

Even unto various kinds of vast utensils—namely, immeasurable and innumerable bowls of gold, silver, and copper filled with precious jewels—he offers them to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, giving rise to inconceivable minds of reverence, faith, and understanding;
or he bestows them upon Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends, and others, giving rise to a mind of rare wonder;
or he bestows them upon all the noble assemblies of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and individuals who abide in the Buddha’s teaching, giving rise to a pure mind.
Or they give to their parents, various ācāryas, and other venerable teachers, giving rise to a mind of respect, intimacy, service, and the desire to seek learning;
or they give to those who are destitute and suffering, acting as unobstructed eyes for all sentient beings and giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.

To state it briefly: if a bodhisattva delights in giving elephant-vehicles, they are seven spans high and sixty feet tall, endowed with six tusks, and their faces are as pure as the color of a lotus. Their bodies are adorned with interlacing golden cords and various exquisite ornaments of diverse jewels; their trunks are raised and tossed in a wondrous golden hue, and those who behold them for a thousand *yojanas* never tire of looking.

If one gives a horse or carriage as a gift, the recipient will travel in the four directions with even and upright steps, their body attaining peace and security; they will command servants and attendants, and their food and drink will be fully provided, adorned like those in the heavens.
Whether giving hundreds of thousands [of coins] and so forth,

or giving to respected spiritual friends, parents, teachers, and elders, and even to all those in the world who are destitute, suffering, and worthy of receiving gifts— doing so with a mind free from stinginess and attachment, through great compassion and great relinquishment— this is the pure profound resolve of the bodhisattva, which gives rise to such immeasurable merit.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas may give couches and seats, such as noble royal thrones and lion beds with lapis lazuli footstools; draped everywhere with jeweled nets of golden cords, adorned with immeasurable soft cushions and countless ornaments, perfumed with various exquisite incenses, and featuring magnificent high banners of great maṇi jewels, all embellished by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of precious gems.
He hung down nets of various jewels, and from each mesh of the nets dangled clusters of precious bells; when stirred by a fragrant breeze, they produced harmonious and pleasing sounds.

Or he provided great thrones, towering so high that one had to look up to see them, arranged in countless rows covering the entire earth. Upon sitting upon these thrones, all the kings and great lords of sovereignty were consecrated, and they attained the wheel of unimpeded authority, commanding the subordinate petty kings to carry out their instructions accordingly.

In this manner, up until the point where the Bodhisattva gives a great precious canopy, which is likewise adorned with great jewels; its jeweled shaft, jeweled bells, jeweled cords, and jeweled nets hang down past the ears and neck, and furthermore, exquisite garlands are fashioned all around from *vaiḍūrya* gems, *maṇi* jewels, and the like.

Furthermore, within the nets, as in the case of the god Nandi, wondrous sounds resounded; pure, harmonious, and elegant, they were like hundreds of thousands of precious torches arrayed in a gathered treasury of jewels.
Furthermore, throughout the entire area, priceless incense was burned—sandalwood, aloeswood, and hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of various firm and exquisite fragrances.
There were also pure jewel canopies, like masses of Jāmbūnada gold light, likewise adorned and embellished with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of ornaments.
With such countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of parasols, he gave as alms with his own mind to all who came to beg, standing before them and bestowing them according to their needs.

Or they may give to the true Buddhas after their parinirvāṇa for the purpose of adorning their stūpas and temples; or they may give to Bodhisattvas seeking the Dharma, to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and to present-day Bodhisattvas and Dharma masters; or to parents, the Sangha, and the Three Jewels, up to all those worthy of receiving gifts who follow the teachings of the Buddha—they dedicate all such roots of goodness in the same manner as previously described.

Whenever there is an opportunity for virtue, one should always draw near to it, making this aspiration and dedicating these roots of goodness: "May I always find a stable dwelling within all worlds, and may I attain true mastery over the pure dharmas."

If all sentient beings, by means of these roots of goodness, have the retributions for their sins in the hells entirely extinguished, and the masses of suffering in the animal realm and the world of Yama are stilled;
and if they dedicate such roots of goodness—then I, regarding those roots of goodness, shall likewise do so.
When dwelling in a house, may all sentient beings extinguish the mass of all sufferings.
When encountering rescue, may all sentient beings be liberated from all afflictions.
When encountering a protector, may all sentient beings be free from all fears.
When walking away, may all sentient beings reach all stages.
When facing toward [the light], may all sentient beings attain ultimate patience (*atyanta-kṣānti*).
Upon seeing the radiance, may all sentient beings attain wisdom free from darkness.
When beholding a flash of lightning, may all sentient beings shatter the darkness of ignorance.
When obtaining a torch, may all sentient beings abide in ultimate purity.
When encountering a valiant hero, may all sentient beings penetrate the true principle of the inconceivable Dharma.
When encountering brave generals, may all sentient beings attain the aggregate of unimpeded wisdom.

Furthermore, may their speech be free from falsehood or artifice, and they dedicate with a deep and firm intention, dedicating with a one-pointed mind, a joyful mind, an exceedingly joyful mind, a supple mind, a mind of great loving-kindness, a mind of affectionate delight, a mind of gathering and sustaining, a mind of protection, and a mind of peace and security; thus do they dedicate.

Furthermore, by these roots of goodness of mine, may all sentient beings achieve the accomplishment of a pure destination; achieve the accomplishment of a pure birth; achieve the accomplishment of a body adorned with the marks of pure merit; achieve the accomplishment of being indestructible; achieve the accomplishment of vast generosity; achieve the accomplishment of a long-enduring mind; achieve the accomplishment of non-forgetfulness; achieve the accomplishment of penetrating wisdom and understanding; achieve the accomplishment of immeasurable awakening; and achieve the accomplishment of the complete perfection of all merits adorning both physical and mental actions.
Furthermore, they dedicate immeasurable roots of goodness to all sentient beings to make offerings to the Buddhas; through these offerings, they attain non-decline.

They repent of all their misdeeds before the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and draw near to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Having heard the Dharma he teaches, they become free from all doubt and confusion; having heard it, they accept and uphold it as taught, thereby attaining the continuity of perfect right practice.
By making offerings to the Tathāgata, one accomplishes all undertakings; through diligent mental cultivation, one is free from all evils and transgressions.
Furthermore, by planting these roots of goodness, I shall ultimately be liberated from all poverty and attain perfection in the seven noble riches.

Following the teachings of all Buddhas, they attain supreme roots of goodness; they are universally able to accomplish vast faith and understanding, entering the wisdom of omniscience. They act as unobstructed eyes for all worlds, their bodies adorned with the marks of excellence, and they purely embrace all merits.
Because they adorn their speech, they achieve the perfection of the faculties (*indriya*).
Through the accumulation of mental cultivation and analytical discernment bound to the Ten Powers (*daśabala*), there is nothing that is not perfected in their conduct, whether moving or resting.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas have attained the state of sublime bliss; may all sentient beings likewise attain it. As it is said in the *Ṣaṣṭipariṇāmanāvidhi*:

"May all sentient beings obtain the food of wisdom; may they thoroughly understand with their minds what should not be eaten, and being resolute, never engage in selective eating; may they take pleasure in not eating meat, and ultimately not give rise to craving or desire."
May all sentient beings, like clouds raining down, attain the single flavor of the Dharma.

May all sentient beings obtain all supreme flavors, becoming fully satiated by resting in the most sublime joy of the Dharma; may they contemplate all Buddha-dharmas with perfect skillfulness so as not to give rise to grasping at signs—namely, the indestructible vehicle, the supreme vehicle, the most excellent vehicle, the swift vehicle, the vehicle of great power, and so forth.
May all sentient beings joyfully behold all Buddhas and never tire of doing so.
May all sentient beings encounter spiritual friends without interruption.
May all sentient beings see no poisonous medicines.
May all sentient beings pacify and eliminate their afflictions.
May all sentient beings behold the pure solar orb.

Having dispelled the darkness, may all sentient beings, according to their inclinations, be taught such bodily marks that illuminate the nature of selfhood; may all sentient beings behold supreme radiance, seeing no harm but only joy, and being virtuous, kind, loving, hopeful, and filled with extreme delight, may they approach the presence of all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the fragrance of ethical discipline, never violating the precepts of the bodhisattva pāramitās.
May all sentient beings cultivate the practice of generosity, relinquishing everything without exception.
May all sentient beings cultivate patience and attain an unshakable mind.
May all sentient beings cultivate diligence and don the great armor of vigor.
May all sentient beings cultivate meditative concentration and, in the presence of the Buddhas of the present, attain samādhi.
May all sentient beings cultivate the bodhisattva dedication.
May all sentient beings cultivate all wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*) and be liberated from all unwholesome dharmas.
May all sentient beings obtain celestial provisions.
May all sentient beings give rise to the practice of great wisdom and obtain the requisites of the noble ones.
May all sentient beings perfume ordinary beings with the bodhicitta and attain the requisites of sublime bliss.
May all sentient beings be free from the suffering of conditioned existence within saṃsāra and obtain the requisites for peace and security.

May all sentient beings dwell in pure buddha-fields and realize the touch of all dharmas—namely, the dwelling in merit, the dwelling in correspondence, the vast and immovable dwelling, and the supreme dwelling of the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings attain proximity to the Buddha’s dwelling place.
May all sentient beings attain immeasurable light that illuminates all Buddha-dharmas.
May all sentient beings attain unimpeded light, capable of illuminating the entire dharma-realm with a single ray of light.
May all sentient beings attain a body of peace and happiness and obtain the body of a Tathāgata.
May all sentient beings be like the King of Medicine, ultimately able to discern the various medical treatises.
May all sentient beings be like medicinal trees, remaining free from harm.
May all sentient beings be like skilled physicians of the world, eliminating diseases and attaining omniscience to reach the state of ultimate peace and happiness.
May all sentient beings be like excellent medicines of the world, being ground, sifted, and compounded according to their profound resolve.
May all sentient beings be freed from all sickness and affliction.
May all sentient beings attain bodies of great power.
May all sentient beings attain the strength to shatter the Cakravāḍa mountains.

May all sentient beings attain the root of mindfulness as vast as the realm of empty space and as limitless as an infinite vessel, universally encompassing and upholding all that is spoken of in both the mundane and supramundane realms, so as to achieve non-forgetfulness.
May all sentient beings obtain a well-purified vessel and realize that the distinctions made by the Buddhas of the three periods of time are pure and free from firm attachment.
May all sentient beings, wherever they aspire to go, attain the practice of the Buddha-ground in all places.
May all sentient beings attain a mind free from malice toward all other sentient beings.

May all sentient beings, in a single moment of mind, take the entire realm of phenomena as their object and travel to all worlds without weariness or fatigue; through this lack of weariness, may they attain the wheel of the supernormal power of the body.
May all sentient beings attain the practice of sublime bliss and, like the bodhisattvas, proceed to the site of enlightenment.

May all sentient beings never feel any inclination to abandon their spiritual friends or their immeasurable roots of goodness; may they recognize kindness, repay it, and remain protected by them accordingly.
May all sentient beings share in the same benefit and happiness as their spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

May all sentient beings, with deep joy in their hearts, be purely embraced by them, dwelling in peace and happiness together with their spiritual friends while practicing meritorious deeds accordingly.
May all sentient beings share in the same great vow as the pure karmic retribution of the roots of goodness belonging to spiritual friends.
May all sentient beings abide in the practices of the Mahāyāna, forever remaining free from the darkness of sorrow, and attain inexhaustibility in omniscience.
May all sentient beings deeply cover their roots of goodness and be protected by all Tathāgatas.
May all sentient beings be shielded by wisdom and virtue, and be liberated from all worldly defilements and attachments.
May all sentient beings be fully endowed with pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) and remain free from distraction, attaining unbreakable conduct within the Buddha-dharma.
May all sentient beings spread the canopy of the Ten Powers (*daśabala*) to provide shelter and protection for all.
May all sentient beings attain the great profound mind and achieve ultimate awakening.
May all sentient beings sit upon the lion throne, attain the supernatural powers of a Buddha, and observe all worlds in this manner.
Furthermore, the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* states:
"The roots of goodness, the Dharma-knowledge, and the skillful means that I have accumulated are all provided as a basis and support for all sentient beings."
The Commentary states:
Regarding the relinquishing of past and future enjoyments, as the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"If one dedicates every moment of wholesome mind and mental factors toward bodhi, this is skillful means."

If future roots of goodness are certain to bring enlightenment to manifestation, one should dedicate all wholesome states of mind arising in the course of various activities toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Commentary states:
Thus, through the cultivation of these mental states and their concomitants, one perfects faith and understanding by relinquishing everything.

This "gathering" (saṃgraha) refers to the very root of liberation from the suffering of the three realms of existence.

Within this state, one naturally and spontaneously enjoys the immeasurable wealth and bliss of both the mundane and supramundane worlds—rewards that would otherwise have been summoned through various deeds performed over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
"I should use the hook of material wealth to pull all sentient beings out [of saṃsāra] and place them on the shore beyond.
