Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the *śramaṇa* of Purple Robes, Subject Rìchēng, along with others, including the Great Master Xuànfàn, Junior Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (*Hónglù Shǎoqīng*). Chapter Eight: On Purity (Part Two). The Treatise states:
Furthermore, one should know that the practice of repentance is now being explained.
As a verse in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says:
"The Honored Ones among two-legged beings, Who dwell throughout the ten directions, With hearts of compassion and pity,
Please bear witness to me."
Whatever vast karmic offenses I have previously committed, I now confess them all before the One Endowed with the Ten Powers.
When I did not yet know the Buddha, nor my parents, nor the distinction between good and evil, I created these transgressions.
Relying on my noble lineage and relying on my wealth and treasures, I committed this sin through youthful arrogance and indulgence.
With thoughts in my mind and words in my mouth, I committed many evil deeds, thinking they were invisible; thus I committed this sin.
My mind was shrouded by afflictions due to the darkness of ignorance; associating with evil friends,
I indulged in worldly pleasures and attachments, or dwelt in sorrow and anger, never satisfied with wealth—
I have committed these transgressions.
I have committed these transgressions through poverty and deceit, arising from stinginess and envy, and by failing to associate with the noble ones.
I have committed these transgressions because fear arose from desire, such that at times of going and staying, I could not attain self-mastery.
Driven by desire, hatred, and anger, my mind was agitated and disturbed; oppressed by hunger and thirst, I committed these transgressions.
Due to these three—food, drink, and clothing—the various fetters and burning afflictions arose, and I committed these transgressions.
The three types of misconduct of body, speech, and mind— possessing such characteristics as these— I confess them all. If,
toward the Buddha’s Dharma and the assembly of śrāvakas, I failed to give rise to respect, I confess it all.
Furthermore, if I failed to give rise to reverence for Pratyekabuddhas and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, I now repent it all.
Or if, toward virtuous Dharma-preachers, I did not rise to welcome them, I now repent it all.
Because I have slandered the True Dharma, I am perpetually devoid of wisdom; and because I failed to respect my parents— I repent for all these transgressions.
May the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time observe and protect me with their compassionate mindfulness.
With a mind moved by unconditional compassion, Pity me and accept my repentance.
Whatever sins I may have committed Throughout hundreds of kalpas, I constantly harbor a heart of anxiety and fear; Out of pity, I pray that you will eliminate them.
Furthermore, my mind is constantly timid and weak;
fearing these various faults, I have never experienced a thought of joy amidst the four modes of deportment.
The Buddhas, endowed with great compassion, remove all fears of the world.
Now I pray that you will take me into your care and liberate me from all fears.
Whatever sins I have previously committed, I confess them before the Tathāgata;
with the water of the Buddha’s great compassion, may he wash away the defilements of my afflictions.
Furthermore, if these sinful evils exist, I confess them all;
whatever sins have already been committed, I shall not dare to conceal them.
Whatever karmic deeds have not yet been committed, I shall never create them again.
"I confess all three types of physical karma, the four transgressions of speech, and the three poisons of mental karma.
The Commentary says:
Regarding the offenses committed by a bodhisattva, their relative lightness or gravity is explained according to their superiority.
Thus, the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"If one were to compare them to the root downfalls, which among these would be even more grave?"
The Buddha said:

"Upāli! Suppose a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna were to commit as many offenses of greed as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and compare them with a single offense of anger; when these two offenses are weighed against one another within the Bodhisattvayāna, the offense of anger alone is the more serious."
Why is this so? Upāli!
One who gives rise to anger abandons sentient beings, whereas one who gives rise to desire protects sentient beings.
Upāli! If one cherishes and protects sentient beings, one will not be afflicted by defilements, nor will there be any fear of calamities or misfortunes in the presence of bodhisattvas.
Therefore, Upāli!... [and so forth].
If there are those who commit offenses of greed, they are all called "guiltless.
What is the meaning of this?
Because those who cherish and protect sentient beings become increasingly superior as previously described, I say that such compassion exists within their profound mind.
The Buddha said: "Upāli!

If a bodhisattva lacks skillful means, they will fear committing the offense of greed; however, if a bodhisattva possesses such skillful means, they will dread committing the offense of anger rather than dreading the commission of that greed."
Why is this? One who possesses skillful means is endowed with both compassion and wisdom and does not abandon sentient beings.
If one were to abandon sentient beings, possessing either only wisdom that realizes suffering and emptiness, or only compassion, they would be diminished by the power of afflictions before long.
As stated in the *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra*:
"O son of good family!
It is like a person who, though bound at the five points by a noose, is able to transcend his bonds through the King of Mantras regarding the dharma he seeks."
By the power of a single mantra-vidyā, one is able to sever all fettering dharmas. Good son!

It is likewise with this bodhisattva’s skillful means in experiencing the pleasures of the five desires; yet he does not disturb his correct practice in what he undertakes. That is to say, if by the power of a single wisdom he universally purifies all desires and pleasures through the mind of omniscience, he shall be born in the Brahma world.
The Commentary says:
What is the meaning of *dveṣa* (hatred)?

It refers to its nature as a great transgression; because it does not give rise to the skillful means of compassion through extensive discernment, one who acts with malice and anger brings no benefit.
What is meant by "fault"?
To tolerate them is to nourish afflictions and diminish compassion; this constitutes a fault.
How to sever these roots shall be seen later.
If a bodhisattva loses the mind of compassion toward sentient beings, then their continuous engagement in the vast benefit of sentient beings will diminish and be lost.
Thus, the "Chapter on the Noble Truths" states:

"One should know that just as a father feels compassion upon seeing his son, if one abandons the compassionate concern for the worldly benefit and happiness [of others], one should also be known as far removed from those who possess wisdom."
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva encourages the practice of desire, they diminish and lose their beneficial purpose; therefore, it is said that the fault of greed results in two kinds of difficulties.
One who is attached to desire is like a blind person who harms his parents; through inferior desires, they give rise to suffering and affliction, and suffer a decline from the celestial realms.
Furthermore, those who are attached to desire violate the prohibitive precepts and distance themselves from the sphere of human beings.
Therefore, to seek one's own happiness while disregarding the suffering of others is not a true view; one should regard the suffering and affliction of others as one's own.
"However, if one does not practice for oneself, two kinds of faults arise.
As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"The Buddha told Ānanda:"

"Suppose there were a person whose body, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, was ablaze with fire, becoming a single mass of blazing flames; and suppose another person came and spoke these words to them:
'I urge you to enjoy the five desires together with me, through song, dance, and play.'"
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "What do you think?
Would this person encourage one to engage in the five desires, singing, dancing, and sporting with this body?"
Ānanda replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This person, through the power of discrimination, gives rise to perverse thoughts regarding song, dance, and amorous play; he urges one to engage this body in the shared enjoyment of the five desires, song, dance, and amorous play."
The Tathāgata is not like this.
In the past, while practicing the conduct for awakening, he saw the suffering of sentient beings in the three evil realms as well as those who were impoverished, and his heart felt no joy.
The Commentary says:

In this world, there are children who do not see the suffering their parents endure in carrying and bearing them; they fail to recognize this great kindness and seek only their own pleasure. Whether toward their own kin or strangers, [the parents] feel compassion and conceal [their hardships].

O guardians of the banner of the sublime Dharma, do not engage in perverse desire; for this may either benefit or harm sentient beings. Specifically, if one is entangled in and relishes such desire, it constitutes a fault;
however, by possessing the pure conduct of brahmacarya, one brings about benefit.

If a bhikṣu enters this sphere of practice, he should serve them as he would his own mother or sister; he should not treat others as if they were fellow practitioners of the holy life, and he must resolutely distance himself from those who seek to bring sentient beings to maturity through such means.
As the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"Whether it be at the proper time or not, one may again set aside what one is doing; or, seeing that there is superior benefit for sentient beings, one likewise abides in this training rule."
Furthermore, the *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra* states:
"In the past, the brahmin Prabhāsa maintained the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) for forty-two thousand years. Having walked seven paces, he gave rise to compassion, thinking:
'Even if they were to violate the prohibitions and undergo the sufferings of hell, I must not abandon them and allow them to pass away.'"
"Good son! At that moment, the brahmin Jyotirasa took her right hand and spoke these words:
'Sister, arise!'"
"Whatever you desire. To speak briefly, noble son:

having given rise to great compassion within such profound and subtle desires, you shall undergo the sufferings of saṃsāra for ten thousand kalpas, after which you will once again practice the holy life.
"O son of good family!
It is by means of the bodhisattva’s skillful means that one is born in the Brahma world.
That sutra further states:

"If there is a bodhisattva who, for the sake of a single sentient being, generates roots of goodness, yet because of their physical form falls into sin and undergoes the torment and boiling of hellish suffering for hundreds of thousands of kalpas."

"Bhagavān! Although those bodhisattvas may give rise to such offenses, they will not experience the sufferings of hell, because they have not abandoned these roots of goodness even with respect to a single sentient being."
That sutra further states:

"Good son! This bodhisattva skilled in means may commit an extremely grave offense: namely, if at some time he encounters an evil friend who exhorts him to realize nirvana within these very aggregates. However, having done so, he will no longer be capable of donning this armor for the sake of future lives; how then could he transform and deliver all sentient beings?"
Therefore, I do not give rise to such thoughts, but revolve like that wheel to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Furthermore, even if such offenses were to exist, by practicing according to the Dharma, one remains free from fault.

"Good son! If a renunciant bodhisattva commits any transgression created by conceptual discrimination—even one of the four grave offenses—and that bodhisattva possesses skillful means, repenting immediately upon its occurrence, it is declared to be without fault."
As clarified in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:
"Committing the ultimate immediate transgression refers to causing a human being to die;
in the Vinaya of the Śrāvakas, this is termed a root offense."
Furthermore, if one feels compassion when skinning deer and the like, it is said to be without fault.
If even a bodhisattva who gives rise to greed is still reborn in the happy realms, then one should not harbor anger toward them.

As it is said, a bodhisattva skilled in means delights in engaging with the darkness of desire; he takes great pleasure in cultivating himself amidst the exquisite forms of women and repeatedly makes the vow to be reborn among them.
Having become weary of that greedy mind and cast off the female body, she attained the marks of a man and achieved a great body.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see such merit as this?"
Although other sentient beings may likewise give rise to such intense greed, they still escape the vessel of suffering and are born in the realms of humans or devas.
Even so, O Great Being, King of Medicine!
"How can a bodhisattva give rise to anger?
For if afflictions arise, how could one possibly bestow various sublime pleasures and the like?
The Treatise says:
If one acts for the sake of such fame, yet employs such skillful means for the benefit of other sentient beings, even if greed should arise, it is said to be without fault.
This is the benefit produced by a bodhisattva through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), who does not abandon sentient beings; this is explained at length as stated therein.
However, it is not that one has attained the sublime practice of the six perfections;
rather, it is because one is perfectly attuned to this investigation that anger and the like find no place.
Furthermore, the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra! There are two great transgressions for a bodhisattva."
What are these two?
They are the mind accompanied by hatred and the mind accompanied by delusion.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
One should first, with sincere resolve, repent of the ten evil deeds and the five kinds of transgressions; these too must be confessed.
This refers to cases where one’s hands act while the eyes look on, making it difficult for the mind to restrain itself, or when one commits two of these [offenses] against a single sentient being.
Śāriputra! Furthermore, it is said that there are five grave ānantarya offenses, namely those committed in their entirety.

This bodhisattva may at times engage in unrighteous conduct with the wives of others, take life with his own hands, or steal property from a Buddha stūpa or the property of the Saṅgha from the four quarters.
At that time, as if having committed those offenses, the bodhisattva should perform a single confession before the thirty-five Tathāgatas throughout the day and night, saying:
“I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.”
“Namo Śākyamuni Buddha. Namo Vajrapramardana Buddha. Namo Ratnārcis Buddha.”

"Thus, before the eyes of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout all worlds, may the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, observe and protect me with their compassionate mindfulness. Whatever karmic obstacles and transgressions I have committed—whether in this life, in other lives, or throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death—including those committed by myself, incited in others, or rejoiced in seeing others commit; whether it be stealing the property of a stūpa or the property of the Saṅgha from the four quarters; or the five deeds of immediate retribution and the ten unwholesome paths of action—whether committed by myself, incited in others, or rejoiced in seeing others commit."

Due to these karmic obstructions and the violation of their precepts, they should fall into hell, or into the realms of animals or the domain of Yama; or else they would be born in border regions as mlecchas, or be reborn among the long-lived gods.
Even if one should obtain human birth, may one not have impaired faculties, be deeply attached to false views, or be separated from the appearance of a Buddha in the world.

Regarding all such karmic obstructions, the Buddha—by means of his true wisdom, true eye, true realization, and true discernment—knows them all and sees them all; I now repent of them all and dare not conceal them.
If I have committed any offenses such as violating the prohibitive precepts, may the Buddha, the World-Honored One, observe me with compassion.

Whether in this life, in future lives, or throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death—even down to the realm of animals—whatever roots of goodness I have cultivated, such as giving even a single morsel of food or observing a single pure precept, practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), delivering sentient beings, generating the bodhicitta, or attaining unsurpassed wisdom—all these roots of goodness, [I dedicate].

Having thus weighed and considered it, there is nothing that is not dedicated toward the fruit of the most supreme and most excellent *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; I now likewise dedicate [it] in the same manner as all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have dedicated theirs.
...and so on, until the verse says:
"I confess all transgressions, rejoice in all merits,
and entreat all Buddhas to proclaim the unsurpassed path."
"To those of the past and the future, and to the Honored One among Men dwelling in the present—
those oceans of boundless merit— I pay homage with my whole being. "Śāriputra!..."
When this bodhisattva has performed this practice before the thirty-five Tathāgatas, those Tathāgatas, through their knowledge of his mental engagement (*manasikāra*), will purify his transgressions.
Because his transgressions are purified, these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, shall appear before him.
Thus, through this liberation, he manifests various marks and signs to benefit sentient beings.

Consequently, foolish ordinary worldlings give rise to doubts regarding this transformative deliverance; even the entire assembly of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is unable to cause that place of transgression to become a ground of purity.

If there is a bodhisattva who constantly upholds and recollects the names of these Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and practices the turning of the True Dharma three times during the day and night, they shall emerge from those transgressions and attain samādhi; this is called the practice of repentance and remediation.
The Commentary says:
By reading and reciting profound sūtras, one attains the extinction of those offenses.
As it is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, yet is treated with contempt by others. Why is this so?
The sinful karma created by this person in previous lives, which would otherwise cause them to fall into the evil realms, is instead extinguished because they have seen these dharmas;
and due to being slighted and disparaged by people in the present life, they shall attain the Bodhi of the Buddhas and other such qualities.
The Commentary states:
Because one who has faith and understanding in emptiness attains purification from sins and evils.
The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* says:
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! There are ten unwholesome paths of action; these constitute great transgressions.”
The most extreme form of killing refers to killing one's father or severing the life of a pratyekabuddha.
The most extreme form of taking what is not given refers to deceitfully seizing the property of the Triple Gem.
The most extreme form of sexual misconduct is to commit an act of defilement against one’s mother or an Arhatī bhikṣuṇī.
The most extreme form of false speech is to declare, "I am the Tathāgata.
The most extreme form of divisive speech is to utter words that cause schism within the Noble Saṃgha.
The most extreme form of harsh speech is the reviling and disparaging of the noble ones and sages.
The most extreme form of frivolous speech is the skillful construction of empty embellishments that disrupt the desire for the true Dharma.
The most extreme form of greed is the arising of a mind intent on seizing and plundering the wealth and benefits of the Right Path.
The most extreme form of hatred is the absence of compassion toward those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution.
The most extreme form of wrong view is the reckless arising of perverse attachments and profoundly treacherous, evil views.

Kāśyapa! If there is a single sentient being who is fully possessed of such great offenses of the ten unwholesome paths of action, the Tathāgata, for this reason, proclaims the essential points of the Dharma in order to cause them to realize and enter into the understanding that there is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-principle, no agent, and no experiencer; that these are merely conditioned activities, karmic constructions, and illusory transformations.

However, the nature of all phenomena is itself the nature of afflictions; by entering into and understanding that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is luminous, and by having faith and understanding that all phenomena are variously pure, I do not say that there are sentient beings who fall into the evil destinies.
Furthermore, the *Sutra on Purifying All Karmic Obstructions* states: "Moreover, Mañjuśrī!

If a bodhisattva perceives what is not the Vinaya as being the Vinaya, they will see transgressions and non-transgressions; if they perceive the realm of saṃsāra as the realm of nirvāṇa, they will see all afflictions as being dependently originated. It should be known that such a person attains purification from karmic obstructions."
Furthermore, the *Tattvasamādhi-rāja-tantra* explains the practice of remediation as follows:

"If one closes the eyes and visualizes all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and having recited the hundred-syllable mantra eight thousand times, opens the eyes and beholds the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others clearly, one shall be freed from those transgressions."

"Alternatively, one may circumambulate a stūpa while reciting eight thousand times the sūtras concerning the stūpa or its image; whichever appears before one, it shall be explained in detail according to the ritual.
Furthermore, the *Cundādhāraṇī Sūtra* states:
"If, after performing the recitation, one even sees such signs in a dream, those transgressions will be extinguished."
If, in a dream, a celestial maiden offers one milk-rice porridge, one shall be freed from those transgressions;
or if one sees the sun and moon rising in the midst of the sky, or fierce fire, water buffaloes, and black men fleeing in terror.

Furthermore, if one dreams of a community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, or milkwood trees, white elephants and white oxen, mountain peaks and boats, or being in a great hall or upon a lion throne while hearing the sublime Dharma, one should know that these are all signs of the extinction of transgressions.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Image of the Tathāgata" explains the practice of counteraction as follows:

"Suppose there is a person whose body is smeared with impurities, foul-smelling and loathsome; if one washes it with water and applies sublime fragrant unguents, that foul odor will immediately depart."

Even one who has committed the five crimes of immediate retribution and fully engaged in the ten unwholesome paths of action may, if they attain faith and understanding and fashion an image of the Tathāgata, be liberated from those sins.
"Because they are free from fault, their wisdom is preeminent and they possess the bodhicitta.
Because of this preeminence, they may either leave the household life and firmly uphold the pure precepts.
As the *Kusuma-rāśi-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
"At that time, the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrīḍita shall abide in the world for a hundred thousand years, bestowing all manner of sublime joys.

After that Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, stūpas for his relics shall be erected. If a person, with the bodhicitta, offers even a single flower to that Tathāgata—whether by joining their palms and reciting his name, sprinkling water for purification, or offering a single garland, ointment, flower, or lamp—even if they merely take a single step toward him, transcending all words and exclaiming 'Namo Buddha,' one should not harbor any doubt regarding that Tathāgata Siṃhavikrīḍita; it is impossible that such a person would fall back into the evil realms for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas."
Furthermore, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabharāja-sūtra* states:

"If one upholds the five precepts, the ten precepts, the four grave bodhisattva precepts, the two hundred and fifty precepts of an ordained bhikṣu, or the five hundred precepts of a bhikṣuṇī, and should happen to violate any of those received precepts and fear falling into the evil realms—if such a person single-mindedly recollects the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabharāja and makes offerings to him accordingly, that person will certainly not fall into the evil destinies."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"If I were to extol all the merits of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharāja, this would be the profound realm of all Buddhas; do you have no doubts and give rise to true faith?"
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, I harbor no doubt or uncertainty."
Why is this? Because there is no virtuous conduct accumulated within the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas that is not pure.
World-Honored One!

These wheels of the sun and moon, though situated at the highest and most remote distances and endowed with great majestic radiance, could be made to fall to the earth; even Sumeru, the king of mountains, could be shaken; yet the words of these Buddhas shall never be otherwise.
“World-Honored One!
Yet there are sentient beings who lack the faculty of faith; upon hearing of the profound realm of the Buddhas, they utter these words:
‘How is it that by merely recollecting the name of a single Tathāgata, one obtains such vast merit and benefits?’”
"Because of this lack of faith, they will give rise to slander, and for a long night they will fall away from benefit and happiness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is impossible that anyone who hears the name of that Buddha should fall into the evil destinies."
Ānanda! This is the profound realm of all Buddhas, difficult to believe and understand. Ānanda!

You who have faith and understanding should know that all of this is established by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata; it is not [the domain] of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have not yet ascended to the stages, with the sole exception of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas bound to only one more birth.
Therefore, that same sutra further states:

"If other sons or daughters of good family with pure faith—whether laymen (*upāsaka*) or laywomen (*upāsikā*)—who have fully observed the eightfold fast for one or three years and, by means of these roots of goodness, vow to be reborn before the Tathāgata Amitāyus in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, should hear the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharāja, then at the time of their death, the eight great bodhisattvas will all manifest through their supernormal powers to show them the right path."
Furthermore, there are various intermediate colors, rare in the world, and lotus flowers made of many jewels arise spontaneously, or they may even grow in the heavens.
Having planted roots of goodness in such places of birth, those [roots] are inexhaustible, and one likewise has no fear of falling into the evil realms.
After passing away from that celestial realm, he was reborn in the human world as a Cakravartin king who ruled over the four great continents.
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* (The Compendium of Bodhisattva Training), Fascicle Eleven; *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Twelve.

Chapter Eight: On Purity, Part Three. “Together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of koṭis of beings, they abide in the ten paths of wholesome action. Subsequently, they are reborn among the great lineages of kṣatriyas, brahmins, and householders, where their wealth and possessions are abundant, their treasuries are overflowing, and they are fully endowed with physical beauty and a retinue of kin.”
That sutra further states:
"If there are women who hear the name of this Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabharāja and uphold it, they shall later transform their female bodies."
Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-guṇavyūha-sūtra* states: "Mañjuśrī said:
'I also pay homage to these bodhisattvas: the Bodhisattva Varapradāna, the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu, the Bodhisattva Cittavaraṇa, and the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya.'"
"If there be any woman who upholds the names of these four bodhisattvas, she shall transform her female body and never again receive it.
The Commentary says:
The practice of remediation has been briefly explained as before; the power of restraint shall now be discussed.
As the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states:

"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abstains from taking life, they bestow upon all sentient beings freedom from sorrow and fear, as well as freedom from grief, affliction, terror, and the bristling of hair."

By the fruit and retribution of these roots of goodness, all karmic obstructions of body, speech, and mind created through killing—whether committed by oneself, incited in others, or rejoiced in by others—which caused one to sink into the ocean of birth and death while riding the wheel of the five destinies throughout the beginningless past—all such things shall be utterly destroyed and extinguished, such that no retribution for them shall ever be experienced.
In this very life, one attains a long lifespan and becomes beloved by both devas and humans. Furthermore, son of good family, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for as long as life lasts,

abstains from taking what is not given, this is equivalent to bestowing upon all sentient beings freedom from sorrow, fear, and feverish affliction, ensuring they are not disturbed, and practicing contentment with one's own wealth and profit, never hoping to acquire gain through unrighteous means.

"By means of these roots of goodness, and specifically because of this distancing from taking what is not given, all karmic obstructions shall be utterly destroyed without remainder, and their retribution shall not be experienced.
To speak briefly, these ten unwholesome paths of action can likewise destroy the wholesome virtues one has cultivated oneself.
As the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* states:

"Regarding the hearing that hearing [insults] extinguishes transgressions: it is said that if one remains established in patient endurance when encountering the false, angry abuse and slander of the foolish and ignorant, all previously committed karmic offenses as well as the anger directed toward Bodhisattvas will be completely exhausted."
The commentary states:
The power of restraint has already been explained as before; the power of reliance shall now be explained.
Therefore, it is said in the explanation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
If one can take refuge in the Buddha, one will not fall into the evil realms; casting off this human body, one will attain birth in the celestial realms.
The same applies to the Dharma and the Saṅgha as stated above.
Furthermore, the *Maitreya-vimokṣa-sūtra* states:

"Regarding the Bodhisattva who purifies all karmic offenses: even if unwholesome dharmas were as pervasive as the great earth, when the kalpa-ending fire arises, there is nothing that would not be consumed by it."

It is even like a person who takes one *liang* of *haṭaka* juice and drops it upon a thousand *liang* of iron, thereby turning it into gold; it is not that the abundant iron can cause the small amount of juice to instead turn back into iron.

The generation of this mind of omniscience is likewise so: by dedicating a single root of goodness through the wisdom of dedication, one is able to encompass all karmic and afflictive hindrances to form the wisdom of all phenomena; thus, no karmic or afflictive hindrance can cause the mind of omniscience to become afflicted.
"Good son! Furthermore, if someone were to take a single lamp and enter to illuminate a dark room, it would immediately destroy the darkness of a thousand years of remote antiquity.

The generation of this mind of omniscience is also like this: when it enters the heart of even a single sentient being—a dark room of ignorance—it can simultaneously destroy the barriers of karma and afflictions from hundreds of thousands of unspeakable kalpas of remote antiquity, giving rise to the radiance of wisdom."
"Good son! Just as a great dragon king, wearing a crown of the sovereign wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel upon his head, has no fear of enemies or adversaries;
so too is this bodhicitta. If a bodhisattva is endowed with a heart of great compassion, he has no fear of the evil realms, enemies, or adversaries."
The *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the Great Vehicle commits an offense during the first part of the day, yet does not abandon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) during the middle part of the day, such a bodhisattva attains the perfection of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*)."

If, at the time of the midday portion, one commits an offense through transgression, yet at the time of the afternoon portion does not abandon the practice of the mind of omniscience, then the bodhisattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline is likewise complete.
"I should further explain this sequence. The Buddha said, "Upāli!"

If a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna should at some time relinquish the precepts and training rules, one must not give rise to regret regarding that bodhisattva, nor follow along with such a lapse.
However, if one were to speak of this to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, it would constitute the offense of disparaging the Dharma.
"However, those who are śrāvakas claim that they have lost the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha);
it should be understood in this way," and so on, as explained at length.
Chapter Nine: On Forbearance (Kṣānti). The Treatise says:

This non-abandonment unfolds through many doors; yet by guarding it well, one causes the precepts to flourish. In this way, one is freed from the bonds of karmic obstructions and breaks the fetters of afflictions, even unto the point where hearing, patience, and lack of patience, as well as decline, loss, diligence, and indolence, all coexist.
Alternatively, some do not hear or know the methods for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because they lack these methods for purifying the afflictions (*kleśa*), they become weary and desist.
They merely hear that one should practice by abandoning distracted conduct, meaning that one should diligently recite and study while relying on mountain forests.

That practitioner may briefly still the distractions, yet his mind lacks meditative concentration (*samādhi*); even this state of stillness, being subsumed under concentration, yields no fruit whatsoever, let alone any other purification of the afflictions. Even if he were to cultivate this contemplation, he would lose even a small measure of virtue, up to and including the purification of the afflictions.
The *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* states:

"It is said that there are three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*): namely, the patience of abiding in suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsanākṣānti*), the patience of discerning the Dharma (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), and the patience of enduring injury from enemies (*paropakramakṣānti*)."
"One who abides in the patience toward suffering attains the ultimate practice that counteracts the fear of suffering and achieves the removal of attachment to the love of pleasure.
As for the other two types of affliction, how are they explained?
This refers to ill will, indolence, and so forth.
The *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* states:
"Those who are attached to pleasure do not abandon suffering."
Furthermore, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"If one harbors sorrow, grief, suffering, or affliction within, one should abide in the patience that subdues through skillful means.
The *Paramārthaviniścaya-paripṛcchā Sūtra* says:
"Furthermore, householder!

A bodhisattva living at home should distance himself from improper harm and not become attached to the eight worldly dharmas. When he acquires a wife and children, or abundant enjoyments such as wealth and grain, he should not be arrogant or complacent; even when faced with decline and misfortune, he should not become dejected or distressed."

One should observe all conditioned phenomena as being created by illusion; one should extinguish the retribution for offenses that arise from arrogance, realizing that these parents, wives, children, slaves, servants, relatives, and associates are not oneself, and that one is not they either.
As a verse says: "If there is something accumulated, from what could sorrow and affliction arise?
Or if there is nothing accumulated, from what could sorrow and affliction arise?"
"Those who are thus assembled are for the sake of being managed.

Because of delusion, anger, vexation, fainting, and exhaustion, one may either cling to ferocity and give rise to great transgressions, or, through deluded confusion and regret, meet with a premature death in an instant; one should distance oneself from such useless hardships.
The Treatise says:
What is the relinquishing of this sorrow and affliction?
It refers to one who gives rise to a mind that is light and supple.
As the *Paramapraśna-sūtra* states:
"Through this seclusion, the mind becomes as supple as tūla-cotton.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:

"One should, like the maiden King Jyotiṣprabha, give rise to such a mind to extinguish all afflictions; with an invincible mind, one should shatter all anger and resentment; and with an unshakable mind, one should not fall back from the profound realm of the mind within the ocean of sentient beings."
The Commentary says:
For one who cultivates this, it is not considered difficult.
As it is, even a fool may still do so.

As for those such as porters, farmers, and hunters, who practice with diligent austerity, undertake menial tasks, and hope for subtle fruits—remaining free from regret or affliction even amidst dust, filth, and impurity—how much more so should these various sublime and joyful practices be embraced by Bodhisattvas, who delight in the most excellent deeds to attain the unsurpassed fruit?

Furthermore, even when those who are base and lowly encounter minor harms that are difficult for the body to endure, they do not abandon their resolve; rather, they focus their minds with fortitude and accept the situation as if competing for victory or defeat.

How much more so for these beings who, for a long time, undergo various sufferings and afflictions without any benefit; why then would they not aspire to acquire even a small portion of the wealth of wholesome dharmas?
Punished by the hells and harmed by worldly thieves, guarded and relentlessly suppressed by the wardens, they encounter extreme agony wherever they go; let them not become one's enemies.

Throughout the vast expanse of time, they have been free from all fetters; enduring toil and suffering, they have utterly destroyed the thieves of affliction without remainder. Clad in the supreme armor within the three realms of existence, they wield weapons to defeat the demonic adversaries and untie the bonds of sentient beings; through prior cultivation, they achieve accomplishment with only slight hardship.

Regarding all sentient beings, one cultivates the perception of pleasure within suffering; that is, when various sufferings arise, one cultivates the perception of pleasure according to their respective locations. One who abides in this perception of pleasure is able to accomplish this fruit and attain samādhi, which is called "Transcending the Pleasure of All Dharmas."
As stated in the *Pitṛputrasamāgama-sūtra*:
"The Buddha said:
'There is a samādhi called "Surpassing the Joy of All Dharmas. "
If a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they experience such pleasure and the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure amidst all objective conditions.

They do not obtain the perception of pleasure from a single cause or condition according to its location; for example, it is as if a person, due to certain causes and conditions, has their hands, feet, ears, or nose severed, yet after the ears and nose are cut off, they obtain the perception of pleasure at those very locations, or even when struck by whips and staves, they perceive it as pleasure, or when imprisoned and subjected to flogging.

That is to say, those who make robes, those who light ghee lamps, those who light oil lamps, and those who crush sugarcane juice for syrup, each dwell in their respective places with the perception of pleasure.

Those who fashion the faces of owls, those who fashion the faces of lions, those who roll out parched grain, and even those who manufacture gold coins, prepare food and drink, or provide elephants and wine, all regard these tasks as if they were music.
Even when their eyes are gouged out, their life-faculties destroyed, or subjected to various harms such as having their heads severed,
they perceive these things as pleasant rather than painful. Why is this so?
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has cultivated such power of aspiration throughout the long night: "May I bring those who are fugitives close to sublime happiness;
and may I also bring those who are offenders close to sublime happiness at all times and in all places by serving, honoring, respecting, and making offerings to them."

If one encounters harsh words, derision, beating, or being cut by blades and weapons, even to the point of having one's life-force destroyed, may all such experiences become the bliss of awakening, leading to the realization of the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Endowed with such mental attention, such activities, and such power of aspiration, and further endowed with the cultivation of intimacy through the knowledge of the inclinations and thoughts of all sentient beings, one performs much practice regarding those karmic results and thereby attains the *samādhi* of transcending all dharmas and joy.

When a bodhisattva attains the samādhi of the bliss of all dharmas, they thereby achieve great immovability and destroy all demonic activities. Through these skillful means, they perfect all forms of relinquishment, accomplish all difficult ascetic practices, fortify all patience, exert all diligence, and assist in the cultivation of all meditative concentrations and wisdom; for this reason, they are ever joyful.
As stated in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"Always joyfully revere [the Dharma] and always abide in right view.
Furthermore, the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"What is joy? It is the pure faith and delight that arises from mindful recollection of the Dharma; it gives rise to a heart of exultation and does not produce indolence; it is free from all feverish afflictions and does not seek the pleasures of the five desires; it never departs from the joy of all dharmas."

By means of the mind, one establishes physical joy and the joy of awakening; one gives rise to a sense of delight and pleasure in the marks and signs that adorn the body of a Tathāgata; one seeks skillful means, listens to the Dharma without weariness, and practices in accordance with the true Dharma.
From the Dharma, they give rise to joy, delight, pleasure, and pure faith; yet, regarding sentient beings, their awakening and understanding are unimpeded.

With the most supreme desire and diligence, they seek the Buddha-dharma and do not abandon the aspiration for the Dharma; with vast faith and resolve, they demonstrate the vehicle of liberation through the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas.
One should give rise to the supreme mind and eliminate the mind of stinginess.
When first giving, whether one has already given, is about to give, or is currently giving, one should practice giving with joy and with the three spheres being pure.

They are also constantly pure in their sublime ethical discipline (*śīla*); by upholding pure precepts, they gather those who have violated the prohibitions, and they always transcend the terrors of the evil realms, turning toward the Buddha’s prohibitory precepts with firmness and without impairment.

Even if others come with malice to revile and insult them, they do not respond with anger in their speech or mind, but endure it with equanimity; they transform themselves through reverence so as to be free from arrogance, their countenance always mild and respectful, far removed from frowning, and they first employ loving speech that is neither sycophantic nor deceitful.

With a pure mind, one is neither crooked nor coarse; even upon seeing those superior to oneself, one does not suppress them with guile. One does not spy for faults or proclaim the failings of others, but cultivates the dharma of harmony and respect. Toward the assembly of bodhisattvas, one respects them as if they were the messengers of the Buddha; toward all the Buddhas' teachings, one holds them dear even at the cost of one's own body and life.
One regards all teachers and elders as one's own parents; protects all sentient beings as if they were an only child; honors one’s preceptors and ācāryas with the thought that they are Buddhas;

treats all those who practice correctly as supreme leaders; regards the pāramitās as one’s own hands and feet; views the Dharma-preachers as various exquisite jewels; and considers all instructions as being like the five sensual pleasures.

Regarding the practice of contentment, it is like being free from illness and affliction; seeking the sublime Dharma is like longing for a wondrous medicine; and confessing one's faults is like encountering a skilled physician.
Thus, by restraining the sensory faculties so that they are free from indolence, this is called "joy."
The Commentary states:
Regarding this statement on "the bodhisattva’s training in adornment," it is as taught in the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*:

"If one delights in the realms of hell and animals, maintaining constant mindfulness and concentration within the hellish destinies, then even while dwelling in the city of hell, one attains a state like that of a traveler at a temporary lodging."
Furthermore, those who delight in hell develop attachment, stinginess, and envy toward the hell realms, causing the fires of hell to blaze even more fiercely.
The Commentary states:
Because it speaks of abiding in the patience of suffering, the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā Sūtra* says:
“There are three kinds of patience.
The Buddha said: ‘Sāgaramati!’”

Within this precious jewel of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has generated, there may arise those who violate his pure precepts through non-human beings—namely, various māras, their followers, the celestial queen of māras, or those possessed by the power of māra—who cause messengers of māra to come and forcibly inflict harm, shaking, agitating, threatening, striking, and hurling him about.

At that time, one should give rise to a deep and firm resolve for this great enlightenment so that it remains indestructible; likewise, one should not allow the compassion and diligence that liberate all sentient beings to be destroyed; nor should one allow the lineage of the Three Jewels to be severed, ensuring its continued prosperity; nor should one allow the accumulation of roots of goodness in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas to be destroyed; nor should one allow the cultivation of meritorious deeds to achieve the primary and secondary marks to be destroyed; nor should one allow the courageous diligence that purifies Buddha-fields to be destroyed; nor should one allow the seeking of all dharmas without sparing body or life to be destroyed; nor should one allow the deliverance of all sentient beings without attachment to one’s own pleasure to be destroyed.
Within this, the profound mind possesses such an intention:
even if one is detested and despised by all sentient beings, or encounters anger, revilement, slander, abuse, and various forms of physical assault, one is able to endure them all.

As for all sentient beings who come to oppress, afflict, crush, and suppress one with malicious intent, one is able to endure them all without weariness, without slackening, without retreating, and without sinking; rather, one manifests the power of courageous diligence, endures toil and hardship, and gives rise to a mind of embracing care.

Furthermore, if someone should approach with an evil mind—whether through anger or abuse, jealousy, malice, or harassment, or through wrathful beating and throwing—one does not retaliate at all against such a mind.

Even if there were someone in the worlds of the ten directions who, brandishing various weapons, pursued one from behind, and wherever that person went—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—if they encountered even a single individual who had resolved upon Bodhicitta and cultivated the mind of generosity up to the cultivation of the mind of wisdom, and if I were to hear them give rise to even a single thought of a wholesome root, I would immediately go to that place. Even if my body were cut and severed limb by limb until each fragment was the size of a jujube leaf, I would endure all such things.

Furthermore, if all sentient beings in the world were to give rise to anger, skillfully uttering evil words to revile, insult, and disparage me, and even went so far as to sever my body, dismembering it limb by limb until each piece was the size of a jujube leaf, at that time I would never, toward these sentient beings, give rise to even the slightest thought of agitation or disturbance.

Why is this so? For throughout the past, as I have transmigrated through immeasurable and innumerable cycles of birth and death, there is nothing I have not done. Whether dwelling in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or the world of Yama, and even now while existing in the human realm, I have indulged in food and drink, enjoyed various sensual desires, listened to what is not the Dharma, pursued a wrong livelihood with arduous toil, and undergone manifold oppressions; yet, regarding my body and life, I have never achieved any fruit or benefit.
Although one may engage in various and manifold activities, they cannot thereby benefit oneself or others.

Even if it were the very limit of my existence in saṃsāra, and all sentient beings were to cut, dismember, and sever my limbs, I would rather endure all such suffering than ever abandon the mind of omniscience, nor would I ever forsake all sentient beings or my aspiration for wholesome dharmas.

Why is this? Although this body of mine is subjected to many kinds of afflictions, torments, and destructions, they do not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even a *upaniṣad* part of the suffering of hell.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, I shall not abandon the object of great compassion—the entirety of all sentient beings.
In short, if there should be any cause or condition that gives rise to anger, I shall eliminate it through the Dharma.
What is the Dharma?
It is that which consists of delighting in the body, being bound to the body, and clinging to the body.
To relinquish this body is to relinquish ill will.
The Buddha said, “Sāgaramati!

One who enters into such a collection of dharmas is able to endure all the afflictions and oppressions of sentient beings; even to the point of not begrudging their own body and being able to relinquish it without attachment or craving—this is precisely what constitutes the cultivation of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).”

Furthermore, when encountering the time when the body is about to perish, if one does not abandon all sentient beings through great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), this is the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

When encountering the time when the body is about to perish, if one is capable of enduring and accepting [suffering] according to the meaning of liberation, and if the power of patience manifests such that the mind remains unshaken and undisturbed, this is the cultivation of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

By means of the power of diligent vigor, one does not abandon the mind of omniscience but upholds it; thus, by initiating various virtuous practices within the cycle of birth and death, one is able to cultivate the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).

Furthermore, when the body perishes, if one manifests the jewel of omniscience within the mind, does not forsake bodhicitta, and observes with reality as it is the supreme, sublime tranquility, this is precisely the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).

When encountering the time when the body is about to perish, one contemplates that the body is an illusory phenomenon, like grass, wood, walls, or rubble; one enters into the realization that the body is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and quiescent. To examine the body with such discernment is precisely what constitutes the cultivation of the perfection of superior wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Even if someone should come with an evil mind to revile and insult him with anger, he immediately thinks:
"This person is indolent and has abandoned the pure dharmas."

I shall now arouse diligence to seek and practice with earnest effort, planting all roots of goodness without ever becoming complacent; I vow that this person shall first sit at the site of enlightenment, and I shall be the last to attain perfect awakening.
To summarize: these sentient beings are called those who are unsubdued, unpeaceful, unguarded, and not yet tranquil; for their sake, he dons the armor of meaningful adornment.
Furthermore, relying on this Dharma, I investigate: what is anger and what is non-anger?
In these two, neither can be apprehended.
Moreover, whether it be anger or non-anger, whether it be oneself or another, both the anger and the one who is angry cannot be apprehended.
"Since these cannot be apprehended, one should further transcend this view; this is what is called 'patience' (kṣānti).
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:
"If sentient beings engage in dispute or contention, they should give rise to this thought:"
"I shall exhort them. It is difficult to find such an occasion for this dispute, whether regarding the disputants themselves or the matter of dispute.
Yet, I act as a bridge for all sentient beings; if I am reviled or slandered by others, why should you respond with such words?"
One should merely resemble a fool or a mute sheep, refraining from engaging in strife.

Even if others approach with malice, reviling one with foul language and insults, one’s mind should remain unharmed regarding the path of speech; one should draw near to others with kind words and not emulate them by giving rise to such faults.
Even if I hear of the faults of others, I shall not emulate them. Why is this?
Because my mind is free from anger.

Furthermore, if there are any exquisite pleasures required by all sentient beings, I shall bestow those exquisite pleasures upon them, even unto nirvāṇa, so that they may realize and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"However, I shall never give rise to anger toward others, nor shall I engage in acts of delusion regarding myself or others; I will cultivate only firm and steadfast diligence.
Because of this diligence, even if my body and life were destroyed, I would feel no resentment or affliction, nor would I knit my brows in a frown.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"If one thus consoles and thoroughly comforts sentient beings who are angry and wrathful, one who abides in this patience will attain the joy of the Dharma that accords with it."
