The Compendium of Training for Bodhisattvas, Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Decree by the Śramaṇa Rìchēng and others, Great Masters of the Propagation of the Dharma, recipients of the purple robe, and Junior Ministers of the Court of State Ceremonial. Chapter Ten: The Perfection of Diligence (*Vīryapāramitā*) The Treatise states:
Although one may hear that diligence arises from abiding in such patience, one might still commit transgressions regarding what has not yet been heard.
As a verse in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* says:
"Arrogant regarding the Dharma and failing to guard the precepts—how much merit can such a person gain?
Even if one has heard much, if the precepts are broken, there is no way to escape the evil realms."
The Commentary states:
Regarding "possessing the superior capacity through hearing," the *Nārāyaṇaparipṛcchā-sūtra* says:
"O son of good family!..."
One attains the nature of supreme wisdom through the understanding of what has been heard.
If one hears that afflictions are pacified and eliminated, then the Māra of Affliction will find no opportunity.
Regarding this, it is explained in detail in the *Maharṣi-pūrvayoga-sūtra* as follows:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, being fully endowed with a profound mind and a reverence for the desire for the Dharma, dwell in other worlds and appear before all Buddhas to hear the Dharma as it is taught.

If Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are diligent in their desire for the Dharma, they store the treasury of the Dharma within mountain forests, attaining immeasurable sūtras and dharma-gates as if placing them in the palm of their hand.”

Furthermore, through the bodhisattvas' diligent aspiration for the Dharma, they attain the manifestation of the Buddha before them, as well as the eloquence of the Buddhas and the devas. Even when their lives are about to end, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the devas increase their lifespan and physical strength; though they do not originally seek it, they abide for a thousand years due to the collective empowerment of the Buddha and the devas, even extending to seeking to abide for an entire kalpa.

Furthermore, all bodhisattvas give rise to reverence for the Dharma; for the sake of removing the suffering of old age and illness for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they receive the bestowal of right mindfulness and the eloquence of thorough penetration, even unto receiving the bestowal of right view, such that according to their vision they are able to preach.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the aspiration for the Dharma through diligence, they will have no fear of any other enemies or adversaries.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who is skillful in the provisions of extensive learning and diligence cultivates and attains such qualities as these.
The Commentary states:
Through how many kinds of practices does a bodhisattva hear and enter into an understanding of the Vinaya?
As stated in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"One enters into understanding by hearing about eighty kinds of practices.

Namely: the practice of aspiration, the practice of profound intent, the practice of firm resolve, the practice of supreme correspondence, the practice of freedom from arrogance, the practice of non-negligence, the practice of reverence, the practice of extreme respect, and the practice of detachment from fame."
The practice of signs, the practice of good speech and conduct, the practice of service, the practice of the benefit of hearing,
the practice of mental attention, the practice of non-distraction, the practice of non-abiding, the practice of the perception of jewels, the practice of the perception of medicine,

the practice of eliminating all diseases, the practice of mindfulness of the vessel, the practice of thorough understanding, the practice of joy in the mind, and the practice of realization and entry.
The practice of never being weary of hearing the Buddha-dharma; the practice of extensive relinquishment; the practice of understanding and subduing [the mind];

the practice of drawing near to those who have heard much; the practice of joyfully accepting what is to be done; the practice of the body leaping with vigor; the practice of the mind being delighted;
the practice of not becoming indolent or regressing upon hearing; the practice of hearing the meaning; the practice of hearing the Dharma; and the practice of hearing the majestic deportment.
The practice of conduct; the practice of hearing others speak of conduct; the practice of hearing the sublime Dharma never heard before;
the practice of hearing of supernormal powers; the practice of not delighting in other vehicles; the practice of hearing of the various *pāramitās*; the practice of hearing of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;

the practice of hearing of the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); the practice of hearing of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); the practice of hearing of the holy life (*brahmacarya*); and the practice of hearing of right mindfulness.
Right knowledge and conduct; skillful conduct arising from what has been heard; skillful conduct arising from what has not yet been heard;
contemplation of impurity; contemplation of loving-kindness; contemplation of dependent origination; contemplation of impermanence;
contemplation of suffering; contemplation of non-self; contemplation of cessation; contemplation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; [and] non-...
The practice of undertaking actions; the practice of undertaking actions well; the practice of establishing true reality; the practice of non-decline; the practice of solitary conduct;
the practice of guarding one’s own mind; the practice of unflagging diligence; the practice of discerning all phenomena; the practice of applying antidotes to the afflictions;
the practice of aspiring toward one's own wholesome qualities; and the practice of subduing the afflictions belonging to others.
The practice of conduct; the practice of relying on the seven riches; the practice of severing all poverty; the practice of praising those possessed of wisdom;
the practice of delighting in the wise; the practice of the equality of the noble ones; the practice of pure faith in those who are not noble; the practice of seeing the truths;
the practice of distancing oneself from the faults of the aggregates; the practice of weighing the faults of the conditioned; and the practice of relying on the meaning.
The practice of conduct, the practice of conducting oneself according to the Dharma, the practice of all forms of wholesome action, the practice of benefiting oneself and others,
the practice of not generating further karma regarding the cultivation of virtue, the practice directed toward excellence, and the practice of attaining all the Buddha-dharmas.
That sutra further states:
"If one accords with the auxiliary dharmas (sahāya-dharma), then one attains such intellectual activity (jñāna-karma).
What is meant by 'according with the auxiliary dharmas'?"

That is to say: having few concerns and few desires, being careful in speech and careful in conduct, during the first and last watches of the night, one listens to those things in the world that accord with reason; one weighs what is beneficial to others and repeatedly investigates it, with a mind free from turbidity and defilement, having removed all hindrances and obstacles.
Regarding other offenses, he departs from them through wisdom and does not give rise to remorse; he initiates and pursues firm, correct practice.
Delighting in the Dharma and revering the Dharma, he makes the Dharma his inner treasury and possesses such diligence as if his head were on fire; seeking wisdom, he makes it his place of dwelling.
Not falling away from the prohibitions and precepts, not abandoning the heavy burden, he proceeds toward the sublime, relinquishing those who are unbeneficial.

Delighting in solitary practice, he manifests mental attention (*manasikāra*) in the *araṇya*, possesses the seeds of the noble ones, and finds joy in the *dhūta* qualities, contentment, lack of distraction, and the delight in the Dharma.
Not dwelling on worldly speech, one seeks the essentials of the supramundane Dharma; free from deluded thoughts, one penetrates meaningful benefit and accords with the true Path.
One understands the conditions for upholding the precepts and is adorned by shame and remorse.

With firm and substantial wisdom, one destroys ignorance; with the eye of supreme insight, which is utterly pure, one awakens to and understands the bonds of the darkness of delusion and ignorance—namely, through vast awakening, non-erroneous awakening, analytical awakening, and direct realization—attaining these not from another.
"Upholding one's own merits and praising the merits of others, such that the wholesome practices one cultivates do not fall under the sway of karmic retribution—
this is called the purity of the activity of wisdom.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"What should one hear?
One should study the Vaipulya sūtras and śāstras in this manner, while also remaining far removed from that which is not beneficial.

Specifically, one should avoid all treatises on worldly affairs, treatises on flogging and punishment, treatises on sorcery and poisons, treatises on silence, treatises on children’s games, and even all those treatises such as the various sectarian expositions of liberation that foster delusion and darkness. Those who are well-established in the Bodhisattva Vehicle should distance themselves from all such things."
Furthermore, as the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"There are four kinds of giving that serve as the provisions for wisdom and bring accomplishment for one who preaches the Dharma."

What are the four? First, paper, pens, ink, and scriptures; second, the adornment of the Dharma seat; third, possessing fame and material gain; fourth, receiving and upholding the Dharma without using flattery or deception to offer praise.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of protection. What are the four?
First, protection of one's own body; second, protection of virtue; third, protection of all worlds; and fourth, protection of beneficial matters.
Furthermore, there are four abodes by which one achieves the accumulation of wisdom.
What are these four? First, abiding as a teacher of the Dharma; second, abiding in the Dharma; third, abiding in gain and offerings; and fourth, abiding in awakening.
"These are called the four kinds.
Furthermore, the *Kusuma-kūṭa Sūtra* states:

"If a person were to give a heap of the seven treasures as large as Mount Sumeru as a gift to a lay bodhisattva, it would not equal the merit of being able to offer a thousand coins to a renunciant bodhisattva, or of giving even a single finger-joint as a difficult-to-practice gift out of faith and understanding in the merit of renunciation."

If all that exists [is attained] only by those who have gone forth, obtaining this great fruit, then for the Tathāgata—who is most supreme and most holy—there is no such possibility for one who remains at home; how much less so for a householder who lacks wisdom and is incomplete in his faculties?
As stated in the *Paramapraśna-sūtra*:
"If one is single-mindedly able to distance oneself from offenses regarding the retinues and so forth of others, this is said to be faultless."
"If they are unable to remain far removed from [worldly attachments] because their nature is difficult to tame, this fault is established for those who live as householders.
Chapter Eleven: On the Āraṇya (The Wilderness Dweller) As stated in the *Paramādhyāyikā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
"One relies upon dwelling in the āraṇya because the nature of householders is characterized by faults."
Furthermore, as a verse in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* says:
"Without giving rise to attachment to desire, remaining far removed from kin and retinue, and renouncing the household life,
one attains the unsurpassed path."
Fearing the household life and distancing oneself from kin, unsurpassed bodhi will not be difficult to attain.
But by constantly remaining at home and dwelling on the plane of desire, one can obtain—
The supreme and wondrous Bodhi:
dwelling in seclusion, far removed from all desires, severing the afflictions,
subduing the demonic adversaries, free from defilement and unconditioned, one awakens to the path of Bodhi.
With food, drink, clothing, and exquisite flowers and ointments, they shall serve the Holy Honored One among men.
If there are those who thus seek awakening and bring benefit to sentient beings, [they shall attain this].
Disgusted with conditioned phenomena, one proceeds toward the empty and secluded;
the merit and reward obtained by taking even seven steps toward this goal are supreme and beyond compare.
If one encounters those who do not share a common lot, yet delights in assemblies and craves wealth and profit,
and follows after such beings— leaving behind that very place— is the hardship of ignorance and darkness.
That sutra further states:
"The wise do not contend with the foolish; one should resolutely abandon them.
Freeing oneself from this most evil state of mind, do not compete in the ways of the foolish."
The wise do not associate with the foolish, for they understand the nature of folly;
though one may remain close to them for a long time, they will later become sources of resentment and envy.
The wise do not rely upon the foolish, for they understand the nature of folly.
That is to say, one whose nature is deluded and dark will naturally seek their own destruction.
Therefore, for such ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), how could there be a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?
If one speaks together with others regarding the Dharma, one should not follow the fault of anger.
This foolish dharma is cruel and poisonous; therefore, the wise do not preserve it.
When fools join with fools, it is like casting filth into impurity;
when the wise associate with the wise, it is like placing ghee within ghee.
That sutra further states:
"In this world, there is not even the slightest portion of a place that is most supremely joyful, whether it be pleasure or non-pleasure;
only the joy of forests and springs, which one may enjoy as they are encountered."
The śramaṇa’s supreme bliss is such that there is not even a hair’s breadth of anything to which he is bound; like the wind turning through space,
he moves like a pratyekabuddha.
The mind is always like the wind, unattached to anything; whether there is pleasure or displeasure, no accumulation occurs.
If one finds pleasure therein, there is neither suffering nor conflict, for one has departed from the two extremes.
"Only this is the bliss of the Dharma; it is not the pleasure of humans.
That same sutra further states:
"He attains the state of permanence, acts in subtle accordance [with reality], and is free from all faults."
Without engaging in even a fraction of dispute,
abiding in accordance with that principle in an araṇya, one shall constantly obtain these merits.
Taking no delight in the world, not increasing outflows, those who dwell in mountain forests attain this supreme capacity and do not give rise to excess.
Through the secrets of body, speech, and mind, and by practicing detachment, those who dwell in secluded places attain great merit.
Having attained that wearying disenchantment, they swiftly awaken to liberation; through the liberation of tranquility, those who dwell in mountain forests abide in liberation itself.
All those who dwell in araṇya and attain these merits, residing among forests and springs,
shall always remain far removed from cities and villages.
"Always like a pratyekabuddha, without any companion; before long, one shall attain this supreme samādhi.
Furthermore, a verse spoken in the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* says:
"Having renounced the household life with its immeasurable faults, which are always unlovely and involve deep, treacherous deliberations;
having attained the joy of mountain forests, the sublime bliss of the sense faculties, and the merit of tranquility;
there are no men or women, nor any talk of play or laughter."
Suppose there comes a person who acts like a pratyekabuddha, whose mind is pure and stainless,
who does not delight in wealth or profit, whose intent is free from attachment, and who is moderate in desire in all circumstances—
one should keep far away from such a person who seeks honor through flattery.
The *Paramapraśna Sūtra* states:
"I should not create a collection of sentient beings; it is not for the sake of a single sentient being that I arouse roots of goodness."

If one who previously heard [the teachings] becomes attached to wealth and profit for even a single moment with an impure mind, then whether they be a deva or a human, all will abandon them; even a single deva or human will likewise abandon them.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*:
"The Buddha said: 'Kāśyapa!'"
It is as if there were a person who, while floating upon a great body of water, died of thirst.

Kāśyapa, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are just like this: though they uphold, receive, read, and recite many teachings, they are unable to sever the thirst of greed, hatred, and delusion; wandering in the great ocean of the Dharma, they die of the thirst and craving of the various afflictions, and subsequently fall into the evil realms.
The Commentary says:
For this reason, one must definitely rely upon an araṇya or a place similar to it.
Furthermore, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:

"If there is a place of residence where one can go for alms that is neither too near nor too far, where there are flowing springs and bathing pools that are pure and stainless, where there is little fear, where leaves, flowers, and fruits are all abundant, which is remote from danger and evil, and abounds in many caves and grottoes of supreme tranquility."
A bodhisattva should rely on this basis in this manner:

first, during the six periods of day and night, they should recite the scriptures themselves with a voice neither too loud nor too low; they should well-restrain the sense faculties so that the mind does not wander outward, and while maintaining this pure livelihood, they should bind their mindfulness to what has been received, skillfully grasping its characteristics without becoming attached to sleep.
If a king, a royal minister, a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, or other officials or attendants should come in person to the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), that bhikṣu should speak thus:
"Welcome, Great King!"
"As has been arranged, you may take this seat.
When the king sits, the bhikṣu also sits;
when the king does not sit, the bhikṣu also stands.
If the King's faculties should become agitated and disturbed, one should praise him, saying:
"Great King! You have attained a great and wholesome benefit."
Within the king’s realm there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess the precepts, virtue, and extensive learning; they dwell therein in peace, unharmed by wicked men, enemies, or thieves.
If the King’s faculties are well-purified and he is capable of receiving the teaching, one should immediately preach the Dharma of skillful means.
If, upon careful examination, he does not delight in skillful means, then one should preach the Dharma of revulsion and detachment.
If, upon examination, they find no joy and feel weary and detached, one should cause them to know that the Tathāgata possesses great compassion and great majestic power;
for the sake of all who come—the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and other officials—one should perform transformative deliverance according to what is appropriate for each.
If they are learned and capable vessels of the Dharma, he causes them to hear the sublime Dharma so that they may subdue their minds.
Those sentient beings, having faith and delighting in this Dharma, attain great joy.
The *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya should contemplate this meaning as follows:"
"How can I dwell in an araṇya?

It is not merely that there are many fierce, wicked, and unruly ones who bear the marks of a śramaṇa; it is not a place of seclusion, nor tranquility, nor restraint, nor correspondence, nor the pursuit of aspiration, where one dwells together with others. Rather, it is a place where non-humans, various evil birds and beasts, thieves, and caṇḍālas dwell together; they do not possess the virtues of a śramaṇa."
"At that time, I shall dwell in an araṇya, and I must fulfill the meaning of being a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, householder, a bodhisattva who has gone forth should observe the practice of the araṇya in this way:
"For what purpose have I come to this araṇya?
It is for the sake of this fear.
What is it that I fear?"
That is to say: the fear of the clamor and bustle of crowds; the fear of assemblies; the fear of greed, hatred, and delusion;
the fear of pride, concealment, and malice; the fear of stinginess and envy regarding wealth and profit; the fear of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; the fear of the *skandha-māra*;
the fear of the *kleśa-māra*; the fear of the *mṛtyu-māra*; the fear of the *devaputra-māra*; the fear of the inversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent; and the fear of the non-existent...
I fear the inversion of taking what is not-self as self; I fear the inversion of taking the impure as pure; I fear the inversion of grasping at suffering as pleasure;
I fear the mind, intellect, and consciousness; I fear the arising of obstructions where there are none; I fear the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); I fear "I" and "mine";
I fear doubt regarding the three periods of time; I fear evil friends; I fear evil associates; and I fear fame, profit, and offerings.
Fear of [not seeing]; fear of claiming to have seen what was not seen; fear of claiming to have heard what was not heard; fear of claiming to have cognized what was not cognized;
fear of claiming to have known what was not known; fear of the defilements of a śramaṇa; fear of mutual anger and resentment; fear of the three realms;
fear of birth within the various states of existence; fear of the three evil destinies; and, in brief, fear of all unwholesome actions.
"I am terrified;
it is because of such evil fears and terrors that I have gone to dwell in the forest hermitage.
... Furthermore, householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya should train in this way:
whenever fear arises, it all originates from the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). To state the essential point:

furthermore, by dwelling in an araṇya and remaining far removed from the grasping at a self, one will be without a self, without what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), without the mark of a self (*ātma-nimitta*), without affection for a self, without the notion of a self, and without views of a self; one will not be sustained by "mine," nor will one calculate things as "mine. Having abandoned the self, one does not dwell in an araṇya for the sake of protection—this would not be beneficial.
Furthermore, householder!
One who dwells in seclusion has no notion of self and no notion of others; if one does not speak of any phenomena, then one does not become entangled with any phenomena.
To speak briefly, householder!
It is like the medicinal herbs, trees, and forests in a wilderness hermitage: they are not startled, nor terrified, nor afraid; nor do they experience any trepidation or bristling of the hair.

It is likewise for this renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in the practice of the araṇya: regarding the body, they conceive of it as medicinal herbs, forests, walls, tiles, and rubble; since the mind is produced like a magical illusion, how could there be any discrimination, fear, terror, or horripilation?

Thus, with such a profound mind, one observes the body: this body does not exist as a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a nourisher, a mind-born, or a youth; these are all false and pervasive conceptualizations.
This fear exists only as a provisional name; it is a false and pervasive conceptual construction that should not be discriminated.
Just as in a forest hermitage there are medicinal herbs and groves that have no owner and belong to no one, so too this forest hermitage has no ownership and belongs to no one.
Having understood all phenomena in this way, one should initiate such practice.
Why is this? One who dwells in solitude is like a stiff corpse; there is no master, nor is there anything to which they belong.
Furthermore, householder!

A renunciant bodhisattva, having understood this while dwelling in seclusion, abides in an araṇya according to what the Buddha has taught; thus he attains the perfection of pure dharmas and deeply plants roots of goodness. Thereafter, he goes out to villages, towns, and cities, and enters royal palaces to preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, householder!

A renunciant bodhisattva who reads, recites, expounds, and explains their meaning and intent should enter among the assembly and receive respect. Within that group, he should draw near to his preceptors (*upādhyāya*), ācāryas, and the elders; likewise, even newly ordained bhikṣus should be respected by him without indolence. He should manage all affairs himself so as not to trouble others, yet he should also not cause those worthy of honor to perform services for him.
One should observe in this way:

Furthermore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is honored and venerated by devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, as well as by all sentient beings; even when performing all his various activities, he manages them himself and does not fear serving others—how much more so should I now, who desire to seek the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa)?
In this way, one serves all sentient beings.
If I serve others and provide for them with everything they require, then all my own tasks will be spontaneously accomplished, and I shall no longer seek to receive service or offerings from others.
Why is that? Householder! This one who honors and serves [the Sangha] takes up violations within the qualities of a bhikṣu’s Dharma.
"Regarding one who forms this grasping, because they have gained the opportunity to serve [the Buddha], I shall not, by means of this dharma, form this grasping.
That sutra further says: "Furthermore, householder!"

Regarding the Dharma for those bodhisattvas in the araṇya: if they see or hear that their upādhyāya or ācārya is ill, even though they are dwelling in a remote wilderness, they should go to inquire after them, which means arriving there at the time of dawn.
One should give rise to this thought:

even if one is requested by others to recite or explain the teachings while residing in a monastic dwelling, one should maintain a mind like that of a forest-dweller (āraṇyaka) and remain free from attachment.
"Thus dwelling in an araṇya, one seeks the Dharma without weariness, perceiving all things as empty and secluded.
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bodhisattvaśikṣāsaṃgraha*, Fascicle 13;
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bodhisattvaśikṣāsaṃgraha*, Fascicle 14.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Propagation of the Dharma, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Rìchēng, et al., by Imperial Decree. The remainder of Chapter Eleven: The Exposition on the Āraṇya. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, regarding the practice of the araṇya: if an ordinary person who has not yet attained the fruits of the path sees tigers or wolves approach, they should not give rise to fear or alarm, but should instead resolve:
'I have come to this araṇya dwelling having already renounced my body and life; I ought not to be afraid.'"
One should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to remain far removed from faults and free from fear.
Furthermore, even if tigers or wolves were to sever my life-root and devour the flesh of my body, one should give rise to this thought:
"I have attained a great benefit; by means of this non-substantial body, I shall obtain that which is substantial."
"If they cannot even be made to eat my flesh, how could those tigers and wolves possibly obtain the pleasure of touch?

To state the essential point: furthermore, regarding the practice of forest-dwelling (āraṇyaka), if non-human beings come—whether beautiful or ugly—one should neither feel attachment nor cause them harm.

If there are devas who have seen the Buddha in the past and come to this forest-dwelling bhikṣu to pose various questions and challenges, that bhikṣu shall explain the Dharma to those devas according to his ability and in accordance with what he has studied.
Furthermore, if there is a time of profound questioning and debate, and an araṇya bhikṣu is unable to answer and the interlocutor does not show respect, he should say to that person:
"I have not yet attained the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)."
"If I were to diligently practice the Buddha's teaching, having heard the Dharma at that time, I would be able to thoroughly understand and answer all questions.
Now, I can only manage to hear this Dharma.
Thus it is summarized: even when dwelling in a forest hermitage among medicinal herbs and trees, one does not grasp at them; how much less so for what is born and what is extinguished?
Observing in this way, one sees that this body is without self, without a sovereign, without an agent, and without an experiencer; who is it that arises and who is it that perishes?
Ultimately, there is no one at all who undergoes arising or ceasing.

This body is likewise thus: it is like grass, trees, walls, or rubble; it has no self, no sovereign, no agent, and no experiencer. It arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and it ceases when causes and conditions disperse.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense, there is not a single dharma that arises or ceases.
That same sutra further states:
“Moreover, one practicing in an araṇya should give rise to this thought:”

"However, as I am now in this forest hermitage alone without a companion, whatever wholesome or unwholesome deeds I may perform, at that time these devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who know my profound mind, shall all serve as witnesses for me."
Furthermore, if while dwelling in this araṇya one roams about with an unwholesome mind and lacks self-mastery;
or if one reaches this most remote place, being alone without companion or associate, without a sense of "I" and without grasping—one should realize these as they truly are:
one should realize as they truly are the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, the thought of cruelty, and all other unwholesome thoughts.
If I were not distinct from this crowd of beings who delight in the clamor of the assembly, I would be deceiving the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
"If one acts in this manner, devas, nāgas, and yakṣas will not reproach or loathe them, and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will be fully delighted.
Chapter 12: Cultivating the Mind (Cittaparikarma) Subsidiary Discussion on the Dhyānapāramitā:
One cultivates this dhyāna-concentration in this araṇya, as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"One who cultivates this perfection of meditative concentration attains a mind free from distraction and benefits all sentient beings. Why is this?

Even for those who give rise to mundane concentrations, such [distraction] still persists; since even a distracted mind cannot be found there, how much less so in the case of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"Therefore, one attains a mind free from distraction, even until the realization of the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
That sutra further states: "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening practices the perfection of meditative concentration, they skillfully enter meditative concentration through mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
If, when seeing forms with the eye, one does not grasp at their signs nor cling to their secondary details,

yet fails to exercise restraint over the faculty of the eye, then— based on false and delusive [perceptions]— one will be afflicted by other evil and unwholesome states of mind that flow forth accordingly;
one who guards the faculty of the eye restrains these so as to bring them to an end.

In this way, regarding sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors known by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and phenomena cognized by the mind, one does not grasp at their signs, nor does one cling to their subtle and excellent characteristics.
If one does not cultivate restraint over the faculty of the mind, then other evil, unwholesome, and unrighteous states of mind will flow forth accordingly;

however, one who guards the faculty of the mind restrains these so that they are exhausted. Thus, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, speaking or remaining silent, at all times and in all places, such a person never departs from *samāhita* (equipoise). Consequently, their hands and feet do not move restlessly, their speech is free from idle chatter and frivolous laughter, and their sense faculties remain undisturbed.

Whether in body or mind, one is entirely free from delusion or error; the three karmas are tranquil, and within both the exoteric and esoteric teachings, one follows the path of ethical discipline. One is content with little and easily sustained, skillfully entering the sphere of practice while remaining far removed from clamor and distraction. Regarding gain and loss, there is no sense of superiority or inferiority, and thus no differentiation.

Thus, regarding suffering and pleasure, defamation and praise, whether lauded or not, whether short-lived or long-lived, there is neither high nor low, and no distinction whatsoever. Whether toward enemies or kin, the mind is always serene; whether among the noble or the ignoble, their voices are unmixed. Regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant, they are like a single characteristic, without high or low, equal and without distinction, transcending all that is adverse or favorable.
Why is this? Because within self-characteristic emptiness (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), and unreality, one perceives that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation.
Thus it is explained at length.
The treatise states:

Those who cultivate joy and bliss distance themselves from all forms of indolence and withdrawal, while those who maintain constant mental attention eliminate mental agitation; these two are the respective objects to be remedied.
A verse from the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* says:
"Throughout immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, All the Buddhas who appear in the world—
By virtue of this Great Sage, One obtains supreme benefit in a single kṣaṇa."
Far removed from negligence, one is liberated from all defiled desires.
These conditioned phenomena are false and illusory, like what is seen in a dream;
they are subject to separation and do not endure for long, nor are all objects of affection permanent.
"Just as one exerts effort in pursuit, so too regarding the stages of the pāramitās up until the awakening to bodhi, one should apply diligence without doubt.
As the *Mahānāṭaka-sūtra* extensively explains in verse:
"The suffering of old age, sickness, and death blazes like a flame; the three realms of existence burn fiercely, with no place of refuge or rest.
Not yet having escaped the cycle of transmigration, one dwells perpetually in ignorant darkness, like a mad bee trapped within a jar."
The three realms are impermanent, like actors on a stage, or like clouds in the autumn sky, arising and ceasing in an instant.
Human life passes away and decays more swiftly than flowing waters; it is as light and rapid as lightning flashing across the sky.
The city of the empty celestial realm pervades the three evil paths; ignorance arises perversely, and craving gives rise to existence.
Like a potter’s wheel, they constantly delight in beautiful forms, exquisite sounds, pure fragrances and flavors, and the pleasure of smooth textures; those who are greedily attached to these—
Like one who is imprisoned,
like a deer caught in a net, or like a monkey bound, they are constantly filled with fear and regard [the body] as an enemy.
These sensual pleasures bring about extreme sorrow and affliction; they are like a sharp, keen blade and like a poisonous drug.
The wise keep far away from them, as one would discard a jar of excrement. The foolish, however, are obsessed with them;
this becomes a cause for fear and a root of suffering.
Bound by craving, one hastens toward old age and decay; those who constantly delight in desire have no refuge or rescue from fear.
In the past, there was a sage who thoroughly understood this desire:
he feared it as a raging fire, as a great mire, as a knife smeared with honey, and as a sword raised in the air.
Furthermore, those who possess wisdom thoroughly understand this desire to be like a jar filled with excrement,
like the head of a venomous snake, like a wooden puppet, like a person smeared with blood,
like the head of a dead dog, and like a malicious enemy.
To understand this desire as being like the moon reflected in water, like an echo in a mountain valley,
like an image in a mirror, like a performer on a stage, and like what is seen in a dream.
Furthermore, the wise realize that these sensual pleasures are like illusions,
like mirages, and like bubbles on water; they endure but for a moment, arising from conceptual construction,
false and unsubstantial.
To think only of one's prime, to rely upon physical form, and to take pleasure therein—this is truly the conduct of a fool.
When old age and sickness arrive, one is swallowed by the suffering of decay; one’s luster fades away like a river running dry.
Abounding in wealth and with storehouses overflowing—those who delight in this are truly the conduct of fools.
Eventually their riches will be exhausted, and later they will rapidly decline and perish; shunned by others, they will be like a desolate forest.
Just as people delight in and long to gather the fruits and flowers of a tree,
yet when it is impoverished, aged, and withered, they abandon it like an owl; so too,
those with abundant wealth and youthful beauty give rise to joy and a pleasant mind.
When one is impoverished, aged, and infirm, others treat one with contempt as if one were a corpse.
Furthermore, this mark of senescence— the years having advanced to extreme decay—
is like the parched, withered tree remaining after a bolt of lightning has consumed it.
This aging and decay are fearsome, Just like a dilapidated old house;
Therefore, the Honored Muni Taught that one must swiftly seek deliverance.
Furthermore, it is like a śāla grove Bound and entangled by creeping vines.
Just as male and female kinsmen wither and rapidly decay,
or like a man mired in mud who suddenly loses his vigor and strength,
so too is this mark of old age: it lacks the agility and swiftness of movement.
Old age transforms the physical form into ugliness; majestic power and strength decline.
One must soon depart from sublime bliss and head toward death, devoid of luster.
These hundreds of kinds of ailments and afflictions are certainly not peaceful happiness.
These signs in the world are as fierce as wild beasts.
To observe old age, suffering, and sickness is to see the afflictions of this world;
having abandoned all pursuit of exquisite pleasures, one speaks of swiftly seeking the essential way of deliverance.
Furthermore, just as frost and snow strip away the lush growth of plants and trees,
so too do the sufferings of illness in this world destroy the life-force, physical form, and vitality.
Though one may amass vast stores in granaries and treasuries, pursuing them to their very limits, [they remain but a source of further craving].
Always like one afflicted by disease, prone to giving rise to anger and resentment,
and facing enemies and adversaries, burning with heat like the sun in the sky;
when the time of death and extinction arrives, both wealth and life are utterly dispersed and destroyed.
Like the current of a river that does not turn back, like fruit or leaves falling from a tree,
and like a log in a river, drifting and sinking without autonomy;
the fruit of karma is difficult to halt, departing alone without a companion.
This phenomenon of death and decay is like the makara fish devouring immeasurable multitudes, like the garuḍa consuming dragons,
like the king of beasts seizing elephants, or like a fierce flame blazing forth.
"it burns all grasses and trees.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra Taught to King Prasenajit* states:
"The Buddha said:"

"Great King! Suppose four mountains were to come from the four directions—solid, firm, and substantial, encompassing everything on all sides, appearing as a single unified mass without any gaps or openings. Within them, the entire realm of space and the earth, including all moving and stationary beings, would be utterly ground to destruction. Who could leap about to escape, or by means of power, incantations, medicinal arts, or wealth, cause them to turn back?"
The Buddha said:

"Great King! There are likewise four kinds of great terrors in the world; who could leap about to escape them, or turn them back through the power of spells, incantations, medicinal arts, wealth, or other such means?"
"What are these four?
They are decay, old age, sickness, and death.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

"Great King! First, when decline arrives, it crushes and overcomes prosperity; second, when the signs of old age appear, they crush and overcome youth; third, when the suffering of illness gathers, it crushes and overcomes well-being; fourth, when death and extinction invade, they crush and overcome life."
"What more is there to say about this?
The Buddha said, "Great King!"

It is also like a lion, the king of beasts, who is fully endowed with a majestic appearance and courageous strength; with its claws and fangs sharp and formidable, it enters the midst of the deer herd and seizes them according to its desire.
"Yet, even if a deer were to leap and bound into the mouth of a fierce beast,
it could do nothing [to escape]. The Buddha said, "Great King!"

The arrow of death that strikes a person is likewise: even one who is stubborn and strong cannot escape it; there is no refuge, no rescue, and nowhere to turn for shelter. One’s limbs are severed joint by joint, blood and flesh wither away, and one suffers from hunger, thirst, and the torment of heat. With mouth agape and heavy panting, hands and feet flail in confusion; one loses all capacity for seeking anything, as saliva and mucus flow profusely and impure excrement soils the body, while the remaining life-force gradually extinguishes.

Within this state, there appear before one the messengers of Yama, arising through the conditions of karma, who are most terrifying. At the final moment of inhalation and exhalation during the division of the dark night, one passes away alone without any companion. Suddenly turning one's back on this life, one flees abruptly to another world, rushing along a great perilous path into vast darkness. One traverses a great wilderness, approaches a dense thicket, and floats upon a vast ocean; driven by the winds of karma, one falls into a direction of profound obscurity where no landmarks exist, with no one left to provide refuge or rescue, and nowhere else to turn for shelter.
The Buddha said: "Great King!
Only the Dharma and the Dharma are the refuge, the rescue, and the place of entrustment."

The Buddha said: "Great King! This wholesome Dharma is like one who is cold obtaining fire; like one who is hot encountering coolness; like a thirsty person drinking clear, cold water; like a hungry person eating exquisite and delicious food; like a sick person meeting a skilled physician and medicine; like one who is terrified finding a powerful companion—it is a refuge and a rescue."
The Buddha said:

"Great King! These wholesome dharmas possess great power in this same way; for those who have no refuge or rescue, they act as a refuge and a rescue; for those who have no place of retreat, they act as a place of retreat."
"Great King!

Therefore, you should know that there are those who manifest impermanence and those who manifest cessation; such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is nothing other than the dread of death.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Great King! The deeds upon which Your Majesty relies are entirely not wholesome dharmas. Why is this so?
"Great King!

As for this body, although it has been protected since time immemorial, adorned with the most exquisite ornaments, and satiated at will with superior food and drink, at the time of death, one cannot avoid dying tormented by hunger and thirst."

Although such a body may be adorned at will with various lovely and wondrous garments, sumptuous and exquisite fine cottons, and decorated according to one's pleasure while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, at the time of death, foul and impure secretions must inevitably flow forth.
"Great King!

Furthermore, although this body may be adorned with immeasurable ornaments such as bathing, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, and exquisite flowers, at the time of death it soon becomes foul and putrid."

Furthermore, although this body is surrounded by queens, court ladies, and retinues, with various musical performances, songs, dances, and amusements, and attended by servants who provide pleasure and delight, at the time of death it cannot escape fear and all manner of suffering and affliction.
The Buddha said: "Great King!

Even though this body dwells within palaces, towers, pavilions, and gabled halls, adorned with decorated windows, balconies, and railings; even though it is surrounded by various flowers and perfumes, lamps and lights, curtains, canopies, couches, seats, rugs, and mattresses; even though one burns various famous incenses and scatters exquisite flowers, with precious vases and incense burners arranged everywhere, and with wonderful jewels, pearls, brocades, silks, and various ornaments and playthings—when the time of death arrives and one reaches the cemetery, the bones, flesh, hair, pus, blood, and foul impurities lie upon the ground, and the corpse remains there entirely without awareness."

The Buddha said: "Great King! Furthermore, this body—though it is constantly mounted upon elephants, horses, and chariots; though it is accompanied by the great music of beaten drums and blown conchs; though it is shaded by exquisite canopies and fanned by whisks; though it is escorted before and behind by immeasurable hosts of brave elephant-riders, cavalry, chariot-warriors, and infantry; though hundreds of thousands of officials and the people of the city and towns join their palms in reverence—it will, before long, lie lifeless upon a bier. The multitude will carry and drag it out through the great city gates. Parents, wives, concubines, brothers, sisters, slaves, servants, and laborers will be bound by grief and affliction; their hair disheveled, they will beat their heads with their hands, wailing and lamenting in sorrowful distress, all crying out, 'Alas, what suffering! They will think, 'For me there is no savior, no kinsman, and no master,' while the people of the city and towns gaze upon it with tears and longing."

Upon reaching the burial mounds, they may be devoured by crows, ravens, eagles, vultures, foxes, wolves, or jackals; or until their remaining bones are burned upon a funeral pyre or cast upon the ground, where wind, rain, and sun expose them until they are reduced to fine dust and scattered in other directions.
The Buddha said, "Great King!
This body is a phantom and an illusion that ultimately returns to destruction; all conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent."
Thus it is said at length.
The Commentary states:
These afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, which constitute a single mass, are abandoned through the cultivation of their respective antidotes.
Therefore, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"To counteract craving, one is able to distance oneself from all conditions that give rise to craving.
What is meant by 'counteracting craving' and 'counteracting the conditions that give rise to craving'?"
If one who is greedy understands well, they should practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) regarding the conditions that give rise to greed.
What is called the contemplation of impurity?

It means that if one observes such things as the body’s hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, blood, tendons, veins, bones, marrow, fat, grease, brain, membranes, sweat, tears, mucus, saliva, the throat, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, spleen, kidneys, the raw and cooked viscera, excrement, urine, and pus—then even a foolish child, a madman, or an unvirtuous person, having understood these things, would not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment; how much less so those who possess wisdom?
"This is how a bodhisattva cultivates the contemplation of impurity.
Furthermore, as the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Moreover, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they understand this body as it truly is.
Subhūti, it is like a skilled butcher or his apprentice who, having slaughtered an ox, divides it into four parts with a sharp knife; whether sitting or standing, they observe it as it truly is.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, it is likewise thus; they observe, as they truly are, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element within this body.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is as if a farmer or a householder has filled a threshing floor with various kinds of grain, namely beans, barley, rice, wheat, sesame, mustard seeds, and so forth.

If a person with clear vision were to examine them closely, they would know those various grains as they truly are: "This is beans and barley; this is rice and wheat; this is sesame and mustard seeds," and so forth.

Subhūti! It is likewise when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā): they perceive that this body, from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, is filled with various impurities such as hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth.

The bodhisattva observes this body as it truly is, seeing that it consists only of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, head, eyes, fat, marrow, liver, gallbladder, spleen, kidneys, the raw and cooked viscera, rheum from the eyes, tears, and other such impurities.

Furthermore, if one goes to a cemetery to contemplate various signs—namely, observing corpses discarded in burial pits that have been there for one day, two days, or even up to five days, their bodies bloated, livid, and foul-smelling, with skin pierced and flesh溃烂 (decayed), as pus and blood flow together.
Having seen this, I realize that my own body is likewise so.
For this body is such by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such by its original nature (*prakṛti*); such is its dharmic nature, which has never been liberated.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, he cultivates the contemplation of the external body as it is observed, even to the point of observing a discarded corpse in a cemetery that has been there for one day, two days, or up to seven days, being devoured by various birds and beasts— crows, ravens, vultures, eagles, hawks, foxes, wolves, and jackals— as well as being gnawed upon by various kinds of ants and insects.
Having seen this, I realize that my own body is likewise so.
For this body is such by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such by its original nature (*prakṛti*); such is its dharmic nature, which has never been liberated.
To summarize: furthermore, if one contemplates a discarded corpse in a burial mound, being gnawed and eaten by maggots, foul and putrid;
this body of mine is likewise the same, as described above.
Furthermore, next, one contemplates a discarded corpse on the path of lamentation: the flesh has wasted away, the bones are exposed, sinews bind them together, and it is stained with blood.
"I and this body are likewise thus," as was explained above.

Furthermore, when one contemplates a discarded corpse on the path of lamentation, where the flesh and blood have completely vanished and the skeletal frame is revealed, yet remaining tendons still bind it together:
"I and this body are likewise thus," as previously explained.

Furthermore, when one observes a discarded corpse along a desolate path, there are only various bones scattered in different directions—namely, the skull, the leg bones, the pelvic bones, the back bones, the neck bones, the arm bones, and so forth.
My own body is also like this, as previously described. Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they go to a place of desolation and contemplate a discarded corpse where only the bones remain, scattered by the wind and soaked by the rain, white as conch shells.
My own body is also like this; the rest is as explained above.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he goes to a cemetery and contemplates a discarded corpse where only the bones remain, which, having lain there for many years, have turned blue-black in color and become like dust when crushed to powder upon the ground.

I and this body are likewise thus; for this body is such by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such by its original nature (*prakṛti*), and within such a dharma-nature there has never been liberation.
The treatise says:

Just as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) serves as the antidote for desire, so too does the cultivation of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*) serve as the antidote for ill-will (*vyāpāda*);

this is what constitutes equanimity. If one does not delight in contemplating sentient beings, one might instead develop attachment to a single meal; consequently, one will seek out and praise the exquisite pleasures of others, finding nothing in them that is not pleasing.
Regarding loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it transcends the conditions of greed and is unattached to defiled passion; this meaning has three aspects.
The *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:

"It refers to the bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment practicing 'loving-kindness conditioned by sentient beings' (*sattvālambanā maitrī*); the bodhisattva who has already practiced and cultivated practicing 'loving-kindness conditioned by phenomena' (*dharmālambanā maitrī*); and the bodhisattva who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) practicing 'unconditioned loving-kindness' (*anālambanā maitrī*)."

Chapter Twelve: Cultivating the Mind (Cíxīn Pǐn), Part Two; also titled the Chapter on the Perfection of Meditative Concentration (Chándìng Bōluómìduō Pǐn). Furthermore, there are [meditations] based on the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, and sentient beings.

Regarding those who take sentient beings as their object: it means that one first delights in bestowing benefit and happiness, and through the mind of meditative concentration, extends loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward them.
Or, there may be acquaintances, guests, or those living nearby; regarding one’s own village as if it were another’s village, and so on, until one attains liberation in this single direction.
In this way, you should never grow weary or indolent in taking the Buddhas of the ten directions and others as your objects of focus.
As it is said in the *Vajradhvaja-pariṇāmanā*:

"For one who fully cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva, if the forms they perceive serve as an antidote to craving—and likewise, if sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena serve as an antidote to craving—then there is no transgression. This is pure, this is wholesome; it is supremely radiant, surpassing all exquisite pleasures. It gives rise to a sense of well-being and engenders pure faith and joy; it produces exultation and establishes one in supreme delight. No distress arises from the discriminating mind; the mental faculty becomes supple, the sense faculties become sharp and keen, and one constantly experiences sublime bliss."

Thus dedicating [merit] to all Buddhas, one further dedicates it to the Prajñā of the Buddhas, thereby attaining the complete and inconceivable wondrous practice of bliss of the Buddhas; yet, one has not yet attained the bliss of the well-sustained samādhi that is identical to that of the Buddhas.

By this power, one is able to successively attain the immeasurable, wondrous bliss of the Buddhas; to be fully endowed with the immeasurable bliss of the Buddha-liberations; to embrace the immeasurable bliss of the Buddha-supernatural powers; to attain the well-secured bliss of the unattached conduct of countless Buddhas; to attain the swift and wondrous bliss of the Buddha’s mastery—reaching far and near like that of a bull king; and ultimately to obtain the immeasurable bliss of the Buddha-powers that thoroughly know all things as quiescent, unborn, and unceasing. Furthermore, within unattached conduct, one constantly and equally attains the wondrous bliss of the non-dual collective practice of all Tathāgatas, free from anger.
This is how a bodhisattva constantly dedicates such roots of goodness to the Tathāgatas and to the bodhisattvas;
that is to say, for those whose aspirations are not yet fulfilled, they dedicate them toward the fulfillment of omniscience.
Regarding those who have not yet attained purity, they purify all the pāramitās through their profound resolve.
Regarding those who have not yet accomplished [the goal], they generate the bodhicitta in order to bring it to accomplishment.
It is like a vajra, causing the armor of omniscience to be without retreat or discouragement.

If the armor of omniscience is without retreat or discouragement, then one will experience the pliancy that accords with the sublime bliss of bodhi; one will not regress from the various paths of virtue, and will dwell in equanimity within all worlds while fulfilling great vows. One cultivates all the practices of a bodhisattva, realizes the sharp faculties and supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, and through these roots of goodness, realizes omniscience.
For the sake of such roots of goodness, one dedicates them toward bodhisattvahood.
Furthermore, those who study the Buddha’s teachings—including all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others—likewise dedicate their roots of goodness in this same manner.

If there are sentient beings who, for even the duration of a finger-snap, hear the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma and show reverence toward the assembly of noble ones, they dedicate these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. That is to say: dedication through recollecting the perfection of the Buddha; dedication through the skillful means of recollecting the Dharma; dedication through reverencing the noble assembly; dedication through never being separated from seeing the Buddha; dedication with a pure mind; dedication through penetrating the Buddha-Dharma; dedication through the immeasurable merits one has cultivated; dedication through purifying all roots of goodness related to supernormal powers; and dedication through severing doubts regarding all dharmas. These are the dedications made by those who study the Buddha's teachings among the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva also dedicates these roots of goodness to all sentient beings, namely: dedication for the purpose of distancing them from the realm of hell-beings;
dedication for the purpose of severing the path of animals; dedication for the purpose of bestowing sublime bliss upon the realm of Yama;
dedication for the purpose of severing the falling into various evil destinies; and dedication to cause the growth of joyful aspiration in those sentient beings.
Dedication toward unsurpassed enlightenment; dedication for the purpose of causing the profound mind to attain the mind of omniscience;
dedication that does not disparage any Buddha-dharma; dedication to ultimately accomplishing the stage of omniscience;
dedication to ultimately purifying all sentient beings—through immeasurable wisdom, one dedicates [the merit] to all sentient beings.
Even regarding all food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness; as well as attending to the body in its coming and going,
sitting and standing, and in various activities while abiding in the path of restraint— he does not give rise to anger toward that path of restraint.

Whether performing the actions of body, speech, and mind with skillful cultivation and disciplined faculties; whether attending to the needs of one’s own body through massage and the like; whether consuming various flavors of food and drink, opening or closing [the mouth]; whether observing or not observing, whether sleeping or waking; and furthermore, when one’s own person goes there to perform service—if a Bodhisattva who is in equal resonance with the object of omniscience does not dedicate these acts, that Bodhisattva’s mind of omniscience delights in the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, even constantly intending to rescue and protect the entire world, thereby generating roots of goodness and remaining far removed from arrogance and negligence.

In brief, it causes all afflictions to no longer manifest, brings one under the protection of the bodhisattvas, ensures the diligent pursuit of the path to omniscience, inspires a joyful affinity for those possessed of wisdom, and enables the cultivation of all roots of goodness until all successive practices are swiftly brought to fulfillment.
In brief, regarding those in the realm of animals, one may give even a small amount of rice so that they all may be reborn in the happy realms;
such is the dedication for their benefit, liberation, and deliverance.

Those who are among the animals constitute an ocean of suffering, are grasped by suffering, are an aggregate of suffering, are called the sensation of suffering, are a mass of suffering, are the flux of suffering, are the limit of suffering, are the root of suffering, and are the basis of suffering; toward those sentient beings, one does not turn back or retreat.

Furthermore, regarding the object of all sentient beings: it refers to directing one's attention toward sentient beings before them; because of the roots of goodness previously cultivated, one generates the bodhicitta and dedicates it toward omniscience. Consequently, one does not fall into saṃsāra, remains free from all perilous difficulties, attains the Buddha’s sublime bliss, and achieves unimpeded presence before them. Thus, one transcends the ocean of saṃsāra, forever severs its continuity, illuminates the Buddha-dharma, and gives rise to great compassion.
As stated in the verses of the *Karunagarbha* chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:
"This Suvarṇaprabhāsa, the most supreme golden drum, Its wondrous sound issues forth,
pervading the trichiliocosm, Able to pacify the hells and the realm of Yama."
Even unto the human realm, may poverty, suffering, and the like be extinguished;
may all worldly obstructions and afflictions be eliminated.
Furthermore, may sentient beings be freed from fear, becoming as serene and fearless as the Honored Muni.
Just as the noble ones, dwelling within the ocean of birth and death, cultivate all-knowledge—
attaining that supreme wisdom, meditative concentration, and the great ocean of merit consisting of the factors of enlightenment.
Having attained this Brahma-sound, as if the Buddha himself had realized it, may you attain supreme and wondrous Bodhi,
turn the pure Wheel of Dharma, and abide for countless eons, preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings and extinguish greed,
hatred, and delusion, along with all afflictions and sufferings.
If there are sentient beings dwelling in the evil realms, being scorched by fire with their bodies constantly ablaze,
upon hearing the sound of this drum, they shall follow its instruction and be led to take refuge in the Buddha Jewel.
Furthermore, may all sentient beings attain the recollection of past lives;
throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of koṭis of births, may they remember the Honored One Lāvaṇya and hear his most profound teachings.
Furthermore, by the sound of this drum, one shall always be near the Buddha,
purely cultivating virtuous conduct and remaining far removed from evil. As the verse says:
"Furthermore, in all lands, may all sentient beings have all their worldly sufferings stilled and eliminated.
Moreover, if there are sentient beings whose physical forms are inferior or whose faculties are deficient,
may they universally obtain all faculties, becoming entirely complete."
With a body that was once frail and weak, wherever he went, he had no one to rely upon;
now, liberated from all ailments, he has attained lightness and ease, and his faculties and powers are fully perfected.
Furthermore, if sentient beings are subjected to the laws of the king, giving rise to various fears and much distress;
if those sentient beings encounter hardships and calamities, the most extreme evils, and a hundred kinds of terrors— may they all be brought to complete liberation.
Or again, they are beaten, shackled, and bound; various instruments of torture press upon their bodies.
Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of grief, fear, sorrow, and lamentation disturb their minds as they are confined within prisons.
Though subjected to flogging, binding, and bitter torment, one is entirely liberated;
though facing execution, one’s life is suddenly restored; and even when manifold sufferings arrive, one remains free from fear.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings oppressed by hunger and thirst, may they obtain exquisite flavors and delicious food and drink;
may those who are blind behold all manner of wondrous forms and appearances.
The deaf shall hear, delighting in harmonious sounds;
those who are naked shall obtain fine, soft garments;
and impoverished beings shall find many hidden treasures, with granaries and storehouses overflowing, adorned with all manner of jewels.
All sentient beings shall obtain this sublime bliss; not a single sentient being shall undergo the retribution of suffering.
Their physical forms will be dignified and majestic, a joy for all to behold;
they shall have an abundance of food and drink, be fully endowed with merit and virtue, and constantly enjoy immeasurable, wondrous bliss.
Harps, flutes, and pipes— multitudes of wondrous sounds— manifest before them in accordance with their mental inclinations at the appropriate time.
Golden lotuses and blue utpala flowers cover everything above.
"According to his mental inclinations, [the offerings] shall appear before him at the appropriate time.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"With scented ointments, flower garlands, and blended powdered incense, three times every day,"
Raining down from the trees,
they made offerings to the inconceivable Tathāgatas of the ten directions,
to the wondrous Dharma of Bodhi, and to all the great Bodhisattvas who have distanced themselves from dust and departed from defilement.
All the assembly of śrāvakas shall be freed from all lowly lineages and the eight states of adversity;
they shall always encounter those free from such difficulties and constantly draw near to the Tathāgatas, the most supreme among kings.
...and so on, until the verse says:
"May all women become men, firm, courageous, and fierce, with wisdom sharp and keen;
may they constantly practice all the paths to enlightenment."
Through the six pāramitās, one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions beneath jeweled trees,
seated upon lapis lazuli thrones; they dwell in peace and bliss, surrounded by those who pay them reverence,
as they hear the preaching of the wondrous Dharma.
The Commentary says:
This briefly clarifies that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) serves as the antidote to hatred (*dveṣa*).
The contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) serves as the antidote to delusion (*moha*); I shall now explain the meaning of dependent origination therein.
The *Śālistamba Sūtra* states:
"What is the dependent origination of internal phenomena as pertaining to causes?
It refers to ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, and so on, up to birth as the condition for old age and death."
If there is no ignorance, one knows that there are no volitional formations; and so on, until: if there is no birth, one knows that there is no aging and death.
Furthermore, if ignorance truly ceases, then volitional formations cease; and likewise, up to: if birth ceases, then aging and death cease.

Furthermore, that ignorance does not think, "I arise from formations," nor do formations think, "I arise from ignorance. In this manner, up to birth, it does not think, "I arise from old age and death," nor does old age and death think, "I arise from birth."

If ignorance were to arise in reality, then the arising of volitional formations could not be apprehended; likewise, up to the point where birth arises, the arising of old age and death could not be apprehended.
One should know that this constitutes the internal dependent origination of phenomena as they are bound to causes.
Furthermore, what are the internal dependently arisen phenomena that are connected to conditions?
They are the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness; their conjunction within the internal is what is connected to conditions.
What is the earth element?
That which causes this body to aggregate and function, having solidity as its nature, is called the earth element.
Furthermore, that which causes the body to be sustained and to perform its activities is called the water element.
Furthermore, that which causes the nature of warmth to manifest in the body and brings food and drink to maturation is called the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
Furthermore, that which produces inhalation and exhalation within the body is called the wind element (*vāyudhātu*).
Furthermore, whatever cavities or apertures exist within the body are called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).

This name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is like intertwined reeds; it causes the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) to be associated with and bound to the outflow-tainted mental consciousness (*sāsravamanovijñāna*), which is called the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*).
If these conditions were not present, the body would not arise.

If the internal earth element is not deficient, and likewise the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are also without deficiency, then through their respective conjunction, the body certainly arises.

However, the earth element does not think, "I can cause the body to be solid and cohesive"; the water element does not think, "I can cause the body to be held together and formed"; the fire element does not think, "I can cause the body to be warm and to digest food and drink"; the wind element does not think, "I can produce inhalation and exhalation within the body"; the space element does not think, "I can form cavities within the body"; and the consciousness element does not think, "I am the condition for birth. It is by virtue of these conditions that the body necessarily comes into being.

Furthermore, this earth element is without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span, without mind-born, without youth, neither male nor female, nor non-male nor non-female; it is without autonomy, without a sovereign, and without "this" or "that," and is utterly non-existent. Likewise, the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are also without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span, without mind-born, without youth, neither male nor female, nor non-male nor non-female; they are without autonomy, without a sovereign, and without "this" or "that," and are utterly non-existent.
Furthermore, as for "ignorance," what is its meaning?

It refers to the arising, within these six elements, of the notion of unity, the notion of combination, the notion of solidity, the notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, the notions of a sentient being, a life-span, a mind-born being, a youth, a sovereign lord, and so forth.
Such various forms of non-knowledge are called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Due to this ignorance, one conceives of objects as truly existent and gives rise to attachment, aversion, and delusion; these very objects of attachment, aversion, and delusion are here called formations (*saṃskāra*). The clear discernment of these phenomena is here called consciousness (*vijñāna*).

At the moment consciousness arises, those four aggregates of grasping are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). Furthermore, the sense faculties that serve as the basis for this name-and-form are called the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The conjunction of these three factors is called "contact" (*sparśa*). From contact, there is experience, which is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Due to attachment to feeling, this is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). Because craving becomes deep and expansive, it is called "clinging" (*upādāna*). Clinging is able to produce "existence" (*bhava*), and existence in turn produces the cause [of birth]. From this, the arising of the aggregates is called "birth" (*jāti*); the maturation of the aggregates is "aging" (*jarā*); and the cessation of the aggregates is "death" (*maraṇa*). Delusion, hatred, defiled attachment, and the fear of death are called "sorrow" (*śoka*); the subsequent lamentation and wailing are called "lamentation" (*parideva*); the intermittent experience associated with the five sensory consciousnesses is called "pain" (*duḥkha*); and the intense suffering resulting from the conjunction of mental attention is called "despair" (*upāyāsa*).
In this manner, they give rise to the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth, up to the general summary.
