Chapter Twelve: The Further Remainder of the Section on Governing the Mind. Furthermore, regarding the true practice and the erroneous practice that have been explained, these refer to the absence of wisdom and ignorance.
From this ignorance, three kinds of formations arise—namely, meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable formations.
This is called "conditioned by ignorance, formations arise.

Furthermore, these meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable formations, according to the consciousness they attract and accumulate, are called "conditioned by formations, consciousness arises. Now, upon careful examination, it appears that a section of the sūtra concerning "conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises" is missing from the original Sanskrit manuscript.
Thus, name-and-form and the growth of name-and-form give rise to the formations at the gateway of the six sense bases; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases.
Furthermore, from these six sense bases, the six groups of contact arise; this is called "with the six sense bases as condition, contact. If there is contact...
When feeling arises, it causes sensation to be produced; this is called "feeling as condition for craving.
If one deeply delights in, takes pleasure in, and becomes attached to delicious flavors, this is called "craving as condition for grasping."

Because one delights in savoring [objects], when one finds pleasure in forms, at the time those forms disperse, one repeatedly pursues them and does not relinquish them; this is called "clinging conditioned by craving."
Thus, the pursuit that causes the arising of bodily, vocal, and mental karma for future existence is called "existence conditioned by grasping.
When that karma passes away and causes the aggregates to arise, this is called "birth conditioned by existence."
Furthermore, when that which has arisen undergoes transformation, reaches maturity, and finally perishes, this is called "old age and death conditioned by birth.

Within this process, the self-nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) serves as the seed, the self-nature of karma serves as the fertile field, and the self-natures of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and so forth, serve as the afflictions (*kleśa*). As for the statement that karma and afflictions cause the seed of consciousness to arise, it means that this karma performs the function of the field for the seed of consciousness.

Craving provides the moisture for the seed of consciousness, and ignorance brings the seed of consciousness to sprout; yet karma does not think, "I am performing the work of a field for the seed of consciousness," nor does craving think, "I am providing moisture for the seed of consciousness," nor does ignorance think, "I am causing the seed of consciousness to sprout. Furthermore, this seed of consciousness itself does not think, "I have been produced by these various conditions."

However, the seed of consciousness abides in the ground of karma; moistened by craving and nourished by ignorance, it gives rise to the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). This sprout of name-and-form is not self-made, not made by another, nor made by both together; it is not emanated by the Lord (*īśvara*), does not arise through the transformation of time, is not born from a single cause, nor is it born without a cause. Without being unconnected to the causes and conditions of the union of father and mother, and through the continuity of defiled attachment, this seed of consciousness produces the sprout of name-and-form within the mother’s womb.

However, this phenomenon is naturally devoid of a sovereign; it is selfless, without grasping, and so forth, like empty space. Its essence and characteristics are illusory transformations arising from unimpaired causes and conditions, such that visual consciousness is produced through five kinds of conditions.
What are these five? They are as follows:
when visual consciousness arises, it depends upon the eye, the object of form, the condition of space, the condition of light, and the condition of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Among these, the eye serves as the support (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness; form serves as the object (*ālambana*); light serves as the illumination; space acts as the non-obstruction; and simultaneous mental attention serves as its arousal. If any of these conditions is lacking, visual consciousness does not arise.

That is to say, if the internal sense-base of the eye faculty is not lacking, and likewise if the conditions of visible form, space, light, and attention are not lacking, then through the conjunction of all these factors, visual consciousness is produced.

The eye does not think, "I act as the support for the eye-consciousness and its object, visible form. Visible form also does not think, "I act as the objective referent for the eye-consciousness. Space also does not think, "I act as the non-obstruction for the eye-consciousness. Light also does not think, "I act as the illumination for the eye-consciousness. Attention also does not think, "I act as the arousal for the eye-consciousness."

In this way, visual consciousness does not think, "I am produced from conditions"; nevertheless, when visual consciousness arises, it truly arises by depending on the convergence of various conditions.
One should explain the arising of consciousness from the various sense faculties accordingly, following this same sequence.
However, there is no dharma that passes from this world to another world; it is merely established by the non-deficiency of the causal conditions of karma and its fruit.
Just as fire does not arise without fuel, so too is the seed of consciousness produced by karma and afflictions.

In each respective place of birth, through the continuity and conjunction [of causes], the sprout of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) arises; such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which is without a sovereign, without self, and without grasping, like space, yet its essence and characteristics are illusory transformations produced by the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
One should know that internally conditioned phenomena possess five characteristics. What are these five?
They are: non-permanence, non-interruption, no point of transition, a small cause yielding a great fruit, and similar continuity.
What is meant by "not eternal"?

It means that when these aggregates at this end die, those aggregates at the other end are born; it is not that the very aggregates which die at this end are the same as those which are born at the other end. This is called "not eternal."

Furthermore, the aggregates at the limit of death do not cease before the aggregates at the limit of birth arise, nor do they arise without the aggregates at the limit of death having ceased; it is like the simultaneous rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale. This is called "non-interruption."

Furthermore, when aggregates arise at the boundary of birth within the bodies of beings of a different class, which do not share the same homogeneous group (*nikāya-sabhāga*), this is called "having no destination.
Moreover, when one performs a small amount of the causal karma of good or evil now, yet obtains a vast amount of retribution in future lives, this is called "little cause and much fruit."
Furthermore, if one performs an action in this life and receives its retribution in a future life, this is called "similar continuity.
The Buddha said: "Śāriputra!..."

Regarding this dependent origination, one constantly cultivates through right wisdom the absence of self, person, sentient being, or life-span as it truly is; thus, being non-erroneous, there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither action nor conditioning, neither opposition nor obstruction, neither fear nor deprivation, and neither exertion nor laxity.

One contemplates that their intrinsic nature lacks any solidity or substance; they are like a disease, like an abscess, like a pain, and like an injury; they are of the nature of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Furthermore, regarding his contemplation that there is no transmigration from the past limit:
"Did I exist in the past? Who said that I existed in the past?"
Did I not exist in past lives? Who says that I did not exist in past lives?
Furthermore, regarding one who does not transmigrate into the future limit: will I exist in future lives?
Who says that I shall exist in a future life?
Who says that I shall not exist in a future life?
Who says that I shall not exist in a future life?
Furthermore, regarding that which does not transmigrate in the present life:
do I exist now? Who says that I exist now? In what sense do I exist now?
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute afflictions (*kleśa*), through which the cycle of existence continues without interruption;
formative action (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*) constitute karma, through which the cycle of existence continues without interruption."
The remaining factors, beginning with afflictions, constitute suffering; their continuous circulation is uninterrupted.
Furthermore, it is said that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); this is called the "contemplation of the prior limit" (*pūrvānta*).
Consciousness, sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth, are called the "contemplation of the present limit" (*pratyutpanna*).
Craving, existence, and so forth are called the "contingency of the posterior limit"; all that has been explained above is termed "cyclic flow" (*pravṛtti*).
Thus, it is through such dependence that there is cyclic flow; if one is free from dependence, there is no cyclic flow.
Through combination there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); if one is separated from combination, there is no cyclic existence.
By this, one understands the manifold faults within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, I shall now sever my attachment and that combination.
Nevertheless, for the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings, one ultimately does not sever the various conditioned activities.
Chapter 13: The Foundations of Mindfulness (Smṛtyupasthāna). The Treatise states:

Having briefly explained how that practice of mental cultivation counteracts delusion through the principle of dependent origination, we shall now proceed to explain the entry into the understanding of the foundation of mindfulness regarding the impurity of the body.
As stated in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*: "Furthermore, noble son, for a bodhisattva who thus dwells in the application of mindfulness to the body, this means:

'This body of mine, from the feet and toes, the heels and ankles, the calves, shins, knees, thighs, and pelvic bones; the waist, spine, abdomen, ribs, chest, and flanks; the fingers, elbows, and wrists; the shoulders, arms, neck, throat, head, cheeks, and skull—this accumulation of various parts is itself karmic existence (*karmabhava*). From this, one produces various afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as well as hundreds of thousands of kinds of false and correct conceptualizations.'"

This body consists merely of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, blood, flesh, skin, bones, liver, gallbladder, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, intestines, stomach, the raw receptacle, the cooked receptacle, fat, grease, brain, membranes, eye-secretions, tears, saliva, nasal mucus, excrement, urine, and a multitude of other impure things; what, then, constitutes the "body"?
By thus observing that the body is like space, one perceives that all phenomena are empty; this is the foundation of mindfulness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
One thoroughly understands that this body arises from two kinds of mindfulness, namely: dispersion and non-dispersion.

This body, when it comes, does not come from the past; when it goes, it does not reach the future; nor does it abide in the interval between the two. It arises solely from the conditioning of inverted views through their conjunction.

Consequently, one experiences this as the fundamental basis for dwelling therein; yet, in reality, there is no sovereign master nor any sense of possession, but rather, based on adventitious karmic traces from previous actions, one relies upon the physical form and its sensory enjoyments as a place of support.

Yet this body is merely a composite of the impure and foul-smelling union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood, taken as one's own essence; it is constantly harmed by the thieves of the three poisons and mental afflictions, a phenomenon subject to disintegration, and a den for hundreds of thousands of various diseases and sufferings.
As stated in the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra*:
"This body is impermanent and does not endure for long; death is its final limit.
Having understood this, one should not give rise to wrong livelihood regarding the body, but should instead cultivate the three kinds of pure giving by means of the body."
What are the three?
They are the pure gift of the body, the pure gift of life, and the pure gift of enjoyments.

This body is impermanent; one should therefore go before all sentient beings to attend upon them and serve them. Whatever they wish to have done—whether acting like a servant or like a disciple—one should remain free from all deceptions, flatteries, and physical faults.
This body is impermanent; its cause for life is merely the inhalation and exhalation of breath—how could one commit evil?
This body is impermanent; one should not give rise to attachment toward pleasant enjoyments, but should relinquish them all.
Furthermore, good son!

When a bodhisattva practices the mindfulness of the body by observing the body, they should contemplate their own body and the bodies of all sentient beings as being identical to the Buddha-body; through the empowerment of majestic spiritual power, they shall attain liberation from all entanglements and fetters.

However, one should observe that the bodies of oneself and all sentient beings, as well as the Tathāgata’s body, are no different from the characteristic of the outflow-free dharma-nature; thus should it be known.
Furthermore, the *Abhayarājadatta-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"This body of mine was not previously accumulated; it gradually disintegrates and perishes, like a mere mote of dust."
The nine apertures overflow like the openings of festering sores.
Furthermore, within all the pores dwell *vāramikās*, which are like venomous serpents taking up residence.

The body is like a mass of foam, its nature frail and weak; it is like a bubble upon the water, arising for a moment and then vanishing, and like a mirage, fundamentally lacking any substantial essence.

The body is like a plantain tree, having no core within; the body is like a magical illusion, being directed by others; the body is like an evil friend, full of disputes and litigation; this body is like a monkey, its nature being only frivolous and restless; this body is like an enemy, constantly watching for one's shortcomings; this body is like a thief, craftily and greedily seizing; this body is like a prisoner, constantly bound and subject to execution; this body is like a mortal foe, not to be cherished or delighted in, and is like an executioner capable of severing one's life.
Furthermore, this body is like an empty village, devoid of a self; it is like a potter’s wheel, never ceasing for even a moment; it is like a vessel of filth, filled with impurity.

The body is like an abscess; when pressed, it is nothing but pain. The body is like a decaying house that will soon collapse. The body is like a leaking boat, incapable of crossing over. The body is like an unbaked earthen vessel that will gradually crumble and break.
Furthermore, this body is like a tree on a riverbank, inevitably tossed and moved by the swift current.

The body is like a temporary lodging, fraught with many hardships; it is like a dwelling where one falsely grasps at a master, or like a watchman for thieves who constantly gives rise to violence and evil. Indeed, this body is like a foolish child that must be guarded and protected.
That sutra further states:
"Such a body, composed of various impurities, is falsely regarded as radiant and pure due to the delusion of ego-grasping (*asmimāna*).
To the wise, it appears like a foul jar from which eye-secretions, nasal mucus, saliva, and other fluids flow; how could one give rise to much craving or pride toward such a thing?"
Furthermore, that verse says:
"Just as a foolish child washes charcoal, wishing to make it white;
even if he were to spend his entire life doing so, he could never obtain whiteness."
It is also like an ignorant person who, wishing to make their body clean,
repeatedly applies baths and washes, yet cannot achieve purity until death.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as a gateway of nine orifices, like sores and pustules.
Eighty thousand families of worms dwell within the body.
When a Bodhisattva contemplates the body, it is like a carved wooden figure, held together by a false conjunction of sinews and bones;
one should know that there is no sovereign master therein.
When a bodhisattva contemplates the body, even when receiving food or drink from others,
they should know that it is like a jackal or wolf coming to eat its own flesh.
The commentary says:
One accomplishes the vast practice through the support of food and drink; this should be understood accordingly in each instance.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), as stated in the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra*: "O noble son!..."

By means of the application of mindfulness that contemplates feelings through feeling, the bodhisattva understands sentient beings; relying upon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they attain such bliss.

If all sentient beings have no liberation, they should practice the application of mindfulness that contemplates feelings through feeling, thinking: "I shall don the armor of great compassion to gather in and subdue all sentient beings, and by means of their own bliss, I shall extinguish all their sufferings."

By means of great compassion, I cause those whose conduct is dominated by greed to understand pleasant sensations and become free from the defilement of greed; by means of great compassion, I cause those whose conduct is dominated by hatred to understand painful sensations and become free from all faults; by means of great compassion, I cause those whose conduct is dominated by delusion to understand neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations and abandon the delusion that arises concomitantly with equanimity.
Furthermore, that pleasant feeling does not destroy painful feeling, nor does it diminish neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
When free from their mutual opposition, there is no ignorance; if there were no ignorance, what could be called "feeling"?
How does one thoroughly understand that all things are impermanent, selfless, and so forth?

This pleasant feeling is itself the nature of impermanence; painful feeling is the nature of oppression; and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the nature of tranquility. Through this, one understands that whether it be pleasure or pain, they are impermanent, selfless, and so on.
Furthermore, the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:

"When experiencing suffering, one should mindfully bring to mind all sentient beings in the evil realms and give rise to great compassion; thereby, one should eliminate anger and remain free from inverted conceptualizations regarding sensation and so forth."
Furthermore, a verse from the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* says:
"It is taught that feeling (*vedanā*) is the act of experiencing; but for whom does this experiencing occur?
Apart from the experiencer, there is no feeling; no distinction between them can be found."
The wise one contemplates sensation, Abiding in this station of mindfulness;
Its characteristic is like bodhi, Luminous and universally tranquil.
— *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, Fascicle Sixteen.
The Compendium of the Bodhisattva’s Training, Fascicle Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu,
Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Xuanfan, invested with the purple robe.
Translated by the śramaṇa subject Rìchēng and others, by imperial decree. Chapter Thirteen: The Remaining Discourse on the Foundation of Mindfulness of Feelings (Vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna). It is said:
This has been a brief explanation of the foundation of mindfulness of feelings.
Next, to clarify the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (citta-smṛtyupasthāna), as stated in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*:
The Buddha said:

"Kāśyapa! Regarding this mind, whether one gives rise to attachment and delight, or conceives aversion and weariness, or becomes deeply attached and clinging—how does one investigate these three temporal limits?"

If it were past, it would have already ceased; if present, it does not abide; if future, it has not yet arrived. It is neither internal nor external, nor is it in between; it is entirely unapprehendable.
Furthermore, this mind cannot be seen as form; it is not something that can be expressed, nor is it an antidote, nor is it contemplation or illumination; it is without abiding and without attachment.
Yet, even all Tathāgatas have nothing to see regarding this mind—how then could others perceive it?
There is no separate objective realm; it is only the conceptualization of phenomena that arises. Kāśyapa!
This mind is like an illusion, being entirely unreal through its pervasive construction; because of what is grasped, various things come into being.
The mind is like space, covered by the adventitious dust of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

The mind is like a river, arising and ceasing without abiding. The mind is like the light of a lamp, produced through causes and conditions. The mind is like a flash of lightning, not remaining for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). The mind is like an evil friend, capable of producing all manner of suffering. The mind is like a fisherman, perceiving suffering as pleasure. The mind is like a malevolent spirit (*bhūta*), causing various disturbances and vexations. The mind is like a yakṣa, watching for and devouring one's vital essence. The mind is like a mad thief, destroying all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). The mind is like a moth, constantly gazing upon its colors. The mind is like a war drum, sounding only to alert one to battle. The mind is like a servant, greedily craving leftover flavors.
"This mind is like a fly that touches a vessel containing pungent grease; this mind is like a pig that, amidst impurity, deems it fragrant and pure.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
When one seeks this mind, it is utterly unfindable; because it is unfindable, there is nothing to be attained.
Since it is unfindable in the past, present, and future, one is then able to transcend the three times and such categories as existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra* states:
"Moreover, this mind does not exist externally and is therefore invisible; it is also invisible within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)."
If one seeks in this way for that which is invisible, by what object of focus (*ālambana*) does it repeatedly arise?
It is said that various minds take such things as their objects.
How, then, can it be said that the mind is invisible?
One should know that this mind is like the edge of a sharp sword; how could it cut itself?
Furthermore, this mind is also like the tip of a finger; can a finger point to itself?
That the mind cannot be seen is likewise so.
It is even as a person traveling a great distance, whose body moves with the lightness and swiftness of the wind, such that no realm he reaches can obstruct him. Noble son!

If a person, regarding these six sense-bases, remains free from attachment in mind and without distraction of body toward what belongs to self or others, then they will attain unobstructed one-pointedness of mind in *śamatha*.
This is the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"One cultivates adornment through corresponding practice, so that within the mind of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is not diminished or lost."
What is meant by adornment?

That mind of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-citta) is identical to an illusion; that is to say, if one relinquishes all that one possesses and is able to dedicate it toward that mind of the nature of phenomena, this constitutes the purification of the buddha-fields.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is also as previously explained.
A bodhisattva does not contemplate the practice of phenomena regarding phenomena, because phenomena are not something that can be contemplated.
If they were neither the Buddha-dharma nor the path to enlightenment, then all phenomena would not constitute transcendence.

Having understood this, they attain the samādhi of great compassion; regarding all phenomena, they perceive neither affliction nor the absence of affliction, and they attain the non-conceptualization of the three spheres.

Why is this? Because one realizes that the nature of all phenomena is without dual characteristics; these afflictions have no nature of accumulation, no nature of greed, no nature of hatred, and no nature of delusion.
"If one can awaken to bodhi in this manner, one realizes that the nature of afflictions is itself the nature of bodhi.
This is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra* states:

“Good son! When a bodhisattva practices the application of mindfulness by observing phenomena with phenomena, they see that when a phenomenon arises, it is born; when a phenomenon passes away, it ceases.

That is to say, regarding phenomena such as a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a nourisher, a man, a pudgala, a mind-born, a youth, or birth, aging, and death—if they accumulate, they proceed through accumulation; if they do not accumulate, they do not proceed through accumulation. Whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable formations, there is not the slightest phenomenon that can arise without its causes and conditions.”
"Furthermore, one deeply investigates this sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) because one does not abandon the bodhicitta of omniscience.
As stated in the *Mahānāṭaka-sūtra*:

"These conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are merely mental constructions; they are impermanent and subject to disintegration, like unbaked clay pots. Formations are like an empty city ruined by rain; like mud that is not firm, they shall gradually wear away and perish."
Furthermore, it is like a riverbank formed by accumulated sand, its inherent nature fragile and easily swept away by the current.

Volition is like a wind-blown lamp, arising and ceasing without staying; volition is like a mass of foam, incapable of being grasped; volition is like a plantain tree, having no core substance within; and it is further like an empty fist used to deceive the ignorant.

Even as grass, kudzu, or other materials are twisted and spun into rope, which can draw water by means of a bottle and pulley, yet never performs that function alone; so too, all the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) revolve through mutual dependence and aggregation, such that they cannot be found at either the prior or subsequent limit.

It is like a person drilling for fire: when the two hands and the wood apply diligent effort without ceasing, fire is produced; yet if the various conditions are separated, the power of the fire is extinguished accordingly.
Once one has been sealed by such a seal of practice, whether oneself or others, one is able to transcend practices such as those of nihilism and eternalism.
"Just as a wise merchant reaches his destination and gains passage through all perilous paths.
The treatise says:

"The aggregates, bases, and elements, which are assembled and brought into being by the causal conditions of karma and afflictions such as ignorance and craving, are all unfindable within the ultimate sense (paramārtha)."
Chapter 14: On Innate Purity The Treatise says: Having already explained the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one next enters into the understanding of the person (*pudgala*).
Once the root has been severed through the definitive accomplishment of the corresponding emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth no longer accumulate or function.
Furthermore, the *Tathāgataguhyasūtra* states:
"The Buddha said:
'O Śāntamati!'"
For example, there is a tree named *palāśa*; if its root is severed, all its branches and leaves will wither away. Śāntamati, it is the same in this case:
if the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, one is able to eliminate all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Commentary says:
There are immeasurable aspects (*ākāra*) for the analytical discernment of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
As a verse in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* states:
“If a person has faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s teaching, And does not violate the Buddha’s training in ethical discipline,
Being able to distance themselves from all women, And knowing that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is eternally empty and quiescent;
They uproot all arrows of sorrow and suffering, Or provide medicine to bring others peace and stability.”
One shall swiftly attain the state of a Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, Knowing that the self-nature of phenomena is eternally empty and quiescent.
If one’s body and life are severed, or if one’s limbs are cut off, And one is struck with staves or beaten, one remains free from resentment and affliction;
The power of patience is supreme, like the moon among men, For one knows that the self-nature of phenomena is eternally empty and quiescent.
Even if one should fall into the evil realms throughout a hundred lifetimes,
one will always maintain a wondrous physical form and likewise attain these five supernormal powers, dwelling perpetually in the presence of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"Moreover, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks of a buddha, they should, throughout all births, maintain mindfulness of the bodhicitta so as not to let it be damaged, remain without forgetting the bodhisattva practices, stay far from evil associates and all faults, and draw near to all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends. Desiring to subdue the hosts of Māras and celestial beings, to purify all karmic obstructions, and to attain non-obstruction regarding all dharmas, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a single thought-moment, they are able to transcend all worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; in every such location, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to dwell in the buddha-fields of the ten directions, they should likewise study the perfection of wisdom; it is to be explained in this same way.

...and so on, as extensively detailed in the teaching that all phenomena are selfless (*dharmanairātmya*). When one extinguishes the bonds of karmic obstructions, one then perceives that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is without cessation.
As it is said in the *Pitṛputrasamāgama-sūtra*:
"The Buddha said:"
"Great King! Thus, these six elements, the six bases of contact, and the eighteen mental investigations arise conditioned by the *puruṣa*.
What are the six elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

What are the six bases of contact? They are: when the eye-base sees forms; when the ear-base hears sounds; when the nose-base smells odors; when the tongue-base tastes flavors; when the body-base directly experiences tangibles; and when the mind-base cognizes mental phenomena.
What are the eighteen mental investigations? They are as follows:
having seen a form with the eye, one may experience pleasure, or experience distress, or abide in equanimity.
In this way, each of the six sense faculties takes those three—pleasure and so forth—as its respective object; these are called the eighteen mental investigations.
Great King, what is the internal earth element?
This refers to the hardness and roughness produced within the internal body, such as the hair, body hair, nails, and teeth.
If the internal earth element were neither to arise nor to cease, there would be no process of accumulation.
"Great King!
When a woman conceives within her own body the image of a man as she contemplates him, and that man likewise gives rise to love and desire, through the union of these two, the kalala is produced."
Furthermore, it is impossible for a being to be born through a union that corresponds exactly to what was conceived.
If two women [conceive], this is impossible; likewise, if two puruṣas [conceive], this is also impossible.
If it were produced through various modes of conceptualization, that too would be impossible, because its own essence lacks reality and is not a composite phenomenon.
How, then, can this be said to possess solidity and hardness?
Great King!
This body stands as a mere semblance of solidity; ultimately, it will rot and disintegrate, with nothing but the cemetery as its final destination.
From where does that solidity and hardness come?
Nor does it go away toward the four cardinal directions, above, or below.
Great King!
"This internal earth element should be understood in this way.
Thus ends the seventeenth fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, the Compendium of Training for Bodhisattvas;
[it continues in] the eighteenth fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Propagating the Dharma, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Rìchēng, and others, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Fourteen, Part Two: On Innate Purity. “Great King!
Regarding this external earth element characterized by solidity and hardness: at that time, the world first established the palaces where the Brahmā gods dwell, which were composed of great jewels.
Furthermore, the palaces where the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) dwell arose, all of them made of the seven precious substances.
"Great King!
If the element of earth (pṛthivī-dhātu) with its quality of solidity had not arisen, from where would it have come?
Furthermore, how could it have become this great earth, eighty-four thousand yojanas in thickness and sixty thousand yojanas in length and breadth?"
Furthermore, the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains arise, firmly established and of one adamantine nature.
Furthermore, Mount Sumeru, Mount Yugandhara, Mount Īṣādhara, Mount Nimindhara, and even the Black Mountains arise.
In this way, once this trichiliocosm has been successively formed, it remains firm and stable.
If the solid nature of the earth element did not arise, from where would it come?
"Great King!
Furthermore, when this world is about to be destroyed, it may be consumed by fire, swept away by water, or blown apart by wind.
When this great earth is scorched by fire, it is like burning ghee or oil; its flames blaze so intensely that even the soot and embers can no longer be seen."
If it were carried away by water, it would dissolve and perish instantly, like salt thrown into water.
If it were blown by the Vairambha wind, this entire trichiliocosm would be completely shattered and destroyed, leaving nothing behind.
Great King!

Furthermore, this earth element is empty when it arises and empty when it ceases; because its intrinsic nature is empty, it possesses neither male characteristics nor female characteristics, being merely that which is manifested through verbal expression.
In this way, the earth element and the nature of the earth element are both unapprehendable; one can understand this through right wisdom as it truly is.
What is the internal water element?
It refers to whatever moist, humid, and similar natures are appropriated within this body.
What, then, are they? They are saliva, sweat, mucus, spittle, fat, marrow, pus, blood, urine, feces, and so forth— these are the internal water element,
Great King.

If at some time one suddenly sees beloved ones with tears flowing from their eyes, or tears flowing because they are oppressed by suffering, or tears flowing out of faith and reverence upon hearing the profound Dharma, or tears flowing because they are struck by a cold wind—whence does such an element of water come?
When the characteristics of water have dried up, where does it go?

Furthermore, when this world-system is destroyed, black clouds arise in thirty-two layers, completely covering the trichiliocosm; from the midst of space, torrential rains fall, with drops as large as elephants, pouring down day and night in an uninterrupted succession.
When such a period has passed through five intermediate kalpas, the accumulated water rises up as far as the Brahma-world.
Great King! From where does this great realm of water come?
Furthermore, when this world is about to be destroyed, two suns appear; once these two suns have appeared, all small rivers and springs are completely dried up.
When three suns appear, even the four great rivers flowing from Lake Anavatapta dry up and vanish.

When four suns appear, the waters of the great ocean decrease by one yojana, or two, or three; they gradually diminish until they reach ten or twenty yojanas, and finally dry up completely until they have receded eighty yojanas.
There remains some water, either as deep as a *tāla* tree, or reaching to the chest, or as deep as a cow’s footprint, down to even a depth of a single finger’s breadth.
At that time, the waters of the great ocean will all be completely dried up, exhausted without remainder. Great King!

This characteristic of the water element comes from nowhere when it arises and goes nowhere when it ceases; it is empty at the time of its arising and empty at the time of its cessation. Because its intrinsic nature is empty, it has neither male nor female characteristics, existing only as what is manifested by verbal expression.
In this way, the water element and the nature of the water element are both unapprehendable.
What is the fire element within the body?
It is whatever nature of warmth and heat is appropriated within this body.

What, then, is that? That which is characterized by warmth and heat, which digests and transforms food and drink, and brings about well-being—whatever is included within the category of heat is called the internal fire element.
What is the external fire element?
It refers to that which is not appropriated and arises as heat and warmth.

Furthermore, if a person seeks the conditions for fire in a wilderness—whether by means of thistleweed, dried cow dung, or cotton wool—and having produced a fire, it burns grasses, trees, forests, villages, and other locations, such that all these places are consumed by the flames.
"Great King!
Thus, this fire element arises from nowhere and ceases with nowhere to go, for its intrinsic nature has been detached from the very beginning.
What, then, is the wind element within the body?"
What is the nature of lightness, mobility, and so forth?

It refers to this internal wind, which at times moves upward, at times moves downward, or remains in the abdomen, the flanks, or the back; it may manifest as eruptions, or coalesce into lumps, or feel like being sliced by a knife, or like being pricked by needles; it includes the inhalation and exhalation that pervade the limbs and the entire body.
The external wind element refers to winds that come from the four directions—some as swift as arrows, others as sharp as blades.
When they arise with violent fury, they break off forest trees and shatter mountain peaks;
when they arise subtly, they cause the body and clothing to flutter and move the *tāla* trees. This is called the external wind element; the rest is as previously explained.
What is the internal element of space?
It refers to that which exists within this body—such as skin, flesh, blood, and so forth—which manifests and increases, being free from the nature of material obstruction.
Furthermore, what is it?

That is to say: the cavities of the eyes, the apertures of the ears, the mouth, and the throat; and the essence of food and drink that has been swallowed and drawn down, which passes through the intestines and stomach and emerges.

When, through the conditions of karma, the six sense bases are produced, and once these bases have arisen, they encircle the space-element—this is called being included within the category of the internal space-element.
But from where does that space-element come?
Furthermore, that which is externally manifested and devoid of the nature of material obstruction is called the external space-element,
Great King!
If form undergoes transformation and decay, all of it is empty. Why is this so?
Because this realm of space is fundamentally inexhaustible; it abides immovably like nirvāṇa, pervading all places without obstruction.
"Great King!
It is, for example, as if someone were to dig a pond or a well in a high plateau.
What do you think?"
"From where does this mark of emptiness within the pond and the well come?
The king replied,
"It comes from nowhere."
The Buddha said: "Great King!
Suppose that person were then to fill it with earth; what do you think?"
"Where does emptiness go?
The King replied,
"Emptiness goes nowhere."
Why is this? Because this realm of empty space has neither coming nor going, it abides neither in the male characteristic nor in the female characteristic. "Great King!
The external realm of space is fundamentally unmoving.
Why is this? Because its intrinsic nature is detached [from movement]; one can understand this through correct wisdom as it truly is.
"Furthermore, Great King, what is the element of consciousness?
It refers to that which, with the eye-faculty as its primary basis, takes as its respective objects visible color, shape, and informative matter; this is called the eye-consciousness element."
If the six sense faculties are taken as primary, and each separately engages with its corresponding object, these are termed the six consciousness elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*).
Furthermore, this consciousness element does not adhere to the faculties, nor does it abide in objects; it is neither internal, nor external, nor in between the two.

However, O Great King, each of these elements of consciousness, having individually cognized their respective objects, immediately ceases and passes away; they come from nowhere when arising, and go nowhere when ceasing.
O Great King!

When consciousness arises, it is empty; when it ceases, it is also empty. Because its intrinsic nature is empty, it does not abide in the mark of male nor in the mark of female, but is merely that which is manifested by verbal expression.
In this way, both the element of consciousness and the nature of the element of consciousness are ungraspable; one can understand them through suchness and right wisdom.
Great King, what is the sense-base of the eye?
It refers to the translucent matter derived from the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
If the earth element is pure, then the eye base is pure; if the water, fire, and wind elements are pure, then the eye base is pure.
Why is this? Because through the purity of the earth element, the sense base of the eye arises, yet within it not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
Thus, up to and including the wind element, through its purity the sense base of the eye arises, yet within it not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
Why is this? Because it is without a sovereign and without agency, for its self-nature is pure, just like nirvāṇa.
Great King!
In this way, each of the sense bases of the eye is sought individually and is found to be unobtainable. Why is this?
Because the earth element is empty, the earth element is pure; and so on, up to: because the wind element is empty, the wind element is pure.

If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature from the very beginning, then how could those realms possess purity or conflict? Since neither purity nor conflict can be apprehended, what form could there be that is visible?

One should know that because the sense base of the eye is ultimately empty, its intrinsic nature is also empty; neither its prior limit nor its subsequent limit can be apprehended, nor can anything created in the future be apprehended.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is detached.
If intrinsic nature does not exist, then there is neither the mark of male nor the mark of female; how, then, could there be desire or attachment?
If one gives rise to attachment and delight, this is the realm of Māra; if there is no attachment or delight, this is the realm of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because if there is no attachment or delight, one is able to remain far removed from all phenomena.
"Great King! What is the sense base of the ear?
It refers to translucent matter derived from the four great elements."
"Furthermore, Great King!

The liberation of all phenomena is definitively manifest as empty like the realm of reality (dharmadhātu); it cannot be established, cannot be displayed, cannot be designated, and is free from any expectation."
"Great King!

Each of the sense faculties delights in and clings to its respective object. When the eye encounters a form, delight and clinging arise; therefore, it is said that form is the objective sphere of the eye."

Furthermore, when this eye faculty encounters the objects of form, there are three modes of observation: toward attractive forms, it gives rise to the perception of desire; toward unattractive forms, it gives rise to the perception of aversion; and toward those that are neither attractive nor repulsive, it gives rise to the perception of equanimity.

In this way, even up to the mind being attached to the sphere of mental objects as its domain: if that mental faculty, taking a pleasing form as its object, gives rise to extreme attachment and pleasure, it is led by that to produce a state of greed; toward an unpleasing form, it produces a state of hatred; and toward what is both pleasing and unpleasing, it gives rise to a state of delusion.
In this way, the three types of objects of perception, such as sound, and their characteristics—such as being apprehended and experienced—should be explained according to what was stated previously.

Great King, you should know that the sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams; it is, for example, as if a person were enjoying themselves with various court ladies within a dream.
"Great King!
What do you think?
Once that person has awakened from the dream, would they consider the entertainment with the court ladies in the dream to be real?"
The king said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"Great King! What do you think?
Would a person who clings to a dream, asserting it to be real, be considered wise?"
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?"
The multitude of people and court ladies seen in a dream ultimately do not exist; how much less could one enjoy oneself with them?
One should know that such a person merely exhausts themselves in vain, for the objects of the dream-world cannot be recovered once the dream has ended.
The Buddha said: "Great King, it is so, it is so."

When foolish ordinary beings see forms with their eyes, a mind of attachment and delight arises, followed by further clinging. Driven by this, they perform actions of craving: three types of bodily action, four types of vocal action, and three types of mental action. These actions, first performed and then ceasing in a single moment, do not abide in the east, south, west, or north, nor in the four intermediate directions, above, below, or in between.

"At the limit of death, when the life-faculty ceases, the karmic retributions of one's own past actions all manifest before one, just as one who has awakened from a dream recalls the events within that dream.
Great King!"

With consciousness as its sovereign and karma as its object-condition, these two factors mutually dependent give rise to the initial consciousness; it may lead to rebirth in hell, or fall among the animals, in the realm of Yama, or among the asuras, or as a human, or as a deva.
The initial arising of consciousness is termed "birth," wherein each receives its respective retribution; the mental factors of the homogeneous class continue in succession.
The final cessation of consciousness is termed the "skandha of death," and the initial arising of consciousness is termed the "skandha of birth."
"Great King, you should know that there is not even the slightest dharma that passes from this world to another world.
Why is this? Because its nature is subject to arising and ceasing."
"Great King!
When body-consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
When that karma arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere."
When initial consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
Why is this? Because its intrinsic nature is detached [from arising and ceasing].

Thus one understands that body-consciousness is empty of body-consciousness, one's own karma is empty of one's own karma, and initial consciousness is empty of initial consciousness; whether it is the emptiness of cessation or the emptiness of arising, one understands that the bonds of karma have no agent and no experiencer, being merely names and concepts.
Furthermore, Great King!
Suppose there were a person who, in the midst of a dream, engaged in battle with various enemies.
What do you think?
"After that person has awakened, do they remember the fighting and other such events from the dream as being real?
The King replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Great King!”
"What do you think?
Would a wise person consider what this man grasps in his dream to be real?
"No, [World-Honored One]."
World-Honored One!
Why is this? In a dream, there ultimately exists no adversary, much less engaging in mutual combat with one.
"This person merely worries and distresses himself in vain;
there is no reality to it at all. The Buddha said, "Great King!

It is so, it is so. When foolish ordinary beings see unpleasant forms with their eyes, they immediately give rise to affliction; they become weary and detached, engage in disparagement, and commit acts of hatred. The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, Great King!
It is as if there were a person who, while in a dream, was tormented by a piśāca; he would give rise to fear in his mind and become deluded and faint.
Great King! What do you think?
Once that person has awakened, does he still remember being tormented by a ghost in his dream? Is it real or not?
"No, World-Honored One!
In a dream, there is ultimately no demon to cause affliction; how much less so for one who is deluded?"
The Buddha said: "Great King! It is so, it is so."
When foolish ordinary beings see these forms with their eyes, they are deluded and fail to understand, thereby creating karmic actions born of ignorance; the rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, Great King, it is like hearing the exquisite singing voices of many people, as well as the music of *vīṇā* lutes, flutes, and various wind instruments within a dream.
"Great King!
What do you think?
After that person has awakened, would they remember all the singing and music within the dream as being real?"
The king said, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
"Great King! What do you think?"
"If this person who dreamed were to grasp at it and claim it to be real, would that be considered wisdom? "No,
World-Honored One."
Why is this? For even the multitude of people within a dream cannot be apprehended, let alone the exquisite sounds of various musical instruments;
such a person merely exhausts themselves in vain, for in the end, nothing exists.
The Buddha said, “Great King, it is so, it is so.”
When foolish ordinary beings hear agreeable sounds, having heard them, they become delighted and further give rise to attachment, thereby performing actions driven by greed.
One should understand that the same applies to each of the other three types of objects—smells and so forth—according to the preceding explanation.
"Furthermore, Great King! Within this Dharma, you should settle your mind well and reflect thus:

'How may I become an eye for those among gods and humans? How may I act as a great lamp to provide illumination? How may I act as a captain to enable them to cross to the other shore? How may I act as a great caravan leader to lead them to the place of jewels? How may I cause those not yet liberated to attain liberation; those not yet at peace to find peace; and those not yet in Nirvana to realize Nirvana?'"
"Great King, you should know that the sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams; yet ordinary beings remain bound and attached to them, never reaching satiety.

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a wheel-turning king named Amitayaśas (Immeasurable Renown). Possessing majestic virtue, fame, wealth, and sovereignty, he ruled over the four great continents as the sole preeminent sovereign. Whatever he desired, he obtained for his enjoyment, and all the trees were perpetually laden with flowers and fruit."

At that time, the people of the world lived in peace and security, free from affliction; furthermore, there fell rains of various exquisite fragrant waters, gold, silver, precious jewels, and all kinds of requisites, so that everything they required was universally and fully provided.
Suddenly, at one time, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where Śakra, Lord of Devas, offered him half of his seat and invited him to sit.

Having conceived a greedy desire, never satisfied, and wishing to usurp that position, he made this thought and immediately vanished; his retinue of ministers surrounded him and all witnessed it together.
It is like fresh butter placed in hot sand that cannot remain for long; it is about to reach the end of its life.
At that time, there was a king named Kāraṇḍava who, having seen this, spoke these words:
"How shall I skillfully explain this matter to all the world?"
Then, Immeasurable Renown spoke these affectionate words:
"In the future, you should speak thus:
'That Immeasurable Renown, because of his insatiable greed, took his own life.'"
"Thus, O Great King! The sense faculties are like illusions and their objects are like dreams; you should settle your mind accordingly and not give rise to faith or compliance.
The body is like a mirage, lacking inherent nature; likewise, the self-nature of form, sensation, perception, and mental formations is unreal."
