Chapter Fourteen: The Section on Innate Purity (Svabhāva-viśuddhi), Part Two. The Treatise states:
This exposition establishes all phenomena based upon the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*); it should be understood in this manner.

When the World-Honored One, with his omniscience, observes the world, he realizes through direct perception that, according to conventional designation, there are six realms of existence: whether gods, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals; beings of high or low birth who experience the retribution of poverty or wealth, decline or prosperity, suffering or pleasure, as well as defamation or praise; and the various forms of existence, such as those of the form and formless realms.

When a Tathāgata appears in the world, and sentient beings develop pure faith toward the Sugata and delight in the teaching of the ultimate truth, at that time the Tathāgata speaks according to his realization for the benefit of sentient beings: that the reality of all phenomena is without fabrication, without conceptual differentiation, without cognition, without manifestation, and without verbal expression; thus, all phenomena are entirely empty.
If this is so, why does the Blessed One further speak of receiving the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Within this Dharma, what constitutes form?
Furthermore, by what means are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness designated as being able to predict unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

From this, one understands that because form (*rūpa*) is fundamentally non-existent, awakening (*bodhi*) is unborn; and so it is for all [the aggregates] up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which are likewise said to be fundamentally non-existent.
Since nothing at all can be apprehended among all phenomena (*dharma*), what could be called a "Buddha"?
What is called "bodhi"?
What is called a "bodhisattva"?
What is called "receiving the prediction" (vyākaraṇa)?

Whether it be form being empty of form, up to consciousness being empty of consciousness, these are established merely in accordance with conventional usage and momentary existence; such discourse is nothing more than names and concepts. Therefore, the wise should not give rise to anger or affliction regarding this.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of all phenomena is ultimately inexhaustible.
Those gods who delight in transformations do not understand this profound meaning; they cling to the notion that a self exists and yet maintain that it poses no obstruction.
The World-Honored One further said:
"Because all dharmas are by nature devoid of the essence of bodhi, if one can awaken to this understanding, that is to draw near to immeasurable bodhi. Why is this so? [Because...]"
"If one is separated from bodhi, there is no nirvana; if there is no nirvana, there is no craving for its bliss, and thus no samsara to be feared.
"World-Honored One!
Just as the 'self' grasped by the gods who delight in emanation cannot be found, how much less could the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) be found?"
At that time, the Lord of the Sahā World, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, immediately attained realization and spoke these verses:
"Just as a person in a dream, though pressed by hunger, Would have no satiety even if they ate a hundred flavors—how could there be fullness?"
Having realized that these dream-appearances are fundamentally empty, one sees that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is likewise so.
Just as when a person skillfully delivers various discourses and others, upon hearing them, all give rise to affection and delight—
yet both the words spoken and the affection felt are ultimately non-existent— one should not give rise to doubt therein.

Just as a lute or a zither produces exquisite sounds, yet the inherent nature of those sounds does not exist, so too should one understand craving for the aggregates: when investigated with sublime wisdom, it cannot be found.
Just as when one hears the great resonance of a conch shell and seeks its source of origin,
finding that the nature of that sound is originally empty, so too does one understand all phenomena of the Great Sage.
Just as various delicacies of exquisite flavor, once eaten, sustain and fill the body, so too this flavor of the body is originally non-existent; thus one realizes all dharmas of the Great Sage.
Just as when the Lord of Devas manifests a jeweled banner, All the devas behold it and give rise to love and joy;
Yet knowing that this sign is originally empty, One then understands all dharmas of the Great Sage.
For example, it is like someone who demarcates boundaries on the earth, Arbitrarily naming them cities and towns where none originally existed;
Likewise, when one realizes that the city of the body is empty of intrinsic nature, One then understands all phenomena of the Great Sage.
Just as when people gather and strike a drum, the multitude hears it together and gives rise to joy;
yet the intrinsic nature of that sound is originally empty—thus one understands all phenomena of the Great Sage.
Furthermore, just as striking a drum produces sound dependent on conditions, yet if there were no moisture, the resonance would not vibrate;
when one seeks the source of these characteristics, from where do they come? Thus one realizes all phenomena of the Great Sage.
Furthermore, it is like striking a drum to produce a deep sound; that sound has no thought or invocation.
Likewise, when such conceptual discrimination is fundamentally non-existent, one then realizes all dharmas of the Great Sage.
The commentary states:
This further clarifies the preceding meaning, namely that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the eye and other phenomena does not exist.

If phenomena do not exist, there is no accomplishment; if there is no accomplishment, there is no arising or ceasing. Consequently, even the three characteristics of the objects perceived by the eye faculty—such as the pleasant, the unpleasant, and so forth—are all unobtainable; they are beyond verbal expression and lack any representation.

For example, it is like showing an empty fist to a small child; it merely deceives them and possesses no reality whatsoever, such that even its name and measure cannot be found. This ultimate emptiness is definitively non-existent [in that sense].

It is like a person who, in a dream, has his head severed by a great seer manifesting a fierce and terrifying form; once the wise person awakens, they understand that everything was a manifestation of their own consciousness, and thereby they are liberated.
As the Kinnara King Mahādruma asked the World-Honored One:
"If all that is taught by the Dharma is entirely empty, how is it that the World-Honored One bestows a prediction of enlightenment upon me?"
I, too, do not know. This self-abiding pavilion neither increases nor decreases, nor does it disintegrate; its enjoyment is inexhaustible.
What is the nature of this phenomenon?
The Buddha said:

“You should understand that the intrinsic nature of all those phenomena is the primordially empty dharmadhātu, just as reflections appear within a mirror or as a wheel is manifested through the gathering of its parts; I say that the intrinsic nature of karmic activity is likewise.”
Furthermore, just as fire is produced when the trees of a forest are struck against one another by the wind, so too, when one reflects in this way, what fire can be found?
My teaching on the performance of action is also like this.
As it is said: "Suppose there is a person whose lifespan reaches a full hundred years; one should know that no accumulation of years can be perceived.
Furthermore, as the *Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra* states:
"The eye and forms are fundamentally without conflict; likewise, the ear and sounds, up to the mind and mental phenomena, are also without conflict."
How is it that there is no contention between the eye and forms?
Because the two meet in harmony without mutual opposition.
This applies likewise up to the mind and mental phenomena (*dharmas*): when these two aspects meet in harmony, there is no contention; if they do not meet in harmony, then there is contention.
World-Honored One!
Dharmas have no duality; therefore, they do not contend.
All dharmas are non-dual and do not cognize one another; because they do not cognize one another, there is no discrimination.

If one is free from conceptual discrimination, there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither increase nor decrease; one neither generates attachment nor feels aversion, neither abides in saṃsāra nor clings to nirvāṇa.
"Bhagavān! If one neither delights in nor feels aversion toward all phenomena, it should be known that there are no such characteristics as defilement or purity. Bhagavān!"
If one says, "Thus do I know," or "Thus do I perceive," all such things are merely false conceptualizations.
World-Honored One!
If, moreover, having thoroughly understood these dharmas such as the eye and so forth, one does not form such thoughts:

"If one can say, 'I am able to discern,' know that such a person does not contend with things; they are then able to accord with the practice of the śramaṇa path, and are one who sees the Dharma, who sees the Buddha, who sees sentient beings, and who sees emptiness."
“World-Honored One!
To see nothing that can be seen is called the non-seeing of all dharmas.
That sutra further states:
The Bodhisattva Asamudgata asked,
“Regarding suchness as emptiness, what is said concerning phenomena?
The Buddha replied:
"That Suchness is empty, neither arising nor ceasing.
If this is so, then all phenomena are empty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anutpāda said:
"It is so, it is so; therefore, the World-Honored One has taught that all dharmas are without arising or ceasing.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you further say that all conditioned dharmas arise and cease?"
"If that were so, then the stupas and temples of the Buddha would certainly be subject to arising and ceasing. "Good son!

The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, teaches the dharma of arising and ceasing in accordance with the world to remove the fear of sentient beings; yet within this, not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, much less arising and ceasing."
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Venerable Subhūti! Regarding 'unborn phenomena' (*anutpanna-dharma*), what is meant by 'unborn'?"
Subhūti said: "Śāriputra!
That which arises is without arising; this is the dharma of non-arising."
The Commentary says:
This is called attaining bodhi through the accumulation of pure meritorious conduct.
By taking sentient beings as the object of pure compassion, and having observed them well, one is free from the notion of a "sentient being."

Furthermore, even if one were to make offerings to the Sugatas of the ten directions, those Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings have already transcended all defilement and are no longer to be perceived.
One should instead make offerings to sentient beings who are suffering; this is the instruction of the Teacher, the Tamer, that one should bestow the supreme offering among humans upon them.
By means of a mind of great compassion, one uproots all suffering and attains the bliss of peace; by generating pure wisdom, one severs the afflictions.
Having thoroughly understood this correct principle, one should abandon doubt and uncertainty; thus, the fruit of such worship is not difficult to obtain.

Having realized the Buddha’s true teaching, one contemplates the body according to that teaching, brings to mind the Eightfold Noble Path, and severs all delusions and defilements. One should relinquish one’s own body to serve the Buddhas, not aspiring for the exquisite pleasures of the worldly devas. One cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whether in stillness or total tranquility, as the path for escaping suffering.
How are conventional phenomena established?
It is said that at the locus of falsehood, through conjunction and correspondence, ordinary beings are deluded and inverted, conceiving the notion of "son" and relying upon its accomplishment.
However, in the context of ultimate emptiness, such characteristics do not exist, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*: "Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
'What is the root of false conceptualization?'"
He replied: "Perverted perception is the root.
He spoke again:
"What is the root of inverted perceptions?
He replied, "Non-abiding is the root."
He asked again:
"What is the root of non-abiding?
He replied:
"Non-abiding is the absence of a fundamental basis. Mañjuśrī!
From this non-abiding as the fundamental basis, one is able to establish all dharmas."
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"One should renounce the household life and dwell with courageous resolve to sever the afflictions, cultivating the *prajñāpāramitā* with a pure and equanimous mind."
Furthermore, the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* states:

"One who skillfully understands emptiness does not rely upon any worldly gain or loss, praise or blame, joy or sorrow, or defamation. Such a person does not give rise to aversion toward various sufferings and afflictions, nor do they give rise to attachment toward various pleasures; they are not destroyed by worldly phenomena."
One who skillfully understands emptiness realizes that within the nature of emptiness there is not even the slightest dharma to be grasped or abandoned.
If there is neither grasping nor abandoning, there is no craving or aversion; this is what is called one who skillfully perceives emptiness.
"One who well understands emptiness has no attachment toward any phenomena; if there is no attachment, then one will have no contention regarding all phenomena.
The Commentary states:
This clarifies that the mind attains purity in each moment, meaning that through the abandonment of the conceit of "I," one lightly relinquishes sentient beings.
One realizes that the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is fundamentally non-existent; if one can sever it through single-minded concentration, such a person will swiftly attain purity of mind.

Observing in this way, one always delights in honoring all sentient beings everywhere, remaining free from objective grasping (*ālambana*) and conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). When self and others are equal, how could there be any contradiction?
To practice and train in this manner is not difficult.
It is like the wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel, which is cherished by all people yet does not regard itself as noble; for this reason, one should give rise to respect toward others.

This means that through inverted conceptualization and attachment, one gives rise to stinginess or disparagement toward sentient beings; all of this is due to being bound by the fetter of *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").
For this reason, one frequently gives rise to praise and blame, which increases feverish affliction.
How could the nose be burning? This sound has no intention regarding praise; how then could such deluded wisdom arise to produce that sense of gratification?
Why give rise to attachment toward the words of others?

Since the joy of others is not one's own, one should always delight in equanimity and take up tranquility for oneself; thus, one unties the bonds of discrimination and leaves behind the marks of praise and blame.
Thus, one understands that there is no benefit or fruit whatsoever.

Furthermore, regarding material gain, it gives rise to much joy and distress; through the habitual practice of stinginess, envy, and crafty seeking, one incurs grave offenses in both favorable and adverse circumstances.

In accordance with correct principle, one should give rise to the antidote; crushing the peaks of the mountain of pride, the mind quickly becomes pure. Free from the faults of speech, one should exclusively delight in silent seclusion, except for the continuous manifestation of instructions.
Having realized that all delusive phenomena lack any solidity or substance, and that the root of suffering cannot endure for long.
15. Chapter Fifteen: On Right Livelihood and Requisites. Furthermore, Householder!
If a lay bodhisattva should delight in right livelihood and enjoy things with equanimity, they must remain far removed from unlawful and wrong modes of livelihood.
As stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:

"How does a bodhisattva not feign the display of dignified deportment through physical actions toward a donor? When lifting the foot, one does not falsely walk slowly; when setting the foot down, one does not look about or manifest the appearance of deep reflection."
How is it that a bodhisattva’s speech is not deceitful and not for the sake of gain, yet manifests subtle speech, gentle speech, affectionate speech, and compliant speech?
How is it that a bodhisattva’s mind is not crooked and not for the sake of gain, yet while his speech manifests few desires, his mind extensively seeks after them, harboring inner feverish distress?
How is it that a bodhisattva is well able to abandon manifesting unusual signs for the sake of gain and offerings? If they see a donor, they never say to themselves:
"I lack clothing, bedding, food and drink, or medicinal requisites for illness; I pray you, grant me these as gifts."
How does a bodhisattva skillfully abandon the empty talk and incitement for the sake of gain and offerings? If they see a donor, they do not utter deceptive words such as:
"The donor so-and-so gave me such-and-such an object, and I repaid his kindness with such-and-such an object."
Furthermore, it is said:
"I give because I am of few desires, uphold the precepts, and have heard much; I embrace them by giving rise to a heart of compassion.

Yet, even those who commit evil deeds with their bodies may run to and fro for the sake of gain and profit, thereby breaking the prohibitions; if they see others who practice the same holy life receiving offerings, they conceive a mind to destroy them.
This is called a bodhisattva seeking gain and offerings while remaining free from treacherous and evil ways.
How does one abandon unrighteous gain and offerings?
It means that this bodhisattva does not practice deception with measures or scales, nor does he cause harm to those who place their trust in him.
How does one abandon impure gains?
This means that the bodhisattva does not treat as interchangeable the property belonging to a stūpa, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha, nor does he consent to accept anything so obtained.
How does one abandon attachment to gain and offerings?

It means that whatever this bodhisattva obtains, he does not take possession of for himself; he does not boast of his wealth nor does he hoard it. Instead, he gives them at the appropriate time to śramaṇas, brahmins, and brāhmaṇas, or to his parents, relatives, and associates.
Or he may use them for his own enjoyment, yet when using them, he gives rise to no defiled attachment.
When the bodhisattva does not obtain gain or support, his mind gives rise to neither suffering nor distress.
"Furthermore, even if there is no object to be given by the donor, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of anger toward them.
Moreover, the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"There is no sentient being who is incapable of receiving a gift; one should bestow whatever has been promised upon them."

When there are those who come to beg, one gives without giving rise to vexation; one gives without being coerced by others; one gives without weariness, without signs of distraction, without contempt, without turning one’s back, without casting away, without disrespect, without discrimination, without not using one’s own hand, without failing to give at the proper time, without partiality, and without causing distress to sentient beings.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Sūtra of the Questions of Varapradāna*:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of generosity, if someone comes seeking whatever they require, they should give it to them by acting in accordance with my [teaching]."
If there are those who delight in alcohol, the Bodhisattva causes them to give rise to right mindfulness and provides them with drink; subsequently, he causes them to abstain from it.
In this way, the Bodhisattva employs pure skillful means to gather in and sustain sentient beings.

If their inner mind cherishes it and refuses to relinquish it, the Bodhisattva will then reprove and condemn the faults of alcohol in various ways, likening them to sharp swords and blades, so that they may certainly distance themselves from it and prevent its continuity.
"One who gives in this manner is without fault.
The Commentary says:

This explains that the practice of giving is purified so as to lead one gradually toward entry [into the path], as is extensively clarified in other sūtras regarding the prohibitions and restrictions.
As stated in the *Gaganagañja-sūtra*: "That is to say:

the pure giving of the self, the pure giving of what belongs to the self, the pure giving of causes, the pure giving of views, the pure giving of signs, the pure giving of various natures, the pure giving of momentary retribution, and the pure giving of a mind equal to space."
Furthermore, just as space has no boundaries, so too is the Bodhisattva’s practice of giving.
Just as space is vast, expansive, and unimpeded, so too is the Bodhisattva’s extensive dedication of merit through the practice of giving.
Just as space has no marks of form, so too is it with the bodhisattva who practices giving while remaining detached from form.
Just as space is without perception, without volitional action, without manifestation, and without characteristics, so too is it with the bodhisattva’s practice of giving.
Just as space pervades all buddha-fields, so too does the great compassion of a bodhisattva extend toward all sentient beings as they practice vast generosity.
Just as space contains and accommodates everything, so too does the bodhisattva’s practice of generosity gather in and sustain all sentient beings.

Even as when an emanated person gives to another emanated person, there is no enjoyment and no conceptual discrimination; so too, the mind realizes that all phenomena are without anything to be sought, being free from "I" and "mine" and naturally pure. With supreme wisdom, one cuts off all afflictions; with the wisdom of skillful means, one does not abandon sentient beings.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice the perfection of generosity as being like space.
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bodhisattvabhūmi-śikṣāsaṃgraha*, Scroll 19;
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bodhisattvabhūmi-śikṣāsaṃgraha*, Scroll 20.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Scattered Official, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Propagating the Dharma, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Rìchēng, and others, by imperial decree.
Part Fifteen of the Second Section on the Requisites for Right Livelihood, Continued. The Treatise states:
This further clarifies the purity of śīla, as stated in the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra*:
"By remaining far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and by not giving rise to regression regarding the bodhicitta, one attains purity in śīla."
"Good son! Just as the nature of space is pure, so too is the purity of a bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts.
Just as space is stainless, so too is the stainlessness of a bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts."
As space is quiescent, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of ethical discipline quiescent.
As space is indestructible, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of ethical discipline indestructible.
Furthermore, just as no one can surpass space, among all sentient beings there is none who surpasses the bodhisattva in the observance of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, just as space is pure and impartial, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of patience toward all sentient beings—impartial, harmonious, and pure.

For example, suppose a person were to enter a śāla forest with a sharp axe in hand to cut off its branches and leaves; one should know that those trees harbor no anger, do not give rise to discrimination as to who is cutting them, nor do they discriminate as to who is being cut.
The bodhisattva’s practice of patience is likewise thus; this is called the bodhisattva’s supreme patience, which is like space.
Furthermore, the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra* states:
"Purity of physical diligence means that this body is like a shadow or an echo, and all speech is by nature indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Knowing that this mind is ultimately empty and quiescent, one should don the armor of compassion."
Wearing the armor, they are fully endowed with all practices and cultivate meditative concentration deeply; they allow no deficiency in the qualities of merit;
they observe all sentient beings with the bodhicitta without deficiency; they delight in practicing generosity up to skillful means without deficiency;
and they are in deep accord with the heart of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity without deficiency.
He is without deficiency in generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and collaborative action;

he is without deficiency in right mindfulness and right situational awareness; he is without deficiency in the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and the noble path; and so on, up to śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Vipaśyanā is without deficiency; having abandoned the karma and afflictions of its own nature, one cultivates self-examination of the body so as not to be negligent.
Constantly diligent in the Buddha-work to mature sentient beings, all attain coolness and abide in tranquility.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the practice of the purity of the dhyāna-pāramitā.
In this same manner, one should understand [the practices] up to the prajñā-pāramitā."
Chapter 16: Increasing Superior Power The treatise states: This explains three kinds of increasing superior power:

namely, being never weary or satisfied with one's practice; not giving rise to indolence or retreat regarding the sentient beings to be delivered; and seeking the wondrous wisdom of the Buddha with firm and courageous vigor. These three powers are such that they cannot be practiced by any of the śrāvakas.
As stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:
"Because all sentient beings are by nature timid and weak, except for Bodhisattvas who manifest and increase [their strength].
Furthermore, the *Tathāgataguhyaka Sūtra* states:
At that time, King Ajātaśatru again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many dharmas must a bodhisattva fully cultivate to be able to obtain such supreme power?”
The Buddha said:
"Great King! If a bodhisattva cultivates ten dharmas, they will obtain these superior benefits."
What are the ten? First, a bodhisattva would rather sacrifice their own body and life than ever abandon the unsurpassed true Dharma;
second, they maintain a sense of humility toward all sentient beings and do not increase their pride.
Third, one gives rise to a mind of compassion toward those who are weak and inferior, and does not cause them harm;
fourth, upon seeing beings afflicted by hunger and thirst, one bestows excellent food and drink;
fifth, upon seeing beings overcome by fear, one bestows upon them fearlessness.
Sixth, seeing sentient beings who are ill, one provides medicine to rescue and heal them;
seventh, seeing sentient beings who are impoverished, one bestows gifts upon them to bring them satisfaction;
eighth, seeing the stupas, temples, images, and paintings of the Buddha, one cleanses and polishes them until they are perfectly pure.
Ninth, uttering words of joy to comfort sentient beings;
tenth, seeing those sentient beings burdened by heavy loads, exhausted, and afflicted, one removes their heavy burdens for them.
If a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they will be able to obtain such supreme power as this.
Furthermore, the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:

“If a bodhisattva can arouse diligence, remaining constantly firm in their earnest application and aspiration, and if the diligence they initiate never ceases, then for such bodhisattvas, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) will not be difficult to attain.”
Why is this? Samudramati!
It is through diligence that one attains bodhi; those who are indolent remain far, even further away, from the bodhi of the Buddha.
"Those who are free from indolence are able to practice generosity, up to and including those who are free from indolence being able to accumulate wisdom.
As the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* states:
"Just as the utpala flower grows within water, one should know that [virtues] increase through successive stages; thus, one should gradually train in and study practices such as generosity."
As it is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"If a bodhisattva abides well in giving, the mass of merit obtained is immeasurable.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it cannot be perfected through minor giving alone; they should bestow upon all sentient beings gold, silver, precious jewels, gardens, groves, and dwellings, providing whatever is required according to their inclinations. By means of the skillful means of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), they should dedicate [the merit] for the sake of immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, and thus they should train in the perfection of wisdom."
The Commentary states:
This clarifies that the self-nature of the Great Compassion Gaganagañja is pure, and that the accumulation of merit and blessings he enjoys increases with rapidity.
If there were no great compassion, it would not be the practice of a bodhisattva; it is the very foundation for establishing all virtues.
When such a profound resolve and firm great compassion manifest, and one courageously practices all corresponding conducts, one will then be able to attain the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Thus, a verse says:
"Just as a person skilled in combat, With sharp weapons and a heart of firm valor..."
"If there is even the slightest laxity or retreat, one will be seized by them.
Furthermore, when Sudhana went to the holy spiritual friend Bhadrapāla, he thought to himself:

"In past lives, this body of mine lacked a courageous mind, lacked a firm resolve, and lacked pure causes; thus it underwent various cycles of rebirth. My mind delighted in wandering and inverted discrimination; through its own wrong reflections, it took pleasure in practicing sensual desires and clung to worldly activities that yield no benefit. Or, regarding the goals and benefits attained for oneself, it gave rise to partiality—all of which I have now utterly abandoned."

In the present life, one should give rise to great fortitude, engage in discernment and analytical investigation with true contemplation, and diligently practice the correct conduct of all bodhisattvas. One should develop a superior resolve toward all sentient beings to bring them much benefit, exert great diligence before the Buddhas to accomplish great wholesome deeds, adorn the sense faculties, and increase the power of aspiration. One should read and recite the scriptures with a mind of pure faith and understanding, maintain control over body and mind without becoming arrogant, and always delight in renouncing the ocean of suffering—birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, and affliction.

Furthermore, in order to joyfully practice the conduct of a bodhisattva throughout the future, one should travel to all buddha-fields to reverently receive the instructions of the Tathāgatas, draw near to and make offerings to teachers who skillfully expound the Dharma, seek with delight the true Dharma of the Buddhas that accords with reality, serve and provide for spiritual friends, and reveal and explain all the Buddha-dharmas.

If a bodhisattva can contemplate and observe in this manner, they will be able to increase the power of their vows and the body of wisdom, thereby delivering sentient beings and planting the roots of all virtues.
As stated in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra*:
"The bodhisattva, solitary and without companion, is courageous and firm, ultimately embracing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
With a profound mind, one cultivates for oneself without relying on the actions of others, adorning oneself with the armor of diligence.
Just as all sentient beings perform wholesome deeds, I likewise shall perform them all.
Furthermore, regarding all the practices cultivated by the bodhisattvas from their first resolution of mind, I too shall practice them.
Generosity is not my companion; rather, I am the companion of generosity.
Ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are not my companions; rather, I am their companion.
The various pāramitās cannot cause me to act; rather, I am able to cause the various pāramitās to act.
All roots of goodness are likewise so.

Even until I sit upon the adamantine seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and destroy the hosts of Māra, in a single kṣaṇa, through wisdom corresponding to equanimity, I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
As stated in the *Vajradhvaja-sūtra*:

"Just as the Sun Deva appears in the world alone and without peer, traversing all realms without ever retreating; he feels no weariness toward those born blind, no weariness toward Rāhu the Asura King, no weariness toward the city of the Gandharvas, no weariness toward the impurities of the regions of Jambudvīpa, no weariness toward the atoms of the earth-element throughout the four continents, and no weariness toward the obstructions of high mountains, smoke, clouds, and the like."

The appearance of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the world is likewise thus: through non-conceptual wisdom and right mindfulness, they clearly understand that even if they are harmed by sentient beings, they do not give rise to a mind of aversion or weariness, nor do they ever retreat.
If there are those who give rise to jealousy toward the vast roots of goodness of a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva does not conceive a mind of aversion toward them and does not regress.
Furthermore, if sentient beings are defiled by the stains of false views, the bodhisattva does not conceive a mind of aversion toward them and does not regress.
If he sees sentient beings constantly bound and entangled by anger, the bodhisattva does not distance himself from them.

If he sees sentient beings obscured by the darkness of ignorance, burdened by the heavy defilements of affliction, and having destroyed the seed of enlightenment such that no one in all the world can protect them, [the bodhisattva likewise does not abandon them].
The bodhisattva does not give rise to contempt toward them. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva, through great compassion, perceives no faults in sentient beings.
It is just as when the orb of the sun appears in the world, causing all things to be clearly manifest and free from obscuration.

Yet, if there are sentient beings shrouded by ignorance—who do not have faith in the Buddhas, do not hear the True Dharma, and do not recognize the field of merit of the Sangha—they create various causes of suffering for themselves and may fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.

At that time, having seen those sentient beings creating such karma, the Bodhisattva’s mind remains undisturbed; he makes no distinction between them and himself, feels no alarm or fear, and gives rise to a firm and courageous heart without retreating, resolving to undergo all their sufferings and afflictions on their behalf.

Why is this? I shall take upon myself the burden of all those sentient beings, even through the hardships of birth, old age, sickness, and death in the world; the hardships of the eight states of no leisure; the hardships of saṃsāra; the hardships of various wrong views; the hardships of the destruction of wholesome dharmas; and the hardships of being born without wisdom—I shall ultimately cause them to be liberated from these hardships.

These sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance, ensnared by the net of craving, and bound by the fetters of existence; confined within the cage of various sufferings, they lack awakening and have no desire for liberation. Constantly harboring doubts and acting contrary to their aspirations, they drift and sink unidirectionally within the ocean of saṃsāra.
I shall abide as the King of All-Knowledge, causing all sentient beings to accomplish their welfare and attain liberation;
I alone am able to provide them with protection and refuge.
Even if all worlds were entirely filled with evil realms, and sentient beings suffering therein were to fill them completely,
I would dedicate all the roots of goodness I have accumulated equally, giving to all without exception.
Until the very end of time, may each and every evil realm be extinguished without remainder, and may every single sentient being attain liberation.
If there should remain even one person who has not yet escaped suffering, I shall offer my own body as collateral to deliver them.

May all sentient beings, by virtue of my body, reach the end of suffering and attain peaceful happiness; may each of them delight in speaking words of truth, never deceiving one another, and never giving rise to harm.

I shall cause them to resolve upon the mind of omniscience, to depart from the objects of the five desires, and to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, ultimately abiding in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
Because these sentient beings are attached to desire, they fall under the domain of Māra and are censured by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

One should know that craving is the root of all suffering; for this reason, they engage in disputes and litigation, or wage war against one another, giving rise to various afflictions. Consequently, they later fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Furthermore, they sever the karma for rebirth in the heavens and distance themselves from the Buddhas; how then could they possibly give rise to the King of Unsurpassed Wisdom?

These sentient beings are submerged by desire and are scorched and boiled by immeasurable afflictions; through the dedication of my roots of goodness with impartiality, I cause all sentient beings to abandon them entirely, so that they may joyfully seek the Buddha-wisdom and attain the bliss of nirvana.
I shall act as their great guide, using the wisdom of skillful means to enable them to reach the other shore.

It is like the rising sun that illuminates the four great continents, causing all realms to become manifest: royal palaces, villages, towns, and cities; the comings and goings of people and the activities they perform; the ripening of crops and the flourishing of plants and trees.
The radiance and majestic virtue of the Sun Deity are uniquely transcendent in the world, certainly without equal.
In this same way, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, when a Bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness, they immediately form this thought:

"I shall rescue and protect all sentient beings; I shall liberate all sentient beings; I shall illuminate all sentient beings; I shall instruct and admonish all sentient beings; I shall lead all sentient beings to understanding; I shall gather in all sentient beings; I shall bring all sentient beings to maturity, causing them all to dwell in peace and sever all doubts."
"Furthermore, just as the solar disc appears in the world and its radiance shines everywhere without depending on anything else, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

appearing in the world to see sentient beings suffering, they provide rescue and protection without waiting for an invitation from others; there is not even the slightest root of goodness that is not dedicated toward awakening, using all sentient beings as their adornment."
Furthermore, the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva does not calculate the number of kalpas while seeking bodhi; from the root of birth and death until this day, the duration of time traversed is immeasurable."

Adorning oneself through many eons, even to the point of beholding a single Buddha and once giving rise to the mind of enlightenment—serving and making offerings to as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges without weariness—one is finally able to comprehend the mental activities of all sentient beings.
This is called the inexhaustible adornment of a bodhisattva.
By thus cultivating the dharma-factors of enlightenment through the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one is able to fully perfect the adornments of the primary and secondary marks.
Furthermore, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:

"The bodhisattva sees that sentient beings are blind and lack the eye of wisdom; they are stubborn and difficult to discipline, violating the precepts and being indolent, fully possessed of all manner of evils."
At that time, the Bodhisattva gave rise to a profound sense of weary detachment and sought rebirth in a Pure Land, vowing, "May I never hear the names of any evils.
Having formed this thought, he further reflected:
"These sentient beings are ignorant, mute, and lack the potential for Nirvana; they do not give rise to faith and remain far removed from all Buddhas. I shall subdue and rescue them."

When this thought is generated, all the palaces of Māra tremble, and the Buddhas of the ten directions praise him with one voice, saying: "This person will, before long, sit at the site of enlightenment and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Commentary states:
By thus contemplating and observing in gradual succession, one can increase an immeasurable accumulation of merit; this should be practiced with a straightforward, profound, and steadfast mind.
As stated in the *Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra*:
"In the Buddha-dharma, straightforwardness is the foundation.
If bodhisattvas lack a straightforward mind, they are far removed from all the Buddha-dharmas."

If one possesses a profound and steadfast mind, one will develop a yearning for the profound and wondrous Dharma never heard before; or, from within the sky, the mountains, forests, or among the trees, the sounds of the profound and wondrous Dharma will spontaneously emerge, leading to understanding and realization.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice in this way:
just as a person with feet is able to travel, so too a bodhisattva who possesses a sincere and profound mind is able to cultivate all the Buddha-dharmas.
Just as a person who possesses a body possesses a life span, so too a bodhisattva who possesses a sincere and profound mind can attain the enlightenment of all Buddhas.
Just as a person who possesses life possesses wealth and profit, so too a bodhisattva who possesses a sincere and profound mind can obtain the noble riches of all Buddhas.
Just as a great torch with its flames blazing brightly, a bodhisattva who possesses a sincere and profound mind can clearly understand all the Buddha-dharmas.
Just as when there are clouds, rain can fall, a bodhisattva who possesses a sincere and profound mind can proclaim the rain of the Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should understand that they must properly protect their own upright and profound mind.

Just as a tree cannot produce branches, leaves, flowers, or fruit if its roots are rotten, if a bodhisattva lacks an upright and profound mind, they will no longer grow in any wholesome dharmas, nor will they be able to attain the bodhi of all Buddhas.
The Compendium of Training for Bodhisattvas (Śikṣāsamuccaya), Fascicle Twenty, and Fascicle Twenty-One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the *Shanshi* (Court Music Master) of the Honglu, the Great Master of Buddhist Propagation, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Rìchēng, and others. Chapter Sixteen: The Remainder of the Section on the Increase of Supreme Power. The Treatise states:
What is meant by "profound mind that fully awakens"?
The *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, this mind is free from deception regarding all its activities; being free from deception means that it does not give rise to flattery."
One who does not give rise to flattery is able to attain certainty;
one who attains certainty eliminates deception and illusion.
Those who eliminate deception and illusion abide in purity;
those who abide in purity are always upright;
those who are always upright are free from crookedness.
One who is free from crookedness and deviousness does so because their nature is lucid;
one whose nature is lucid does so because they are skilled in awakening to and understanding [reality];
one who is skilled in awakening to and understanding does so because they have attained the truth.
That which has attained reality cannot be destroyed;
that which cannot be destroyed has attained firmness;
that which has attained firmness has attained immovability.
"One who attains immovability does not abandon sentient beings;
therefore, this is called the profound mind of awakening.
This sutra further states:

“Cultivating the most supreme and profound resolve, dwelling in tranquility, and covering all sentient beings with loving-kindness; honoring and respecting those who are virtuous, and compassionately rescuing those who are not;

acting as a protector for those without protection, a refuge for those without refuge, an island for those adrift, a sovereign for those without a sovereign, and a companion for those without a companion.”
To act as their companions; to cause those who are crooked and deviant to become upright; to cause those who are violent and cruel to become gentle and compliant;
to cause those who are sycophantic and flatterous to become impartial and honest; to cause those who are deceptive and fraudulent to become truthful and sincere;
to cause those who are treacherous and villainous to become pure and guileless; and to cause those who do not recognize kindness to come to recognize kindness. In [those who are...]
He brings peace to those who suffer; he provides benefit to those who lack it; he causes the arrogant to become humble;
he causes those who disparage others to offer praise; he provides instruction to those who err;
he acts as a protector for those without protection; and he perceives no fault in those who oppose him.
"Blame; one should give rise to pure conduct toward all teachers and elders, show respect with skillful means and an impartial mind, and remember and not forget their instructions.
The Commentary says:
When one thus gradually cultivates through a profound mind, one is able to increase superior power and bring forth the manifestation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
As it is said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:"
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva does not need to study many dharmas; if one upholds a single dharma, one will be able to thoroughly know all Buddha-dharmas.
This single dharma is what is called great compassion.”
If bodhisattvas are able to practice great compassion, they can grasp all the Buddha-dharmas as if they were in the palm of their hand.
World-Honored One!
It is like the wheel-treasure possessed by a universal monarch (cakravartin); wherever it goes, everything follows along with it.
“World-Honored One, it is just the same for a bodhisattva: when great compassion arises, they naturally attain all the Buddha-dharmas.
World-Honored One, it is like the rising sun illuminating the world, whereby all the activities and tasks of sentient beings are successfully accomplished.”
"Bhagavān, it is likewise for a bodhisattva: if they illumine all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) with great compassion, they become easy to cultivate.
Bhagavān, it is just as all the sense faculties, having the mind as their basis, are able to apprehend their respective objects."
When a bodhisattva dwells in great compassion, they practice each of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) individually and act in accordance with the truth.

World-Honored One, it is just as all other faculties exist in dependence upon the life-faculty; likewise, if a bodhisattva possesses great compassion, they are able to cultivate all the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Furthermore, the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"For example, just as a person's life-faculty has inhalation and exhalation as its basis,
so too, when a bodhisattva practices and studies the Mahāyāna, they take great compassion as its basis."
Furthermore, it is like a householder who has but one son; his affection for him is so deep that he never abandons him even for a moment.
When a bodhisattva attains great compassion, their love for all sentient beings is likewise like that of a parent for an only child.
The Commentary says:
How is this to be contemplated?
It means cultivating the mind through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), regarding all sentient beings with affection as if they were one's own children.

In past lives there were immeasurable sufferings and afflictions; in the present life there is the great ocean of the suffering of illness; and in the future there are the perils of long-term saṃsāra. As stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*:
"The classes of ignorant and deluded ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have had countless bodies that have already perished, are currently perishing, and will yet perish."

Having ceased in this way, they are unable to develop revulsion toward the body; instead, they further increase the machinery of manifold suffering. Following the stream of birth and death, they cannot escape or relinquish the clinging to the aggregates (*skandha*). They cannot distance themselves from the poisonous snakes of the great elements, nor observe the six sense bases as an empty village. They cannot sever the notions of "I" and "mine," nor extract the poisoned arrows of views and conceit. They cannot extinguish the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor shatter the darkness of ignorance. They cannot dry up the surging waves of craving, nor seek the Great Sage Teacher endowed with the ten powers. Entering the dense forest of error, they follow the faction of Māra, drifting solely upon the ocean of saṃsāra, wrapped in the thick membrane of the eggshell of ignorance, and constantly oppressed by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death.
I now act as a protector for all sentient beings out of compassion; having accumulated immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom, I cause all these roots of goodness to attain ultimate purity.
That sutra further states:

"These sentient beings gallop through the perilous and evil paths of birth and death—the realms of hell, animals, and Yama—obscured by the darkness of ignorance and lacking a great guide. They even sink into the eddies of the river of craving, transmigrating without leisure to contemplate the cessation of the thoughts of desire, ill-will, and harm. Having no means to abandon the habitual tendencies of greed, they are seized by the rākṣasa of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi). With the island of pride as their only refuge, they have no one to rely upon; unable to transcend the villages of the six sense bases, they lack even the slightest root of goodness with which to cross over."

Therefore, by the power of my great compassion, I shall now rescue those sentient beings, causing them to be liberated from suffering and hardship, to be free from defilement and to abide in tranquility, so that they may dwell securely upon the great jewel-island of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

These sentient beings are driven by and bound to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; they are fettered and constrained by the shackles of craving, and for a long time have been shrouded by ignorance, guile, and deception, seeking no escape from the prison of the three realms.
"I shall cause all to be liberated from various fears and manifest sufferings and afflictions, so that they may attain peace and security without hindrance.
The Commentary says:
Thus, through a firm and profound resolve toward others, one is able to increase the meritorious practice of great compassion.
Furthermore, the *Paramapraśna Sūtra* states:

"During the six periods of day and night, wearing fresh and clean robes, one should pay homage to all Buddhas with constant reverence and cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra in successive order."
Furthermore, the *Tripiṭaka-sūtra* states:
"By prostrating with one's head at the feet of all Buddhas in reverent salutation, one is able to repent of and eliminate all defilements of sin.
The 'Three Aggregates' refer to the merits of repentance, entreaty, and sympathetic joy."
Furthermore, in the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*, only the single benefit of making an exhortation is clarified: it unravels the snares of Māra and brings about the realization of impermanence.
Furthermore, one should equally practice respectful homage toward all Buddhas, as described in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra*.
Regarding the meritorious conduct obtained through the confession of both oneself and others, it is as explained in the four verses of the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*.
Regarding the practice of rejoicing in meritorious deeds, it is as explained in the "Chapter on Rejoicing" of the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*.
In other sūtras, these three types [of merit] are fully elucidated.
Next, the characteristics of the practice of vast offerings and dedication are clarified, as stated in the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*:

"If bodhisattvas, with flowers that have been produced, various incenses, sandalwood trees, kalpavṛkṣa trees, and jewel trees—even those without an owner or one who possesses them—direct their minds toward making offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, six times throughout the day and night."
Furthermore, the *Tri-samaya-sūtra* states:

"One should, for a long duration, direct the mind as previously described in offering all the jewel-mountains born of earth and jewel-mountains born of water found in the lands of the worlds of the ten directions; all sublime medicinal herbs; the most excellent food and drink upon pure waters; and all gold and jewels, up to the forest creepers, the essence of the earth, and the naturally fragrant rice—the most supreme and delightful objects of enjoyment—found in Uttarakuru."
The Commentary states:
Having heard as explained above regarding the vast approach, service, and offerings made to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others,
one should ultimately practice with a single mind according to the teachings, making vows and dedicating the merit.
As it is taught in the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*, the *Vajradhvaja-paripṛcchā*, or the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:

furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they bring forth ten kinds of vast vows, namely, serving and making offerings to all Tathāgatas, thereby accomplishing pure and superior resolve (*viśuddhādhimukti*).

With such modes of practice, equal to the realm of empty space and identical to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one shall perform great offerings without ceasing throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
This is the first great vow he undertakes:

desiring to receive and uphold the Dharma-eye taught by all Tathāgatas and to skillfully protect the true teaching of all Buddhas, throughout the entire realm of empty space and the equal nature of phenomena, for as many eons as reach the end of the future, he shall embrace the True Dharma without ceasing.
This is the second great vow that he undertakes:

to be among those who, when the Buddhas appear in the world, first dwell in the Tuṣita heaven, descend to take conception in a womb, remain there in the womb, are born, grow up, leave home to practice the ascetic path, sit at the site of enlightenment, subdue all Māras, turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma, and manifest the signs of parinirvāṇa—to first apply oneself with diligent effort to go and pay homage to them, and to simultaneously turn the supreme wheel of Dharma in all places.

Throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and for all kalpas extending to the end of the future, may all Buddhas who appear in the world be entreated to turn the wheel of Dharma without ceasing.
This constitutes the formulation of the third great vow.

It is for the purpose of eliciting the vast and immeasurable practices of all bodhisattvas, as well as the perfect purity of the non-conceptual *pāramitās*; and to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas so that they may resolve their minds upon awakening by correctly and unerringly revealing the general and specific characteristics, the similarities and differences, and the phases of formation and disintegration of the stages (*bhūmis*) encompassed therein.

Throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and for all kalpas extending to the limits of the future, one’s practice of the right path shall never cease.
This is the formulation of the fourth great vow.

Desiring to bring to maturity the realm of all sentient beings—those of the form and formless realms, those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those bound to the three realms and the six destinies; and those comprised within name-and-form—he causes them to be forever severed [from suffering]. He causes all categories of beings to enter into the teachings of the Buddhas, so that they may ultimately abide in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) without exception.

Throughout the entire realm of empty space, equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and for all kalpas extending to the limits of the future, one brings sentient beings to maturity without ceasing.
This is the formulation of the fifth great vow.

Desiring to enter into and understand the worlds of the ten directions—whether vast or narrow, coarse or subtle, inverted or upright, or abiding in chaotic disorder—each with distinct positions like the divisions of Indra’s net, they realize them through the manifestation of corresponding wisdom.

Throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and for all kalpas extending to the limits of the future, they are able to enter into and comprehend such worlds without ever ceasing.
This is the formulation of the sixth great vow.

Desiring to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields, one shall travel from one Buddha-field to another, universally illuminating and embellishing them with light; becoming free from all afflictions, one shall establish pure lands filled with sentient beings of great wisdom who universally enter the vast realms of all Buddhas, manifesting impartially according to the inclinations and aspirations of all sentient beings to bring them all joy.

Throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and for all kalpas extending to the limits of the future, as well as throughout the number of all Buddha-fields, may they be universally purified and adorned without ceasing.
This is the formulation of the seventh great vow.

Desiring to share the same intention as the assembly of great bodhisattvas to accumulate roots of goodness, to abide in the state of equality through the same objects of focus, to constantly encounter all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, to never be separated from them according to one’s wishes, to manifest the power of the Buddhas and awaken the mind in common with them, and furthermore to attain non-retrogressive supernormal powers so as to be able to travel to all worlds, to manifest bodies corresponding to those in the great assemblies, to delight in cultivating the correct practices of a bodhisattva, and to realize the inconceivable, wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna.

Throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and for all kalpas reaching the limits of the future, they continue to awaken to and enter the Great Vehicle alongside all bodhisattvas without ceasing.
This constitutes the formulation of the eighth great vow.

Desiring to mount and govern the bodhisattva practices of the non-retrogressive wheel, such that the actions of body, speech, and mind are never in vain; so that by merely briefly beholding their deeds, one attains certainty within the Buddha-dharma; and by merely briefly hearing their voices, pure faith is born, enabling the arousal of right wisdom and the eternal severance of afflictions.

May this body be like a great medicinal tree that relieves all suffering from disease, and like a wish-fulfilling jewel that aids all who are destitute, so that I may extensively benefit sentient beings by practicing the bodhisattva path.
Throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and for all kalpas extending to the limits of the future, they shall never cease from their practice.
This is the initiation of the ninth great vow.

In order to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in all worlds throughout the ten directions, one is able to manifest for those beings to be converted—whether they be one or many—their descent into the world, renunciation, attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment, turning of the great wheel of Dharma, and entry into parinirvāṇa; displaying the power of wisdom within the realm of the Buddhas, one causes all sentient beings to awaken universally in a single instant according to their respective inclinations, making a true dedication for the entire realm of sentient beings toward the sole, vast nirvana of Bodhi.
They all proclaim the essentials of the Dharma with a single voice, causing the minds of all sentient beings to be filled with joy.

By means of their supernormal powers, they are able to pervade all worlds; by manifesting great wisdom-power, they are able to establish all dharmas; and by manifesting great nirvana, they do not extinguish any of the conditioned activities of existence.

Throughout the entire realm of empty space, equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and for all kalpas extending to the limits of the future, they attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) without ceasing.
This is the bodhisattva’s arousal of the ten kinds of vast vows.
The treatise says:
Thus, with deep resolve and diligent application in visualization, one performs this dedication in all circumstances.
As it is said in the *Avalokiteśvara-vimokṣa-sūtra*:
“By dedicating all roots of goodness performed by me with equanimity, may all sentient beings be freed from the fear of falling;
may all sentient beings be liberated from the fear of attachment to kinsmen and loved ones; may all sentient beings extinguish the fear of ignorance;
may all sentient beings sever the fear of bondage; and may all sentient beings be free from the fear of death.”
...to cause all sentient beings to be free from the fear of poverty; to cause all sentient beings to be free from the fear of untimely death;
to cause all sentient beings to be free from the fear of slander; to cause all sentient beings to be free from the fear of saṃsāra;
to cause all sentient beings to be free from the fear of the majesty and power of the great assembly; and to cause all sentient beings to be free from the fear of all forms of death. To cause all...
May all sentient beings be freed from the fear of the evil realms; may all sentient beings be freed from the fear of darkness;
may all sentient beings be freed from the fear of encountering those they hate; may all sentient beings be freed from the fear of separation from those they love;
may all sentient beings be freed from the fear of hatred and envy; may all sentient beings be freed from the fear of physical and mental affliction; may all sentient beings...
"Severing sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, and fear.
Furthermore, this briefly clarifies the dedication of merit, as stated in a verse from the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra*:
"The pure and courageous Honored One Mañjuśrī, And Samantabhadra who has attained supreme excellence—likewise [is it for me]."
I shall follow and practice the dedication taught by those two Great Beings.
Regarding the pure teachings on dedication spoken by all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three times,
I now gather all roots of goodness, making them entirely identical to the supreme conduct of Samantabhadra.
17. Chapter on Paying Respect through Making Offerings. The treatise states:
This clarifies the sequence for paying respect to the various Buddhas and increasing one’s meritorious conduct; how should this be understood?
As a verse in the *Lokānuvartana-sūtra* says:
"If for even a single moment one serves the Buddhas,
the retribution I say they shall obtain is to be forever free from the eight states of no leisure."
Their physical form is most excellent, adorned with the marks of perfection;
dwelling securely within the Buddha-dharma, they are free from all indolence.
Such persons, in this present life, enjoy every abundance in full measure.
Always honored by the multitude, free from illness with a radiant body,
he was later born into a householder’s family, revered beyond compare.
He extensively practiced the giving of alms, possessing precious jewels without any stinginess.
Furthermore, he became a Wheel-Turning King, ruling over the four continents;
the people were all virtuous and compliant, and the lands were entirely prosperous and joyful.
He was fully endowed with majestic power and virtue, and his seven treasures were all most extraordinary.
By diligently practicing offerings at all times,
one will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; dwelling freely upon the summit of Mount Sumeru as Śakra,
Lord of Devas, one shall uphold the pure teaching.
If a person, at a stūpa of the Buddha, joins their palms and circumambulates it to the right,
they shall receive inexhaustible merit for ten million kalpas.
Furthermore, if one arouses the mind and pays homage at a stūpa of the Buddha, [the merit is likewise boundless].
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, they shall be free from congenital blindness, lameness, or paralysis;
by firmly establishing all roots of goodness and possessing courageous diligence,
they shall swiftly attain Bodhi— this is due to bowing at the Buddha’s stūpas.
If, in this evil age, one takes refuge in the Buddha even for a moment,
one has already drawn near to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas;
such a person is the most supreme and unsurpassed in the world.
A sovereign among men and sages, Of peerless and exquisite beauty;
If one offers a garland of flowers To a Buddhist stūpa,
Upon passing away from this human world, They will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Riding upon exquisite palanquins and carriages, adorned with rare jewels,
amidst palaces and towers, they are constantly surrounded by celestial maidens;
there are pure ponds and pools, overflowing with water of the eight virtues.
The ground is strewn with golden sand, and the banks are made of lapis lazuli and crystal;
they enjoy supreme and wondrous happiness, and their lives are all long-lasting.
When they pass away from this celestial realm, they are reborn into noble and wealthy families.
For hundreds of billions of kalpas, they receive supreme and boundless merit;
constantly offering exquisite flower garlands in every place,
they become universal wheel-turning monarchs and Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
The Devaputra Maheśvara and the World-Lord Mahābrahmā,
by virtue of making such offerings, attained the aforementioned merits.
Having offered exquisite, fine cotton cloth to the Buddha, the Great Guide, [they obtained these fruits].
Such a person shall achieve all goals and benefits within the world.
Furthermore, by taking garments and garlands and offering them as alms to a Buddha-stūpa,
one will leave behind low-born lineages and never again be born among them.
Surrounded by a constant retinue, free from the suffering of separation,
one shall always become a great king, receiving offerings and praise;
or one may be born among devas and nāgas, or as a wise person in the world.
Possessing courageous majesty and spiritual power, their meritorious retribution is peerless.

Whether it be a kingdom, a city, or a clan, if one offers even a small amount of incense— subtle as a mustard seed— at the stūpas and shrines of the World-Honored One, [the merit shall be immeasurable].
With a mind of resolute faith, one offers worship;
listen now as I describe the merit thereby obtained:
it forever leaves behind all defilements, being a firm and pure heart.
Free from illness, affliction, sorrow, and grief, with a countenance and deportment of supreme clarity and vigor,
he shall become a Wheel-Turning King, endowed with great wisdom and majestic power;
wherever he may go, his merit and strength shall be fully realized.
Whether they be kings or common people, all shall joyfully and constantly revere them.
By offering exquisite robes as gifts to the Buddha’s stūpas,
such persons, in their future lives, will possess limbs of extreme radiance and purity.
The celestial garments of the Kośika devas manifest simultaneously,
constantly emitting a pleasing fragrance that brings joy to all who hear it.
Furthermore, with golden threads, they weave together these most excellent robes.
Skillfully and well-arranged are the various forms of lions;
later, one is reborn among the gods, where no wish goes unfulfilled.
Precious jewels and various necklaces arise from the palm of the hand according to one's thought.
If a person offers a magnificent banner, suspended as a gift at a Buddha-stūpa,
they will be reborn in the lands of the various Buddhas according to their aspirations;
they shall obtain a golden-hued body, fully endowed with all the primary marks.
With various superior delicacies and all manner of sweet flavors, they all joyfully offered them as tribute.
Furthermore, with silks and cottons, fine furs and wool, and various precious garments,
as well as *tūla* and *kāśika* fabrics, they fashioned banners and offered them to the Buddha.
In their future lives, these people’s treasuries shall all be overflowing;

they will be free from the afflictions caused by their kin; possessing firm and immeasurable wisdom, they will be dignified and graceful in both upper and lower parts of their bodies, and the multitude will always look up to them with joy and reverence.
They will not be burned by fire, nor harmed by the infliction of swords and staves.
If one holds up a single lamp and makes an offering at a Buddha-stūpa,
by virtue of making such a gift, one shall obtain a long life.
With a pure mind and clear comprehension, their physical form is perfectly complete;
such a person, in a future life, will be born in the Pure Land of the Golden River.
With wondrous arms that emit radiance, they shall possess great and steadfast power.
Wandering through the world, they are free from all terrors.
Even if there were as many Buddha-fields as there are nayutas,
filled with mustard seeds such that their number could be known by weighing them—
I say that this karmic reward could not be exhausted even throughout an entire kalpa.
By holding up vast silk canopies and offering them to a Buddha stūpa,
such a person will before long attain the possession of the thirty-two marks.
He constantly emits wondrous radiance, incomparable and inconceivable;
That light is ever-bright and shimmering, as translucent as a river of gold.
Like *kusuma* flowers in full bloom, they intermingle as a decorative ornament.
His fame is universally pervasive; endowed with extraordinary supernormal powers, his enjoyments are boundless.
Having attained the highest peace and security, he is constantly approached and served by gods and humans alike.
Having few desires and possessing dignified deportment, Firmly upholding the pure precepts,
dwelling in the tranquil forest, Delighting in the cultivation of various meditative concentrations,
With wisdom that never diminishes, and never abandoning the bodhicitta.
Contented and free from longing, practicing loving-kindness with equanimity;
if one performs music as an offering to the Honored One among Men,
they will be freed from afflictions and sorrow, and attain the perfection of the mark of a sublime voice.
The eyes are exceedingly clear and bright, gazing with unwavering focus;
the ears constantly hear wondrous sounds, and the pure mind is as joyful as can be.
The nose is high, long, and straight, endowed with all majestic marks in their full perfection.
His tongue is ever supple and smooth, Red and lustrous like coral;
His voice is like that of a celestial being, Hearing a full *koṭi* of sounds.
Free from the foul retribution of being tongueless, He shall never again be born among snakes.
With a most supreme and excellent body, upright and free from lameness or curvature,
you constantly give rise to a virtuous and pure mind without even a moment’s interruption;
all devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and mahoragas [revere you].
"Wherever one travels through the world, one shall be comforted and protected.
By making such gifts as these, one obtains the aforementioned rewards of merit.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Proclaimed Grandee,
