"If there be a person who, after my parinirvāṇa, is able to repair and maintain the Buddha’s stūpas and temples,
for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas their towering physical marks will all be majestic and beautiful;
with the most supreme and pleasing sandalwood fragrance, they shall construct palaces and carriages."
Though they obtain superior rewards, they remain unattached; this is due to having repaired and adorned the Buddha’s stūpas.

When the Buddha’s true teaching is about to perish, they are not reborn in the various lands of Jambudvīpa, but dwell in celestial palaces according to their inclinations; this is due to having repaired and adorned the Buddha’s stūpas.
Repulsed by the defilements of the five desires, They dwell securely in the cool and pure aggregate of ethical discipline.
They cultivate the holy life extensively and universally; This results from applying fragrant ointment to the Buddha’s stūpa.
Having passed away from here, one is born in the heavens, where joy and abundance are immeasurable;
furthermore, one is able to transform and guide all devas and humans—this is due to offering scented ointment at the Buddha’s stūpa.
With a perfectly rounded countenance always radiant and joyful, the speech they utter gives rise to manifold virtues;
all who behold them conceive hearts of love and reverence—this is due to having offered scented ointment at the Buddha’s stūpa.
Far removed from the suffering of boundless evil realms, They constantly gain proximity to all Tathāgatas;
Extensively cultivating pure deeds to benefit all beings— This results from applying fragrant ointments to the Buddha’s stūpas.
If a person, for even a mere moment, is able to sweep away the dust and webs from a Buddha-stūpa, the retribution for such a person is difficult to measure:
they will forever leave behind the eight difficulties and be born where there are no hardships;
they will be courageous, wise, and fully enlightened, and the objects of the five desires will no longer pursue them.
One is always able to transcend all saṃsāra, This results from sweeping the Buddha’s stūpa with a pure mind.
Fully endowed with the prohibitive precepts without transgression, Hearing the profound and wondrous Dharma, one gives rise to joyful reverence;
Never regressing from the bodhicitta, This results from sweeping the Buddha’s stūpa with a pure mind.
Such a person, within this degenerate age, will always remain free from slander and all faults;
they will accumulate vast and supreme merit and wisdom, all because they purified their mind by sweeping the Buddha’s stūpa.
Obtaining delicacies of the finest flavors and adorned with exceptionally pure garments,
always experiencing sublime tactile sensations that satisfy all the faculties— this results from sweeping the Buddha’s stūpa with a pure mind.
If one gives rise to joy toward a Buddha-stūpa and is able to remove all withered flowers,
by relying upon the Great Guide endowed with the Ten Powers, one shall be freed from the deep enmity and harm of the five desires;
one’s physical form will be exceptionally sublime and rare in the world, such that the multitude delights in beholding it without weariness or aversion.
The king constantly gives rise to a heart of love and reverence, Because he removed withered flowers from the Buddha’s stūpa.
He is fully endowed with all the precepts of a bodhisattva, And has extinguished all perilous and evil paths;
His mind is always clear and far removed from delusion, Because he removed withered flowers from the Buddha’s stūpa.
Having cast off the afflictions and all obstructive defilements, one is forever free from the bonds of the suffering of illness;
one attains pliancy in all places by removing withered flowers from the Buddha’s stūpa.
One shall receive the foremost offerings among humans, And further, the most supreme of all honors;
Adorned with a body of pure merit and wisdom, This results from removing withered flowers from a Buddha stūpa.
Furthermore, if one takes fresh and exquisite flowers— whether *maṇḍārava* or *pāṭala*—
and exchanges them for those that have withered at a Buddha-stūpa, such a person shall obtain a most excellent reward.
If a person can, at the stūpas of the Buddhas, diligently join their palms and offer prostrations,
praising the virtues of the Buddha well, they shall cause all who see them to bow their heads; kings, ministers,
and commoners alike will develop faith and respect for them, as will devas, nāgas, spirits, and mahoragas.
Like a wondrous flower blooming in the world, you are able to skillfully expound the essentials of all dharmas;
because of that skillful exposition of the True Dharma, you abide in the Buddha’s wisdom without deficiency,
causing sentient beings to leave the evil realms behind and increasing their supreme benefit as humans and devas.
Fully endowed with the power of merit, mindfulness, and wisdom, their retinue is vast and always virtuous and compliant.
I declare that such persons in this world, according to their inclinations, possess peace of mind;
they constantly utter gentle and tranquil sounds, instructing all living beings so that they may attain liberation.
One does not give rise to craving for wealth or pleasure, because one has joined the palms in worship at the Buddha’s stūpa.
One is able to practice generosity and kind speech, as well as beneficial conduct and impartiality;
likewise, one does not give rise to anger when reviled by others, because one has joined the palms in worship at the Buddha’s stūpa.
Sometimes they go to the heavens as Śakra, or remain in the world as kings of men;
wherever they go, they possess mastery according to their will—all this results from joining their palms in worship at the Buddha’s stūpas.
Without attachment or defilement toward the objects of desire, Always content amidst worldly wealth and nobility,
Never falling into the miserable realms— This results from joining palms in worship at the Buddha’s stūpa.
The words they speak are rich in meaning and flavor, Always in perfect accord with the sūtras;
They are constantly born into noble families within the human world— This results from joining their palms in worship at the Buddha’s stūpa.

If, with a most supreme and pure mind, one takes a handful of flowers and scatters them upon the Buddha, the retribution obtained will be that of becoming a king; dwelling securely as before, he shall bring forth virtuous benefits.
Being able to clearly comprehend the five desires, he will not be oppressed by sorrow or affliction.
“His physical form is upright and majestic, a joy for all to behold; his nature is quiescent, and he is free from all fear.

Suppose there were someone who, for even a moment, could give rise to a single pure faith and mindfully recollect the Buddhas, holding a single flower and scattering it into the air as an offering; that person shall attain the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, Śakra Devānām Indra, or Mahābrahmā, and will immediately be able to transcend the ignorance of the past limit and the cycle of birth and death throughout future kalpas.
Ānanda! Let this matter rest for now.

Suppose there were someone who, even within a dream, could scatter a single flower into the air as an offering; I say that the limit of the merit and reward obtained by this person through such roots of goodness would be unknowable.
Furthermore, the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"If a bodhisattva draws near to the Buddhas, they will be able to obtain eight kinds of superior dharmas."

What are these eight? First, to transform sentient beings by causing them to behold the wondrous marks of the Buddha; second, to serve and make offerings to the Tathāgata; third, to praise the supreme virtues of the Buddha within the great assemblies; fourth, to keep the Tathāgata in mind and fashion his images; fifth, to exhort and transform sentient beings so that they are never separated from the Buddha; sixth, to constantly hear the name of the Buddha wherever one goes; seventh, to always aspire to be reborn in the lands of all Buddhas; and eighth, to have a will free from cowardice and to joyfully seek the wisdom of the Buddha.
"These are the eight kinds of superior dharmas.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, how do they increase the meaning of excellence?
This means that by performing acts of service toward the Buddha, one shall attain bodhi.
As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, the name of the Buddha is difficult to hear."
How much more so for those who gain proximity, Who forever sever all doubts and delusions.
The Tathāgata, the light of the world, Thoroughly penetrates all dharmas;
Universally generating merit throughout the three periods of time, He causes all beings to become completely pure.
The Tathāgata has appeared in the world as the great field of merit for all beings;
he universally guides all sentient creatures, causing them to accumulate meritorious deeds.
If there are those who make offerings to the Buddha, they will forever eliminate the fear of the evil realms.
Extinguishing all suffering, one accomplishes the body of wisdom.
If one beholds the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings and is able to give rise to the vast mind,
such a person will always encounter the Buddhas and increase the power of their wisdom.
This sutra further states:
"The Tathāgata, with great compassion, appears in the world;
for the sake of all living beings, he turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
Throughout countless kalpas, the Tathāgata has undergone diligent toil for the sake of sentient beings;
how could those in the various worlds ever repay the Great Teacher’s kindness?
It would be better to undergo the sufferings of the evil realms for immeasurable kalpas [than to fail to repay his grace].
Never shall I forsake the Tathāgata while seeking liberation;
I would rather dwell in the various evil realms And always hear the name of the Buddha,
Than be born in the good realms And for even a moment not hear the Buddha.
For what reason would you wish to dwell for long within all the evil realms?
By beholding the Tathāgata, the power of wisdom increases.
If one beholds the Buddha, all suffering is diminished and eliminated.
One is able to enter the realm of great wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
If one attains the vision of the Buddha, one abandons all obstacles,
nurtures inexhaustible merit, and accomplishes the path to Bodhi.
The Commentary says:

If even a momentary sight of an image yields such a reward, how much more so for one who personally beholds the physical form and marks of the Tathāgata and receives his instructions; the merit obtained is exceedingly great.
As stated in the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*:

"Mañjuśrī! If there were a son or daughter of good family who, for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, were to daily provide offerings of food of a hundred flavors and exquisite garments to as many pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all worlds; yet, [if another were to]..."

Mañjuśrī! If there should be another person who is able, even for a moment, to gaze upon and honor a single painted image of the Buddha and various scriptures, this merit would surpass the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas.

How much more so for one who joins their palms, offers a single flower, or a single incense or unguent, or even lights a single lamp as an offering; this merit surpasses the former by immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
The Commentary states:
This clarifies the increase of merit through skillful means (*upāya*).
As it is said in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*:
"If one is able to restore and maintain ancient stūpas of the Buddha, one shall obtain four kinds of pure great vows:

first, a most excellent physical appearance with no equal; second, upholding the sūtras with diligence and without weariness; third, being able to behold the Tathāgata in every place of rebirth; and fourth, being endowed with all the marks upon the body in one's future birth."
This sutra further states:

"If a person can reverently make offerings at a stūpa of the Tathāgata with various kinds of famous flowers and various types of fragrant unguents, they will further obtain eight kinds of non-decrease:

first, no decrease in physical appearance; second, no decrease in enjoyments; third, no decrease in retinue; fourth, no decrease in the precepts; fifth, no decrease in meditative concentration; sixth, no decrease in extensive learning; seventh, no decrease in wisdom; and eighth, no decrease in supreme vows."
Furthermore, as the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:

"Suppose sentient beings were to fill the three realms of existence, and each were to construct a stūpa for the Tathāgata, as high and vast as Mount Sumeru, and each were to offer various kinds of supreme and exquisite offerings for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
"If a bodhisattva, with a mind that does not abandon all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-citta*), offers a single flower as a gift to that stūpa, the mass of merit obtained will exceed even that.
This sūtra further states:

"Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were each to become a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*) abiding in the Mahāyāna, and each wheel-turning king were to take a vessel for oil as large as the great ocean and a wick equal in size to Mount Sumeru, and each were to thus make offerings to the Buddha’s stūpa; [the merit of one who offers a single flower with the thought of all-knowledge would still surpass it]."

If a renunciant bodhisattva can take a small amount of oil, apply it to a wick to make a lamp, and offer it to a stūpa or temple of the Tathāgata, the merit obtained will surpass that of the previous gift of lamps; the former does not equal even a hundredth part, a karoṭi-th part, or even an upaniṣad-th part of the latter.
Furthermore, while that Wheel-Turning Sage King may offer various articles of pleasure as alms to the assembly of monks before the Buddha,
if an ordained bodhisattva constantly practices begging for food and, having obtained some, shares it with those who see him, the merit he acquires is incomparably superior to the former.
Furthermore, if a Wheel-Turning Sage King were to heap up saffron robes as high as Mount Sumeru and offer them as a gift before the Buddha and his assembly of bhikṣus;

and if a renunciant bodhisattva were to take whatever surplus items they possess beyond their three robes and, according to the circumstances, offer them to the Buddhas present, to the community of bhikṣus established in the Mahāyāna, or to the stūpas of the Tathāgata—the merit obtained by the latter would be double that of the former offering.
Furthermore, if each of those Cakravartin kings were to offer every kind of exquisite and sublime flower filling all of Jambudvīpa as an offering to the Buddha’s stūpas;

yet if a renunciant bodhisattva were able to offer even a single flower to a stūpa of the Tathāgata, this would surpass the former offerings such that the former would not equal even a hundredth part, a *kalā* part, or even an *upaniṣad* part of the latter.
The Commentary says:
To explain the characteristics in detail, as stated in the "Chapter on Successive Transcendence":
"Once that renunciant bodhisattva has understood this, if they can make offerings to the Tathāgata in his presence, they will immediately obtain four kinds of virtuous merits:"

First, one constantly receives the highest honor and offerings; second, having seen them, one follows and trains according to their example; third, one is able to make the great bodhicitta firm and stable; fourth, one increases roots of goodness and manifests the vision of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Furthermore, the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "Moreover, Sāgaramati,
there are three kinds of dharmas that are called 'making offerings and serving the Tathāgata.'"
What are these three?
First, the arousal of the bodhicitta without regression; second, the ability to uphold all true dharmas; and third, the generation of great compassion toward sentient beings.
Furthermore, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will remain undefiled by the impurities of the womb."

What are these ten? First, creating images of the Tathāgata with pure faith; second, repairing the old stūpas and temples of the Buddhas; third, adorning them by applying various exquisite incenses; fourth, bathing the Tathāgata with fragrant waters; fifth, sweeping, sprinkling, and smearing the ground within the Buddha-stūpas; sixth, personally serving one’s own parents; seventh, personally making offerings to one’s preceptors and teachers; eighth, constantly providing for fellow practitioners of the holy life; ninth, practicing generosity without hoping for its reward; and tenth, through these roots of goodness, causing all sentient beings to be born unstained by the impurities of the womb.
"Good son! If one can be fully endowed with these ten dharmas, then one will be able to give rise to a profound mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the Great Vehicle, they should first give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
If these bodhisattvas are able to practice this conduct, they will attain non-retrogression in the Great Vehicle.”
The Buddha said:
"Kauśika! Suppose there were someone who could weigh the trichiliocosm; its measure could be known. However—"
"The merit obtained by these bodhisattvas through their resolve and sympathetic joy is beyond calculation.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If bodhisattvas, from their initial generation of the mind of awakening until they attain perfect and complete enlightenment, perform immeasurable roots of goodness through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) during that interval, yet [other] bodhisattvas neither hear of them, nor know of them, nor take them up, you should know that such persons are possessed by Māra.
The Buddha said:

“Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to swiftly realize the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, they should give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Mahāyāna.”
Furthermore, regarding the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they neither cling to them nor abandon them, yet they are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward them.

It should be known that such a person, in whatever place they are born, will always encounter the ten wholesome paths of action; they will obtain offerings, respect, honor, and praise, and among all forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles they perceive, nothing will be disagreeable to their mind. They will forever leave behind the evil realms and be reborn in the heavens.
Why is this? Because whatever this person does accords with their benefit, causing all sentient beings to attain happiness.

By means of these roots of goodness, they can cause immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of people to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*), whereby they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This sutra further states: "Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were to each resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and each were to practice the four dhyānas for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, abiding in tranquility and free from distracted thoughts."

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able, through skillful means, to gather and weigh together the concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation cultivated by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as all the morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle and the śrāvaka vehicle. Having thus collected and weighed these various roots of goodness, they rejoice in them all with a mind that is supreme, ultimate, most excellent, most wonderful, vast, immeasurable, and peerless. Furthermore, Subhūti, they dedicate these roots of goodness born of such rejoicing toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The merit obtained thereby surpasses the merit of the previous bodhisattva’s cultivation of meditative concentration; it cannot be compared, for it exceeds it by a factor of a hundred, a *kalā*, or even an *upaniṣad*.
The Commentary says:
This concludes the explanation of the merit of exhortation following the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
As stated in the *Paramapraśna Sūtra*:
"If one is able to uphold the True Dharma, then one has already protected the life-span of the Buddhas across immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields.
Chapter 18: Mindfulness of the Three Jewels. The Treatise states:
To clarify that virtuous conduct increases merit in successive stages, this cannot be obtained through any other cause; rather, one must constantly cultivate faith and the other [roots of virtue].
As it is said in the *Guhyamahāyānasūtra*:
“The Buddha said:
‘Great King!...’”

You should now know that there are four kinds of dharmas; if one can practice them according to principle, then one will abide securely in all the wholesome dharmas that lead toward the supreme path of the Mahāyāna, without any loss or decline.
What are the four? Great King,
the first is that faith enables one to proceed toward the supreme path.
Furthermore, what is meant by faith?
Because one possesses faith, one is able to accord with the lineage of the noble ones and refrain from all that ought not to be done.
Second, through reverence, one is able to turn toward the supreme path.
Out of respect, one listens attentively and receives the sublime Dharma spoken by the noble ones.
Third, being free from pride, one is able to advance toward the supreme path.
Because one is free from pride, one is able to pay respectful homage with faith to all those in the assembly of noble ones.
Fourth, diligence can lead toward the supreme path.
By means of diligence, both body and mind attain pliancy, and all wholesome dharmas one undertakes are brought to fulfillment.
The Commentary says:
This explains that which is constantly cultivated within faith; thus, it specifically clarifies the five faculties, beginning with faith.
As stated in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra*:
“What are the five faculties?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
What is the faculty of faith?”
It refers to having deep patience and aspiration for four dharmas:

first, practicing mundane right conduct within saṃsāra and having faith in karmic retribution; because one creates karma, its retribution will certainly exist, and thus one would never commit a transgression even at the cost of one's life.
Second, they have faith in and delight in the correct practice of bodhisattvas, seeking no other vehicle and following no views.

Third, within the ultimate truth, they understand the absence of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, or a person, and they are able to deeply believe in and comprehend all phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless.
Fourth, to give rise to resolute faith in the Buddha’s qualities, powers, and fearlessnesses, thereby severing the web of doubt—
this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). What is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?
If a dharma is embraced by the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), and one applies oneself to that dharma with diligence and without interruption, this is called the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*).
What is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
If a dharma is cultivated by the faculty of vigor, and one never forgets or loses that dharma, this is called the faculty of mindfulness.
What is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?
If a phenomenon is subsumed under the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), and that phenomenon is single-minded and undistracted, this is called the faculty of concentration.
What is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?
If a dharma is subsumed within the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), such that this dharma is self-observed and not understood through another, it is called the faculty of wisdom.
When these five faculties arise in continuous succession, they are able to bring all Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, one should constantly cultivate the dharmas such as the power of faith.
As the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra* states:
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s purity of vigorous practice?

It means that one has no timidity regarding the sense faculties; all evil Māras cannot disturb or confuse them; śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot cause them to regress; and all afflictions cannot destroy them. Thus, they are able to firmly abide in the Mahāyāna, fulfilling their long-held vows with a pure mind and courageous vigor, while secretly guarding the faculty of the body to attain supreme purity.”
The Commentary says:
Thus, by constantly cultivating the faculties and powers such as faith, the merit of the practice of loving-kindness increases.
As a verse in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* states:
"Within nayuta-billions of Buddha-fields, all the various implements for making offerings to the Buddhas,
even if used entirely to worship all the Tathāgatas, do not equal even a small fraction of a single thought of loving-kindness."
The Compendium of the Bodhisattva’s Training (Śikṣāsamuccaya), Fascicle Twenty-two and Fascicle Twenty-three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Subject Rìchēng, a Grand Master of Buddhist Propagation (Xuánfàn Dàshī) and Junior Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù Shǎoqīng), who was conferred the purple robe. Chapter 18, Part 2: Contemplating the Triple Gem. The Treatise states:
By means of faith and other [faculties], one is able to take the merits of the Buddhas as an object of contemplation.
As stated in a verse from the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"I prostrate to the True Golden-Hued Tamer, Whose face is like the full moon, pure and stainless;
Whose merit and noble wisdom are truly inconceivable, And who has no equal within the three realms of existence."
The Sage’s conch-like topknot is deep azure-blue, Lofty, prominent, and pure as Mount Sumeru;
The tuft of hair between his brows shines forth universally, While his uṣṇīṣa is invisible to all beholders.
The Tathāgata’s eyes are pure like blue lotuses, Compared to the kumuda flower, the conch, and the moon;
With compassion he gazes upon all sentient beings— Therefore, I now prostrate and pay homage to him.
The Tathāgata’s tongue is copper-colored in appearance, long and broad enough to cover his face;
he proclaims the Dharma of ambrosia to moisten all living beings—for this reason, I now bow my head in worship.
The Tathāgata’s forty teeth are even and closely set, pure white, firm, and sharp as vajra;
they utter words of truth that radiate brilliance—therefore, I now prostrate in worship.

The Tathāgata’s physical marks are most extraordinary; his majestic light shines brilliantly across hundreds of thousands of lands, such that all the radiance of Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and the various devas can no longer be seen.
The Tathāgata’s calves surpass those of the deer king; his chest is as broad and expansive as that of a lion.
As he gazes down and walks with steady grace like an elephant king, the great earth, its mountains and rivers, all tremble.
The physical marks of the Tathāgata are most sublime and majestic; Resplendent like golden light and lustrous, they are peerless among all worlds;
Sentient beings who behold them never grow weary of or abandon them.
In the past, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the Tathāgata was able to give away all that he cherished;
out of compassion and pity for all sentient beings, I now prostrate and pay homage to him.
The Tathāgata’s aspiration is to cultivate all the perfections; his morality, generosity, patience, and diligence are virtuous and firm;
his meditative concentration and supreme wisdom are perfectly clear and bright; therefore, I now prostrate in homage to him.
The Tathāgata roars the lion’s roar amidst the assembly; With valor he can crush all heterodox arguments.
The defilements of the three poisons are exhausted without remainder; Therefore, I now prostrate and pay homage to him.
The Sage’s three karmas transcend the three realms of existence, Like a lotus flower unsullied by water;
With the pure and wondrous voice of the kalaviṅka bird, I now prostrate myself before him with full reverence.
Knowing that the world is entirely an illusion, like an actor changing his form and color,
or like a mirage and a dream, it is devoid of self, devoid of person, and devoid of a life-principle.
The Dharma is fundamentally empty and quiescent, without arising; unable to awaken to this, beings wander along with the stream.
With great compassion, you universally guide all who are deluded, skillfully proclaiming the True Dharma according to their capacities.
Observing the various sufferings and afflictions of the world, Which are perpetually entangled by the many diseases of greed and the like,
The Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Great King of Physicians, Applies specific remedies for each, causing them to be liberated.
Manifesting birth, old age, death, grief, sorrow, and suffering, As well as the various afflictions such as separation from what is loved—
The Muni protects and delivers the world, Causing all to feel weary of and detached from them, so that they may be utterly severed.
In the perilous and evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, all sentient beings revolve according to the wheel;
out of compassion for those who have no kin and no teacher of the Way, you point them toward the path of truth so they may ascend it.
The Buddhas of the past appeared in the world, And with sovereign mastery proclaimed the profound meaning of the Dharma;
In this same way, the World-Honored One speaks as they did, Causing all sentient beings to realize the Path of the Sages.
The Buddha’s voice is deep and far-reaching, surpassing that of Brahmā; its resonance is moist and crystal clear, giving rise to manifold virtues.
The musical sounds produced by the gandharvas and kinnaras all fade into insignificance before it.
Having accumulated all pure merits and proclaimed boundless words of truth,
hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings, upon hearing them, each gave rise to the aspiration for the three vehicles.
If one can make offerings to the Tathāgata, One shall obtain supreme and wondrous happiness;
Wealthy, noble, and sovereign, revered by all, One will later become a monarch in this world,
Or a Wheel-Turning King who governs the four continents, Fully endowed with the seven extraordinary treasures.
Constantly benefiting sentient beings through the ten wholesome paths, they give rise to pure karma by means of the Tathāgata.
Some become lords of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, some kings of Yāma or Tuṣita,
even reaching the Mahābrahmā of Paranirmita-vaśavartin— all this is due to making offerings to the Tathāgata.
Having thus beheld the Buddha and made offerings to him, and having conceived faith and reverence for the Dharma they have heard,
they are all able to forever sever the causes of suffering and realize the peace that is free from defilement.
The World-Honored One thoroughly understands what is the path and what is not the path;
He is able to cease evil and cause all to return to goodness, Enabling all sentient beings to attain auspiciousness, And causing them all to dwell securely in the Noble Path.
If a person seeks merit by making offerings to the Buddha, they will constantly obtain an inexhaustible treasury of supreme merit,
immeasurable throughout millions of eons, until they eventually realize the fruit of enlightenment.
The subtle and wondrous land is most excellently adorned, as delightful as the Heaven of Others' Emanations;
dwelling therein by the power of their vows, their physical, verbal, and mental actions are ever pure.
Such various and wondrous fruits of merit all arise from making offerings to the Tathāgata;
though such a person dwells within the world, they experience the bliss of the dragon palaces and the heavens.
The Tathāgata possesses vast renown, heard and known throughout all buddha-fields;
amidst infinite assemblies, the Buddhas of the ten directions all offer praise.
Forever free from all worldly afflictions, Manifesting peerless great compassion,
Supreme tranquility, honored among men— Therefore, I now prostrate in homage.
Having now attained the five supernormal powers, I stand in the void and offer praise:
I bow my head to the courageous Great Teacher, who discerns all phenomena as pure and stainless.
Now, in this great assembly of devas and humans, I extol the manifold virtues of the Sugata;
may all these vast and supreme fields of merit together bring all sentient beings to perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:

"Moreover, noble son, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are adorned with great merit and wisdom; they take great compassion as their sphere of activity and serve as protectors for all worlds. Acting as great physicians who skillfully extract the poisoned arrows [of affliction], they dwell perpetually in the sublime samādhi of quiescence, remaining unattached to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa."
Even toward all sentient beings, he acts like a father and mother; with a heart of great compassion, he regards the entire world with impartial pity, being without fault.
Through his corresponding wisdom, he serves as a light for the world, surrounded by sentient beings of great intelligence, whom all people always delight in serving.

They distance themselves from personal pleasure and extinguish the suffering of others; they uphold the True Dharma, take the Dharma as their master, and attain mastery over the Dharma. They take the Dharma as their food, the Dharma as their medicine, and the Dharma as their gift, relinquishing everything.

Discerning with wisdom and never being heedless, he acts as a bridge over perilous and difficult places; like the royal road, it is level and free of obstacles, such that even his pure physical body never tires those who behold it.
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess such immeasurable merits; I shall accomplish all those benefits.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the Buddha.
What is the recollection of the Dharma?

"The Bodhisattva clearly understands that the boundless merits of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are all born from the Dharma, transformed by the Dharma, obtained through the Dharma, preeminent because of the Dharma, existing because of the Dharma, having the Dharma as their sphere, relying upon the Dharma, and accomplished through the Dharma; even all worldly and supramundane matters of happiness are likewise born from the Dharma and accomplished through the Dharma."

Therefore, as I seek the Bodhi of all Buddhas, I should respect the Dharma; I should rely upon the realm of the Dharma, the refuge of the Dharma, the certainty of the Dharma, the steadfastness of the Dharma, and the practice of the Dharma.
This is called the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the Dharma.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should preach the Dharma to all sentient beings with equanimity; because the Dharma has no high or low, my mind is equalized with that Dharma.
The Dharma does not preach by approaching from the front; because the Dharma has no factionalism, my mind is equal to that Dharma.
The Dharma does not preach according to temporal seasons; because the Dharma is inwardly realized within the mind, my mind is equal to that Dharma.
The Dharma is not taught for the superior nor withheld from the inferior, because each person is capable of entering into and understanding it; thus, my mind is equanimous toward that Dharma.
The Dharma is not taught for the sake of purity, nor is it taught for the sake of impurity; because the Dharma is free from defilement, my mind is equanimous, being identical with that Dharma.

Furthermore, this Dharma is not taught for the sake of the noble ones, nor is it not taught for the sake of ordinary beings; because the Dharma is free from all views, my mind is equalized with that Dharma.

The Dharma is not taught only by day and not taught at night, nor is it taught only at night and not by day; because the Dharma is constantly sustained by its own power, my mind is equal to that Dharma.
The Dharma is neither disciplined nor transgressed, for the Dharma is without grasping or attachment; I am equal to that Dharma, my mind being equanimous.
The Dharma neither diminishes nor increases, for the Dharma is like space; I am equal to that Dharma, my mind being equanimous.
The Dharma does not weary of sentient beings, and sentient beings are able to protect the Dharma; I am identical to that Dharma, and my mind is equanimous.
The Dharma does not seek a place of refuge, yet it serves as a refuge for the world; I am identical to that Dharma, and my mind is equanimous.
The Dharma is free from harm and affliction, for the Dharma is devoid of the characteristics of being harmed; I am equal to that Dharma, and thus my mind is equanimous.
The Dharma is free from enmity and jealousy, for the Dharma is free from all fetters and latent tendencies; I am equal to that Dharma, and thus my mind is equanimous.
The Dharma neither fears saṃsāra nor delights in nirvāṇa, because the Dharma is free from conceptual discrimination; my mind is equal to that Dharma.
When a bodhisattva thus accumulates right mindfulness in this way, it is called "mindfulness of the Dharma."
What is the recollection of the Saṃgha? Regarding this, it is further said: "They are those who teach the Dharma;

those who practice the Dharma; those who contemplate the Dharma; those who are fields of merit for the Dharma; those who uphold the Dharma; those who rely upon the Dharma; those who make offerings to the Dharma; those who act in accordance with the Dharma; those whose sphere is the Dharma; those whose domain is the Dharma; those who have accomplished the Dharma; those whose nature is upright; those whose nature is pure; those who follow instructions; those who give rise to great compassion; those whose sphere is the wisdom of discernment; and those who constantly cultivate pure and white dharmas."
The Commentary states:
When a bodhisattva contemplates the Saṃgha in this manner, they are able to accomplish the true merits of all sentient beings.
As a verse in the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra says:
"Sometimes they manifest old age, sickness, and death, bringing all sentient beings to maturity;
yet they understand these things to be like illusions and transformations, attaining unimpeded penetration.
Sometimes they manifest the conflagration at the end of an eon, wherein heaven and earth are all set ablaze."
The multitude harbors the notion of permanence; he illuminates them so they may know impermanence.
Countless billions of sentient beings all come together to invite the Bodhisattva;
arriving at his dwelling at once, he transforms them and leads them toward the Buddha-way.
Whether it be the scriptures, incantations, and arts, or the various crafts and skills,
they manifest the practice of all these things to benefit all living beings.
Regarding the many paths and dharmas of the world, they renounce the home life within them all.
By this, one resolves the delusions of others and does not fall into false views.
Sometimes one becomes a deity of the sun or moon, or the Brahmā King, lord of the world;
at other times one becomes earth or water, or again, wind or fire.
In kalpas of pestilence, he manifests as various medicinal herbs;
those who take them are cured of illness and their many toxins eliminated.
In kalpas of famine, he manifests his body as food and drink.
First one rescues them from hunger and thirst, and thereafter instructs people with the Dharma.
When there are weapons and warfare in an eon, one gives rise to compassion for their sake;
transforming all those sentient beings, one causes them to abide in the ground of non-contention.
If there should be a great battle array, he establishes them with equal strength;
the Bodhisattva manifests his majestic power to subdue them and bring about peace and harmony.
Within all lands, wherever there are places of hell, [he brings relief].
I immediately go there to deliver them from their suffering.
Throughout all lands where animals devour one another,
I manifest birth among them all to bring them benefit.
Manifesting the enjoyment of the five desires, yet also appearing to practice dhyāna,
he causes the mind of Māra to be confounded, so that it cannot find an opportunity.
For a lotus flower to grow amidst fire— this may be called truly rare.
To practice dhyāna while remaining within the realm of desire is likewise a rare occurrence.
Sometimes she manifests as a courtesan to attract those who lust after beauty;
first drawing them in with the hook of desire, she later leads them into the wisdom of the Buddha.
Sometimes acting as a leader of a village, or serving as a guide for merchants,
or as a national preceptor or a great minister, he brings benefit and protection to sentient beings.
To all those who are poor and destitute, he manifests as an inexhaustible treasury.
I therefore exhorted them, causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
To those whose minds were arrogant, I manifested as a great strongman to subdue their pride and cause them to abide in the Unsurpassed Way.
To those who are fearful, he stands before them to offer comfort;
first bestowing fearlessness upon them, he later inspires them to resolve for the Way.
Or he manifests as one free from lust, appearing as a seer endowed with the five supernatural powers.
He guides and instructs all sentient beings, causing them to abide in precepts, patience, and loving-kindness.
Seeing those who require service, he manifests as their servant;
having gladdened their hearts, he then inspires in them the mind of the Way.
According to whatever they require, they are enabled to enter the Buddha-way;
by the power of skillful means, he is able to provide for them all sufficiently.
Thus the Way is immeasurable, and its practice has no limit.
His wisdom is boundless, delivering countless multitudes.
Even if all Buddhas were to praise his merits for countless billions of eons, they would still be unable to exhaust them.
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the merit of making offerings, as stated in a verse from the *Ratnaprabhāsa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*:
“Emitting great light, adorned with garlands, Various subtle and wondrous clouds of garlands like an ocean—
Such exquisite garlands pervade everywhere, Performing the Buddha-work through vast offerings.”
Emitting great radiance adorned with fragrance, A vast ocean of clouds of various subtle perfumes;
Such wondrous scents pervade everywhere, Performing the work of Buddhas through this vast offering.
Emitting great light adorned with flowers, A vast ocean of clouds of various subtle and wondrous blossoms;
Such exquisite flowers pervade everywhere, Performing the work of a Buddha through this expansive offering.
Emitting great light adorned with necklaces, a wondrous ocean of clouds of various necklaces,
such necklaces pervading everywhere, performing the Buddha-work of vast offerings.
Emitting great radiance, he manifests jeweled banners, Adorned with alternating patterns of blue, yellow, red, and white;
Composed of various kinds of rare treasures, They serve to adorn the Buddha-field.
The colors of the mani-jewel nets intermingle and reflect one another;
Countless silk banners are suspended as canopies, And hanging pearl necklaces proclaim the Buddha’s voice, Adorned and covering the Tathāgata above.
Making offerings to a single Tathāgata, one brings forth all manner of ornaments from the palm of one's hand;
it is the same for immeasurable Buddhas—this is the samādhi of sovereign manifestation.
The power of your supernormal knowledges is wondrous and inconceivable; you are extensively able to transform and benefit all sentient beings.
Through the supreme samādhi of miraculous transformations, you manifest hundreds of thousands of gates of skillful means.
The gateway of making offerings to all Tathāgatas, The gateway of generosity that relinquishes everything,
The gateway of ethical discipline through the virtues of *dhūta* practices, The gateway of patience that is inexhaustible and immovable,
The gateway of diligence through tireless and heroic exertion, And the gateway of meditative concentration abiding in tranquility.
The gate of supreme wisdom that penetrates all meanings and purposes; The gate of pure cultivation of the brahma-faring and supernormal powers;
The gate of joy through practicing the four means of attraction; The gate of accumulating merit and wisdom to benefit others;
The gate of liberation through the Four Truths and dependent origination; The gate of the excellent path through the cultivation of the faculties and powers.
Awakening to the gate of liberation of the Śrāvaka vehicle, Contemplating the pure gate of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
Cultivating the gate of spiritual transformations of the Supreme Vehicle; Sometimes manifesting the gate of impermanence and suffering,
Thoroughly understanding the gate of selflessness and the absence of a life-principle, Practicing the contemplation of impurity to depart from greed.
The gate of samādhi of true, eternal bliss— Through such various gates of skillful means,
Equally and universally shared with all sentient beings, All are able to realize that gate of liberation.
Manifesting in various forms to respond to the capacities of all beings, your miraculous powers and preaching of the Dharma are inconceivable;
you bring sentient beings to maturity in accordance with their needs, so that each may give rise to love and respect and abide in peace and happiness.
Constantly contemplating the causes for renouncing the world, he sought to realize the pure samādhi;
whenever famine or various hardships arose, he provided for all according to their needs.
He is extensively able to compassionately pity all sentient beings, freeing them from all sorrow and fear so they may always be at peace and secure.
With the most excellent and sublime food and drink, various garments, and diverse treasuries,
as well as kingdoms, cities, and all that is dear to him, he is able to relinquish everything, performing great acts of giving within those worlds.
Some manifest physical forms of supreme distinction, adorned with various ornaments and majestic power;
with skillfully applied perfumes and multitudes of flower garlands, their towering features are peerless.
Such complexions and deportments cause each person, upon seeing them, to delight in gazing upon and honoring them.
For their sake, he manifests the sound of the Dharma through skillful means, universally causing all living beings to resolve upon the Way.
He may manifest the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, the sounds of the kumbhīra and the kunāla, or the exquisite drum-sounds of the kiṃnaras;
from all these, he expounds the meaning of the Tathāgata’s liberation.
That which the Buddha proclaimed upon appearing in the world— The eighty-four thousand treasuries of true Dharma—
Such classifications of the various Dharma gates All bring benefit to sentient beings.
Whether manifesting suffering or joy, or performing deeds that are beneficial or harmful,
they guide beings according to what is appropriate to inspire their resolve, and are able to practice and act together with them in all such ways.
If one sees various obstacles, perils, and calamities, Or diverse oppressions that are difficult to endure,
One should, with a courageous and great compassionate heart, Take upon oneself the suffering for the sake of those sentient beings.
In places where there was no Dharma of liberation, nor any forest-dwelling renunciation,
through the power of the king’s merit, he caused them all to give rise to pure faith.
If one is freed from the bonds of craving for household life, One thereby transcends the causes of the world;
Having utterly eliminated all objects of desire, Such a person is an illuminator of the world.
If one can be fully endowed with all virtues, Such a person is called a Great Being who practices the Dharma;
Able to cultivate all the wondrous deeds of the Muni, That person shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
Where their lifespan is vast and beyond measure, Experiencing supreme and wondrous joy as they eliminate all delusions.
Birth, old age, and the suffering of illness cannot invade him; he attains mastery amidst impermanence.
He reveals the various faults of greed and hatred, which burn and scorch incessantly;
likewise, he manifests the four marks of existence to cause all deluded beings to awaken.
The Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses, And the eighteen unique qualities—
I now praise and vow to take refuge in them, May they constantly bring benefit and welfare to the world.
Just as various illusory beings Can manifest a multitude of forms,
So too does the Tathāgata appear in the world, Displaying transformations through his supernormal powers.
Able to employ skillful and expedient means to extensively bring benefit to all sentient beings,
their pure intention is inconceivable, like a lotus flower rising above turbid water.
Sometimes they manifest playful discourse and words, adorned with necklaces and dancing in turns;
displaying various arts for all to behold, they reveal that all forms and appearances are like illusions.
Sometimes he is the leader of a village, camp, or settlement; sometimes he is a householder or a merchant;
sometimes he is a prime minister or a high official, a great sage whose eloquence in debate is peerless.
Sometimes he becomes a great tree in the wilderness; sometimes he becomes an inexhaustible treasury of precious jewels.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem that provides whatever is needed, it acts as a guide for those who have lost their way.
It manifests various activities and crafts, such as diverse paintings and works of art,
and the bustling pursuit of cultivation and planting, so as to lead them to realize that this world is not a place for long-term dwelling.
Sometimes manifesting as enemies or kin without hatred or affection, causing all to dwell in peace and attain auspiciousness;
thoroughly mastering medical prescriptions to save all living beings, and skillfully teaching and showing them the Way of the Muni.
Some expound the supreme Dharma of the Muni, universally causing devas and humans to leave behind delusion;
they cause those who have left the home life in heterodox paths to resolve their minds and turn toward omniscience.
Thus these non-Buddhist practitioners of asceticism, who constantly observe silence like the Gautamas,
who are naked, Jains, or called śramaṇas, each able to rely upon and follow the teachings of their own masters.
Some constantly maintain the practice of self-sacrifice, holding it to be supreme and unsurpassed;
others observe the vows of the long-tufted youth with braided hair, each able to rely upon and follow the instructions of their venerable teachers.
Some scorch their bodies with the five heats; some observe the prohibitions of dogs, oxen, and the like;
some are constantly clad in deer skins; each is able to rely upon and honor the instructions of their venerable teacher.
Some constantly delight in celestial wisdom, where there is neither good nor evil, nor even cause;
subsisting only on roots, fruits, and clear springs, each is able to rely upon and honor the teachings of their master.
Some squat or stand on one foot; some lie upon thorns or smear themselves with ashes.
Holding their staffs to keep the mind from wandering to other objects, each is able to rely upon and honor the instructions of their teacher.
Even unto each and every non-Buddhist practitioner, who is able to cultivate ascetic practices with fierce intensity—
I transform them so that they may forever sever the causes of suffering, causing them all to seek liberation with a profound mind.
Thus, all the various divergent views in the world arise from relying upon teachers;
now, in order to guide those followers of false paths, I shall reveal the true meaning of the Tathāgata.
Some expound the subtle phrases of the Mahāyāna; some proclaim the phrases of secret mantras;
some manifest direct and explicit phrases; some delight in the phrases of celestial speech;
some employ phrases that analyze through letters; and [some utter] the adamantine phrases of definitive, wondrous meaning.
With wisdom, he subdues all heterodox arguments; he abandons and turns his back on unrighteous discourse.
At times he reveals the phrases of human vidyā-mantras; at times he manifests the supreme and wondrous phrases of the devas.
[He also manifests] the phrases of the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and bhūtas.
The words spoken by the kinnaras, garuḍas, and mahoragas—
each is able to comprehend their speech and proclaim the Tathāgata’s Dharma of liberation.
That is to say, by realizing the true meaning, one’s mind becomes resolved within the Buddha-dharma;
this state of linguistic wisdom, a realm of marvelous inconceivability, is the supreme samādhi.
It is said that by attaining those samādhis, one is able to radiate pure light everywhere;
that light gathers and transforms beings according to their capacities, causing them to attain pliancy and constant tranquility.
Some emit a light named "Excellent Vision," Through which sentient beings receive illumination and give rise to faith;
They are all able to observe the causes of manifold virtues, And become fully endowed with the unsurpassed wisdom that is never in vain.

Once this radiance has shone everywhere, one beholds the boundless Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as well as the Tathāgata’s reliquaries and the various sacred traces; each and every one is extolled and honored with offerings.
Again, he emits a light named "Victorious Lamp," its brilliance so dazzling that nothing can compare;
desiring to adorn and purify the world, it is able to shatter all darkness within even the finest atoms.
Having illuminated sentient beings with that light, each held up a lamp as an offering;
they made inconceivable offerings to the Tathāgata and further bestowed many lamps as gifts.
Whether with lamps of ghee or oil, Or with pine resin, bamboo, or reeds,
Even lamps made of various fragrances and wondrous jewels— Having offered these, may I receive the prediction of enlightenment from Dīpaṃkara.
Again, he emits a light named "Summoning," which is able to awaken and gather all sentient beings;
through this instruction of those deluded multitudes, they are liberated from the ocean of craving within saṃsāra.
Thus, having universally illumined with the light of loving-kindness, may each and every sentient being attain awakening;
may they forever be freed from the four torrents, and manifest the constant peace and joy that dispels all sorrow and affliction.
The Compendium of the Bodhisattva’s Training (Śikṣāsamuccaya), Fascicle Twenty-three and Fascicle Twenty-four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu...
The Imperial Commissioner of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Grand Master of Dharma Xuanfan, recipient of the purple robe, proclaims: "Wherever there are roads and rivers, Those who can construct bridges, causeways, and rafts,
Universally benefiting and bringing joy to all sentient beings, And praising tranquility to inspire joyful awakening."
He emits a great light named "Eliminating Thirst and Craving";
this light awakens all sentient beings, causing them to abandon the five desires and focus exclusively on seeking the profound and wondrous Dharma of liberation.
If one can abandon the five desires and focus exclusively on seeking the profound and wondrous Dharma of liberation, [one shall attain it].
Thus, he is able to rain down the Buddha’s nectar, universally extinguishing all thirst and craving in the world;
he provides gifts of ponds, wells, and flowing springs, and diligently seeks the path of unsurpassed Bodhi;
he reviles the five desires and praises meditative concentration—therefore, his light is named "Extinguishing Thirst and Craving."
He emits a great radiance named "Transformation-Maker"; this light can awaken all sentient beings, causing those who see it to long for the Buddha’s bodhi.
They resolve their minds to realize teacherless wisdom and fashion images of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, adorned with all the marks and seated upon lotus thrones.
Constantly praising the supreme virtues of the Buddha, this light is therefore named "Beloved.
It emits a great radiance called "Joy," which can awaken all sentient beings,
causing their hearts to delight in the Buddhas, to delight in the Dharma, and to delight in the Sangha.
If one’s mind always delights in the Buddhas, And likewise delights in the Dharma and the Sangha,
Then, within the holy assembly of the Tathāgata, One will attain the profound *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*,
Awakening immeasurable sentient beings, Universally causing them to keep the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha in mind.
And demonstrating the meritorious conduct of generating the bodhicitta— therefore, this light is named "Joyful Delight.
It emits a great radiance called "Accumulation of Merit," which can awaken all sentient beings,
causing them to practice various forms of giving and to seek the unsurpassed path through these vows.
He established a great assembly of offerings without restriction, satisfying all who came to beg so that their hearts felt no lack;
for this reason, this light is named "Accumulation of Merit."
He emits a great light named "Endowed with Wisdom"; this light can awaken all sentient beings.
It brings understanding of many dharmas within a single dharma-gate, and in a single kṣaṇa, it brings comprehension of many dharma-gates.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he analyzes and explains them, definitively and thoroughly knowing their true meaning.
He is well able to extensively explain without diminution; therefore, this light is named "Possessing Wisdom.

He emits a great radiance named "Lamp of Wisdom"; this light can awaken all sentient beings, causing them to know that the nature of sentient beings is empty and quiescent, and that all phenomena are non-existent.
Phenomena have no sovereign and are primordially empty, Like illusions, mirages, and the moon in water;
They are also like dreams and reflections— Therefore, this light is named the Lamp of Wisdom.
He emits a great light named Dharma-Sovereignty; this light awakens all sentient beings, causing them to attain inexhaustible dhāraṇīs.
They fully uphold the treasury of all Tathāgatas and respectfully make offerings to those who uphold the Dharma, serving and protecting them as they would sages.
Bestowing various teachings upon sentient beings, Therefore, this light is named Sovereignty of Dharma.

It emits a great radiance named Endowment of Renunciation; This light awakens stingy sentient beings, Causing them to know that all wealth is impermanent, So that they may delight in practicing generosity without parsimony.

Skillfully taming those who are stingy, Understanding that wealth is like a dream or a floating cloud, They increase their pure mind of generous giving; Therefore, this light is named "Possessing Renunciation."
He emits a great light named "Remover of Heat," which awakens those who have violated the precepts,

causing them all to abide securely in pure morality. It inspires them to resolve to realize untaught wisdom and encourages all sentient beings to uphold it, keeping the ten paths of wholesome action ever pure.
Furthermore, they cause [beings] to set their minds upon Bodhicitta; therefore, this light is named "Heat-Dispelling.

It emits a great light named "Adorned with Patience," which awakens those who speak much anger, causing them to eliminate resentment and pride, so that they delight in practicing patience and remain ever gentle.
Sentient beings are violent and evil, yet he practices patience with difficulty; for the sake of Bodhi, his mind remains unshaken.
He extols the merit of supreme patience; therefore, this light is named "Adorned with Patience."
He emits a great light named "Diligent Valor"; this light awakens those who are indolent, causing them to always revere and make offerings to the Triple Gem without weariness.
If they always revere and make offerings to the Triple Gem without weariness, [they shall attain liberation].
Thus one can transcend the realms of the four Māras, Swiftly achieve the unsurpassed Bodhi of a Buddha.
Exhorting all sentient beings to arouse diligence, Constantly extending offerings to the Triple Gem,
And single-mindedly protecting and upholding the Dharma when it is about to perish— For this reason, this light is named "Diligent Valor."

He emits a great light named "Tranquility," which can awaken those with distracted minds, causing them to distance themselves from greed, hatred, and delusion. Their minds become unshakable as they dwell in right concentration;
they abandon all evil associates and all meaningless talk or defiled conduct.
Praising meditative concentration and the forest hermitage, this light is therefore named "Tranquility.
Emitting a great radiance named "Wisdom-Adornment," this light awakens the ignorant and deluded,
causing them to realize the Truths and understand dependent origination, so that their faculties and wisdom are all fully realized.
If one can realize the Truths and understand dependent origination, And if all faculties and wisdom are fully mastered, Then one attains the *Sūryapradīpa* Samādhi;
With the radiance of wisdom, one achieves the fruit of Buddhahood.
Able to relinquish kingdom, wealth, and even oneself, One seeks the True Dharma for the sake of Bodhi.
Having heard it, he expounded it extensively for the multitude; therefore, this light is named "Adorned with Wisdom.
A great radiance is emitted named "Buddha-Wisdom"; this light awakens all sentient beings, causing them to see immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, each seated upon a precious lotus flower.
Praising the Buddha’s majestic virtue and liberation, Expounding the Buddha’s sovereign supernormal powers,
Revealing the Buddha’s inconceivable and wondrous strength— Therefore, this light is named "Buddha’s Wisdom."
He emits a great light named Fearlessness; when this light touches them, all terrors are removed.
Whether struck by non-humans or bound by them, all calamities and misfortunes are caused to be extinguished.
Bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings, he is able to stop all afflictions and harms whenever they are encountered.
He rescues those in distress, the orphaned, and the destitute; therefore, this light is named Fearlessness.
He emits a great radiance called Tranquility; this light can illuminate those who are ill, causing all their pains and afflictions to be removed, so that they all attain the bliss of supreme samādhi.
Bestowing excellent medicines to save all from affliction, With wondrous jewels and life-prolonging incense smeared upon the body,
And various foods and drinks surging forth from the palms— Therefore, this light is named "Peaceful Security."
He emits a great light named "Beholding the Buddha," which awakens those who are about to die;
according to their recollections, they behold the Tathāgata, and at the end of life, they attain rebirth in that Pure Land.
Seeing those approaching death, he exhorts them to mindfully recite the Buddha’s name, and further displays sacred images for them to gaze upon with reverence.
Causing them to take deep refuge and look up to the Buddha, this light is therefore named "Beholding the Buddha.
It emits a great radiance named "Delighting in the Dharma," which can awaken all sentient beings,
causing them to always rejoice in the True Dharma by hearing, reciting, and transcribing it.
When the Dharma is about to perish, one is able to expound it, causing those who seek the Dharma to have their minds fulfilled;
by loving the Dharma and diligently practicing it, this light is therefore named "Delighting in the Dharma."
He emits a great light named "Wondrous Sound," which awakens all bodhisattvas;
it causes every sound within the three realms to be heard as the voice of the Tathāgata by those who hear it.
With this great resonance, they praise the Buddha and offer bells, chimes, and various musical instruments.
Causing the sound of the Buddha to be heard throughout the world, this light is therefore named "Wondrous Sound.
It emits a great radiance called "Nectar," which awakens all sentient beings,
causing them to abandon all heedless conduct and to fully cultivate all meritorious virtues.
Conditioned phenomena are not secure, being entirely filled with immeasurable suffering and affliction;
because one always delights in praising the bliss of nirvana, this light is named "Amṛta" (Nectar).
He emits a great light named "Most Supreme," which awakens all sentient beings,
causing them to universally hear from the Buddha the superior dharmas of precept, concentration, and wisdom;
they constantly delight in praising the Great Muni’s supreme precepts, supreme concentration, and supreme wisdom.
Thus, for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed path, this light is named "Most Victorious.
It emits a great radiance called "Jeweled Adornment," which can awaken all living beings,
enabling them to obtain inexhaustible treasuries of jewels, and with which they may make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
By offering various kinds of supreme and wondrous jewels to the Buddha and his stūpas,
and by likewise bestowing gifts upon the poor and destitute, he has attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Fragrant Adornment," which can awaken all sentient beings;
those who hear it find their minds filled with joy, and they will certainly attain the merit of Buddhahood.
Adorned with the exquisite fragrances of humans and devas, they shall make offerings to the Supreme Lord of All.
Furthermore, by constructing stūpas and images of the Buddha, one attains this radiance.
A great light named "Exquisite Adornment" is emitted, with countless jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies;
incense is burned, flowers are scattered, and various musical instruments are played, filling both the interior and exterior of cities and towns.

By means of the sounds of subtle and exquisite music, and with various adornments such as diverse fragrances, wonderful flowers, banners, and canopies, they made offerings to the Buddha; therefore, they have attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Adornment," Which makes the earth level like the palm of a hand, Adorning the Buddha-stūpas and their sites; For this reason, he attains this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Great Cloud," Which is able to spread densely to rain down fragrant water.
Because he sprinkled fragrant water upon the Buddha-stūpas, he has attained this radiance.
He emitted a great light named "Ornament," which caused those who were naked to obtain fine garments;
because he gave as gifts exquisite objects for adorning the body, he has attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Supreme Flavor," Which enables those who are hungry to obtain fine food;
By bestowing gifts of various rare delicacies, He has therefore accomplished this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Supreme Wealth," Causing those who are destitute to obtain treasuries of jewels;
By bestowing inexhaustible goods upon the Triple Gem, He has thus attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Eye," Able to enable the blind to see all forms.
By offering lamps to the Buddha and the Buddha-stūpas, one thus achieves this radiance.
Emitting a great light named "Pure Ear," it enables those who are deaf to hear clearly;
by performing music as an offering to the Buddha and the Buddha-stūpas, one thus achieves this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Nose," through which he can now smell all fragrances never before heard;
because he offered incense to the Buddha and the Buddha’s stūpas, he has thus attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Tongue," Which can eliminate coarse, evil, and unwholesome speech;
Because he praised the Buddha with beautiful sounds, He has therefore attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Body," which causes those with impaired faculties to become complete;
because he prostrated his body before the Buddha and the Buddha’s stūpas, he has thus attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Intention," which causes those who have lost their minds to regain right mindfulness;
through the power of mastery in the cultivation of samādhi, he is thus able to accomplish this radiance.
He emits a great light named Pure Color, Causing all to behold inconceivable and wondrous forms;
Because he offered exquisite flowers to the Buddhas and their stūpas, He has thus attained this radiance.
They emit a great light named "Pure Sound," Contemplating that sound arises dependently like an echo;
Thoroughly understanding that the nature of sound is originally empty, They thereby achieve this radiance.
He emits a great light named Pure Fragrance, Causing all that is foul and impure to become fragrant and clean;
Because he bathed the Buddhas and their stūpas with scented water, He has therefore attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Taste," Which can eliminate all poisons within flavors;
By constantly making offerings to the Buddha, the Sangha, and his parents, He has therefore attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Touch," which can cause all hard textures to become soft.
Spears, lances, swords, and halberds rain down from the sky, yet he causes them all to transform into exquisite flower garlands;
for in the past, upon the roads, he had smeared them with fragrant unguents, scattered flowers, and spread out garments.
Because he welcomed and honored the Tathāgata while treading upon him, he has attained this radiance.
He emits a great light named "Pure Dharma," which causes all the pores of his body to expound inconceivable and wondrous Dharma-gates; those who hear it all rejoice and attain liberation.
Self-nature is unborn, arising from conditions; The nature of phenomena is eternally abiding, equal to space.
To realize that the Buddha-body is the Dharma-body— It is for this reason that this radiance is attained.
Such gateways of light as these, As numerous as atoms, beyond measure, All emerge from the pores of the Great Sage; The deeds they perform are each distinct.
Just as the light emitted from a single pore, Is as vast as the number of atoms in space, so too are all others.
All the pores are likewise so; this is the power of the Great Sage’s samādhi.
Just as he has cultivated all merits, according to his past conditions and shared in pure conduct, now he emits such radiance; this is the Great Sage’s mastery over wisdom.
In the past, we together cultivated supreme meritorious deeds; We were able to give rise to love and joy, and all rejoiced together.
What is done now is likewise so; Therefore, this radiance has been attained.
If there are those who personally cultivate various meritorious deeds, repeatedly making offerings to the Buddhas,
and constantly and diligently seek the virtues of the Buddhas, they are awakened by this radiance.
For example, though one born blind does not see the sun, it is not said that the sun does not arise in the world;
all those with eyes perceive it clearly, each engaging in their respective activities accordingly.
The radiance of the Great Being is likewise: those with wisdom all behold it, while ordinary people, those of false faith, and those of inferior understanding cannot perceive this light at all.

The maṇi palaces and celestial carriages, polished and adorned with exquisite jewels and divine incense—all these are spontaneously present through supreme merit; they cannot be inhabited by those lacking virtue.

The radiance of the Great Being is likewise: those with profound wisdom all receive its illumination, yet when the ignorant and foolish—possessing false faith and inferior understanding—enter [this realm], none are able to be struck by this light.
If there are those who hear of these distinctions of light And can give rise to pure, profound faith and understanding,
They will forever sever all webs of doubt And swiftly perfect the banner of unsurpassed merit.
Furthermore, he manifests the supreme samādhi, With his retinue and adornments all sovereign;
Throughout all lands in the ten directions, He is surrounded by assemblies of the Buddha's sons.
There is a wondrous lotus flower adorned with light, Its magnitude equal to the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system;
His body sits upright, completely filling it, Manifesting the supernatural power of this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are as many adorned with exquisite jewel lotuses as there are atoms in ten lands;
the sons of the Buddhas dwell therein—this is the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi.
Having accomplished virtuous causes and conditions in past lives, and having fully cultivated the merits of a Buddha,
he is thus surrounded by this assembly, all of whom join their palms and gaze upon him without weariness.
Entering samādhi within the body of a youth, he arises from concentration within the body of a man in the prime of life;
entering samādhi within the body of a man in the prime of life, he arises from concentration within the body of an old man;
entering samādhi within the body of an old man, he arises from concentration within the body of a laywoman.
Entering samādhi in the body of a female lay devotee (*upāsikā*), he arises from concentration in the body of a male lay devotee (*upāsaka*);
entering samādhi in the body of a male lay devotee, he arises from concentration in the body of a bhikṣuṇī;
entering samādhi in the body of a bhikṣuṇī, he arises from concentration in the body of a bhikṣu.
Entering samādhi within the body of a bhikṣu, he arises from concentration in the bodies of those in training and those beyond training;
entering samādhi within the bodies of those in training and those beyond training, he arises from concentration in the bodies of pratyekabuddhas;
entering samādhi within the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, he manifests in the body of a Tathāgata and arises from concentration.
The Tathāgata enters samādhi within his own body and arises from concentration within the bodies of the devas;
he enters samādhi within the bodies of the devas and arises from concentration within the bodies of the great nāgas;
he enters samādhi within the bodies of the great nāgas and arises from concentration within the bodies of the yakṣas.
Entering samādhi within the body of a yakṣa, he emerges from meditative concentration within the body of a bhūta;
entering samādhi within the body of a bhūta, he emerges from meditative concentration within a single pore;
entering samādhi within a single pore, he emerges from meditative concentration within all pores.
Entering samādhi through all pores, Arising from concentration at the tip of a single hair;
Entering samādhi at the tip of a single hair, Arising from concentration at the tips of all hairs;
Entering samādhi at the tips of all hairs, Arising from concentration within a single atom.
Entering samādhi within a single atom, Arising from concentration amidst all atoms;
Entering samādhi within all atoms, Arising from concentration at the adamantine limit;
Entering samādhi within the adamantine limit, Arising from concentration amidst mani-jewels.
If the Maṇi-jewel enters samādhi, he arises from concentration within the Buddha’s radiance;
if he enters samādhi within the Buddha’s radiance, he arises from concentration within the element of water;
if he enters samādhi within the element of water, he arises from concentration within the element of fire.
If one enters samādhi within the element of fire, one emerges from meditative concentration within the element of wind;
if one enters samādhi within the element of wind, one emerges from meditative concentration within the element of earth;
if one enters samādhi within the element of earth, one emerges from meditative concentration within a celestial palace.
If one enters samādhi within a celestial palace, And arises from concentration in space with an undisturbed mind,
This is called the inconceivable liberation, The samādhi of sovereign merit.
All the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions could not exhaustively describe them even in immeasurable kalpas;
all the Tathāgatas together proclaim that the karmic retributions of sentient beings are like the transformations of dragons.
The Buddhas possess sovereign and great supernormal powers, as well as inconceivable entry into meditative concentration;
while the Hearers dwell their minds in the eight liberations, they can manifest many bodies from a single body,
and again manifest a single body from many bodies, entering the fire-concentration within the midst of empty space.
If even one who lacks great compassion and does not seek the Buddha-way for the sake of sentient beings can manifest this inconceivable feat, how much more so those who bring vast benefit?
Just as the sun and moon travel through the void, their light pervading all places throughout the ten directions,
appearing in springs, ponds, marshes, and water in vessels, and manifesting in all rivers, seas, and precious waters.
The physical form of the Bodhisattva is likewise so: universally manifesting throughout the ten directions in an inconceivable manner.
All of this is the power of mastery over samādhi, which only the Tathāgata can directly realize.
In the ocean there is a deity named Good Sound; his voice universally accords with the sentient beings of the sea, making all their speech eloquent and clear, causing them all to rejoice.
If that deity, though still possessing greed, anger, and delusion, is yet able to skillfully understand all forms of speech,
how much more so could one with the sovereign power of dhāraṇī fail to bring joy to the multitude?
Just as a master illusionist, skilled in the arts of illusion, Can manifest boundless and ingenious feats,
Showing in an instant the passage of days, months, and years, And cities abundant and full of great peace and joy—
Though the illusionist possesses greed, hatred, and delusion, He can still, through the power of illusion, delight the world.
How much more so for one liberated in the various dhyānas and samādhis—how could such a person not cause the multitudes to rejoice?
Rāhu, the asura, manifested his power, standing upon the adamantine foundation in the midst of the ocean;
though the seawater was deep, it submerged him only to his waist, while his head stood level with Mount Sumeru.
If even those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion can manifest such great supernormal transformations,
how much more so for the Lamp that Illumines the World, who has conquered Māra— could he lack sovereign and majestic spiritual power?
When the devas and asuras were engaged in battle, Śakra, possessing sovereign supernormal power, manifested bodies equal in number to his own host so that he was peerless;
