the asuras then thought: "Śakra Devānām Indra is coming toward me."
They will surely seize my body with its fivefold bonds, Because of this, that host is filled with grief and fear.
Śakra manifests his body with a thousand eyes, Holding a vajra from which flames erupt;
Clad in armor and bearing a staff, he is full of majesty; Seeing him from afar, the asuras all retreat and submit.
Since even by the power of a mere trifling merit one can thus destroy great enemies,
how much more so for one who delivers all beings— how could such a one not be sovereign over their own virtues?
Just as the wind raises clouds and brings down great rain, it can also extinguish all vapors,
ripen all crops, and bring peace and happiness to all living beings.
They cannot study the pāramitās, nor do they study the various merits of the Buddhas, yet they still accomplish inconceivable deeds;
how much more so those who have fully perfected all their vows?
The Commentary states:
Whatever actions a bodhisattva performs are all for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
Apart from this general principle, there are specific explanations regarding the causes for increasing merit, as stated in a verse from the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:
"If all Bodhisattvas, having adorned themselves with incense and flowers, offer them to the Tathāgata and to the Buddha stūpas and temples,
they dedicate these merits, vowing that all sentient beings may be free from the defilement of broken precepts and attain the fragrance of the Buddha's morality."
With pure scented water, sweep, sprinkle, and smear the ground; dedicating this merit,
may all sentient beings leave behind improper conduct, cultivate virtuous methods,
and become disciplined and perfect.
And with this offering, I dedicate these merits, wishing that all sentient beings may be freed from the heat of afflictions.
May all sentient beings enter the city of Nirvana. When departing from the monastery, [I pray thus].
Giving rise to such a thought, may I cause all sentient beings to transcend the prison of birth and death.
Just as one opens a door or a window, giving rise to such a thought, may I cause all sentient beings to open the gate of noble wisdom.
If closing doors or windows, one should give rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings close the gates to the evil realms.
When sitting down in a peaceful manner, one should give rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings sit upon the field of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)."
When lying on the right side, he gives rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings dwell securely in nirvāṇa.
When rising from his reclining position, he gives rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings be free from the hindrances of entanglements and obscurations."
If one goes to relieve oneself, one should give rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings proceed upon the path to Great Enlightenment.
While actually relieving oneself, one should give rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings extract the arrows of the three poisons."
When washing [the body], one should give rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings wash away the defilements of affliction.
When washing the hands, one should give rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings be freed from defiled and turbid karma."
When washing the feet, one should give rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings be freed from the dust and grime of obstructions.
When chewing the tooth-stick, one should give rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings abandon all defilements and stains."
Whatever wholesome deeds are performed by the body, I dedicate them all for the benefit and peace of all sentient beings.
And at the stupas and temples of the Buddha, they give rise to such a thought:
"May all sentient beings always be honored and revered by humans and devas."
The Compendium of Bodhisattva Training, Fascicle Twenty-four and Fascicle Twenty-five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Subject Nichijō, a Grand Master of the Propagation of the Dharma and Junior Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, who was conferred the purple robe. Chapter Eighteen, Part Four: Contemplating the Triple Gem. The Treatise states:
When Bodhisattvas encounter various difficult circumstances due to causes and conditions, they apply correct mindfulness as an antidote so that no fear arises.
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should encounter the peril of ferocious beasts, he gives rise to neither agitation nor distress, nor does he feel any fear."
Why is this? This bodhisattva reflects thus:
"For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I shall relinquish everything."
If any predatory beasts wish to devour me, I shall give myself to them, so that I may swiftly bring the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) to completion.

I vow that when I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), my land shall be pure, and even the names of such evil insects and beasts shall not be heard there.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to agitation or distress, nor experience fear, even amidst the perils of hostile bandits. Why is this? "
If this bodhisattva is able to relinquish everything he possesses,
he then forms this thought:
"Should any enemies or bandits come seeking what they require, I shall give it to them."

Even if one were to rob me of my life-force, my physical, verbal, and mental actions would remain free from anger and resentment; thus, I shall swiftly fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) and attain the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
"May it be that when I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, my land shall be pure, and even the names of such enemies and bandits shall not be heard there.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva encounters the hardship of thirst and exhaustion, they likewise have no fear.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has attained the benefit of the Dharma and is free from sorrow and affliction.
He then formed this thought:
"I shall now proclaim the essential Dharma for all sentient beings to sever their craving.

Even if this body of mine should be overcome by thirst and reach its end, I will again give rise to great compassion in future lives; lamenting that these sentient beings have meager merit and are thus reborn once more in this hardship of waterlessness, I shall cause them to cultivate right practice and perfect supreme wisdom, thereby enabling them to fulfill the perfection of diligence."
May it be that when I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, my land shall be pure, and even the name of such thirst and deprivation shall not be heard there.
The sentient beings therein shall be fully endowed with merit, and the water of eight virtues shall exist spontaneously.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to fear or alarm amidst the calamity of famine. Why is this? "
This bodhisattva dons the armor of diligence, firm and without weariness, and forms this thought:
"These sentient beings are currently suffering from famine; they are deeply pitiable."

May I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and may my land be free from even the name of famine; may the sentient beings I transform be contented and at peace, experiencing natural happiness like that of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; may all their desires appear immediately according to their minds, and may they possess firm life-spans and dwell in tranquility.
The Commentary states:
Such actions as these can increase vast causes of merit, and the supreme state is likewise the same.
As stated in the *Vimala-sūtra*, if one practices the gift of Dharma without generating expectations, the superior retribution obtained therein is seen in the *Gambhīracittānuśāsana-sūtra*.
If a person does not crave fame or material gain and is able to practice the gift of Dharma, they will obtain twenty kinds of meritorious qualities of a compassionate mind:
first, abiding securely in right mindfulness; second, being able to give rise to awakening; third, setting out upon the supreme path;
fourth, upholding all virtues; fifth, increasing the life of wisdom; sixth, attaining transcendence from the world.
1. Wisdom; 2. Elimination of the fault of greed; 3. Elimination of the fault of hatred; 4.
Elimination of the fault of delusion; 5. Māras finding no opportunity; 6. The empowerment of all Buddhas; 7. Protection by all devas; 8.
A radiant and lustrous complexion; 9. Non-humans and evil friends being unable to gain access.
Fourteenth, one is always loved and respected by virtuous friends and spiritual teachers;
fifteenth, one’s speech is truthful; sixteenth, one attains fearlessness; seventeenth, the mind is always joyful and serene;
eighteenth, one’s good reputation spreads abroad; nineteenth, one possesses clear memory and never forgets; twentieth, one always delights in the Dharma.
Giving. This is called the merit of a compassionate mind.
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Suppose a śrāvaka were to universally expound the Dharma of the śrāvakas for all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, teaching it exactly as he has realized it, so that they all attain the fruit of arhatship.

Ānanda! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can use phrases and meanings associated with the perfection of wisdom to reveal and explain them for even a single sentient being, this surpasses the merit obtained by all sentient beings in the three thousandfold world system who have realized arhatship.
"Furthermore, regarding the merit accumulated by those arhats through their practice of generosity and observance of the precepts—what do you think?
Is this not great? Ānanda replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so.”
“Sugata! The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

Although that merit is great, it does not equal the merit of a bodhisattva who, for the sake of others, expounds this Dharma-gate associated with the perfection of wisdom; the latter's merit surpasses the former.

Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to analyze and explain this profound Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā for others within a single day, or even if they skillfully proclaim it for a single moment, a single hour, or a single *muhūrta*, [they shall obtain vast merit].
Ānanda! Such Dharma-giving by that bodhisattva cannot be compared with the roots of goodness possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
"This is because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, regarding the gift of Dharma, as stated in a verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"At times, the bodhisattva enters a quiet chamber and, with right mindfulness..."
Contemplating the Dharma according to its meaning,
one provides seats upon the pure ground; having anointed the body with oil and washed away all impurities,
one dons fresh, clean garments, so that both internally and externally one is entirely pure.
Seated upon the Dharma throne, he teaches according to the questions asked.
To the bhikṣuṇīs as well, he removes their sense of remorse and regret, as well as thoughts of indolence;
free from all sorrow and affliction, he preaches the Dharma with a compassionate heart, teaching constantly by day and by night.
The unsurpassed Way of the Buddha,
through various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables, is revealed and shown to sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
Regarding food, drink, medicine, and so forth, within these things, one harbors no expectations; rather,
with single-minded devotion, one contemplates the causes and conditions for expounding the Dharma, vowing to attain the Buddha-way and to cause all beings to do likewise.
"This is indeed a great benefit; it is a peaceful and joyful offering.
This sutra further states:
"Because one accords with the Dharma, one speaks neither too much nor too little; even for those who deeply love the Dharma, one does not speak excessively."
Furthermore, a verse in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* says:
"If an elder asks a question, And you wish to offer the gift of Dharma, You should first say to them: 'I have not studied extensively.'"
Furthermore, he spoke thus: "The Venerable One is most wise;
how could one dare to speak rashly before such a Great Virtue?
When speaking, do not be hasty; you must discern whether the listener is a fit vessel or not."
Once you have discerned their faculties, you should preach even without being asked.
If, amidst the great assembly, you see those who violate the precepts, do not praise the observance of the precepts;
rather, you should praise such practices as generosity.
If one sees those with few desires who are endowed with the observance of precepts,
one should give rise to a heart of great compassion and praise their fewness of desires and their keeping of the precepts;
having found such excellent companions, one may then praise the observance of the precepts.
The Commentary states:

A Dharma teacher such as this should bathe and put on fresh, clean robes; cultivating his person with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he should expound [the teaching] for the assembly, so that no *māra* can find an opportunity against him.
As seen in the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the dhāraṇī is as follows: "Tadyathā:
śame, śamāvati, śamidāsthu, aṅkuri, marajiṭi, grā—"
1. Niḥ 2. Ki-yu-li 3. U-kha-va-ti 4. U-hu-ka-ya-ti 5. Vi-śu-dha-ni 6. Ni-rma-ri 7.
Ma-ra-pna-ye 8. U-kha-ri 9. Kha-ru-gra-se (Note: The transliteration follows the standard IAST conventions for Indic scripts.)
15. *prasaṃ* (ā) 16. *hi-mukhe* 17. *a-mukhe* 18. *śvetani-sarvatrāgāra-hamadhāni* 19. *kṛhīta-sa*
Ṛvaparāvartana vi-mukta-mārapakṣa svabhāva-buddha-mūrdhna samudgati-ta.
“Sarvamāra-āttṛptadānapariśodhaya-vigaccha sarvamārakarmāṇi. The Dharma-preacher shall perform the recitation using this mantra.
Having done so, he takes his place upon the Dharma-seat and, surveying the entire assembly with a mind of vast compassion,
should conceive of himself as a King of Physicians, regard the Dharma as medicine, view those who listen to the Dharma as patients,
perceive all Tathāgatas as true sages, and regard the Eye of the True Dharma as something to be made long-enduring.

By means of this mantra, when one manifests its application and explains the Dharma of the True Principle as is appropriate, at that time, within a radius of one hundred *yojanas* on all sides, none of the hosts of Māra-devas will be able to come and perform demonic deeds;
even if the various Māra-kings should arrive at the site of the Dharma assembly, they likewise will be unable to create any obstacles or difficulties.
The treatise states:
Such impartial giving of the Dharma can increase the great bodhicitta.
As it is said in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*:
“Mañjuśrī! It is like the trees and their foliage, which grow lush and abundant, all because they depend upon the four great elements for their growth. Mañjuśrī!”

In this way, the bodhisattva gathers all roots of goodness through various gateways, encompassing them all within the bodhicitta and dedicating them toward omniscience for the sake of increasing enlightenment.
The treatise says:

If bodhisattvas, desiring to extensively demonstrate the training in the sphere of the Buddhas, first abide in right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samprajanya*), they will thereby be able to accomplish the right abandonments (*samyak-prahāṇa*) and heedfulness (*apramāda*). This means that by initiating diligence and aspiration, they guard against the arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states; they completely sever those evil and unwholesome states already arisen so as to bring about purification; they cause unarisen wholesome states to arise; and they further increase those wholesome states already arisen.
To always abide in heedfulness is the root among all wholesome dharmas.
As a verse in the *Candrapradīpa Sūtra* says:
"Regarding the wholesome dharmas as I have taught— namely, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and patience..."
"Taking heedfulness as its root—this is called the supreme wealth of the Sugata.
What is meant by heedlessness?
It refers to that which arises from vain pursuit of false teachings and evil companions.

It is like a person carrying a vessel filled to the brim with medicine for the king to drink, traveling along a perilous and slippery path; one should know that such a person is filled with terror and anxiety—how could they have any heedlessness?
Furthermore, the *Tathāgataguhyasūtra* states: "What is non-negligence?
It refers to being able to first restrain and harmonize the sense faculties."
When seeing forms with the eye and so forth, one does not grasp at their signs nor become attached to their beauty; this applies likewise up to the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*).
Having understood this, one neither grasps nor becomes attached to anything, does not give rise to defiled craving, and constantly seeks liberation.
Furthermore, having well disciplined one's own mind, one is also able to appropriately restrain and protect the minds of others, effectively pacifying their afflictions and defiled attachments;
this is called heedfulness (*apramāda*).
If a person has faith and understanding in the dharma of heedfulness (*apramāda*), they will be able to accord with all matters of diligence and further accumulate the merit of pure faith.
By cultivating pure faith and the dharmas of heedfulness and diligence, one is then able to practice right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right situational awareness (*samyak-samprajanya*).
By means of right mindfulness and right situational awareness, one does not lose or impair any of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
One who possesses pure faith, heedfulness, diligence, right mindfulness, and right situational awareness is able to ardently cultivate the profound and firm Dharma.

If a bodhisattva thoroughly understands profound and firm phenomena, they will be able to realize existence and non-existence as they truly are, even to the point of explaining that the eye and so forth exist within the context of conventional truth.
The verse in that sutra says:
"The Dharma of nectar is constant non-negligence; To benefit sentient beings, one gives rise to the bodhicitta.
The profound, firm, and tranquil mind is likewise so; It is the root of all happiness, free from grasping."
The Commentary states:
If one is able to accumulate all practices associated with meditative concentration, then superior merit will increase for both oneself and others.
Thus, it is said in verse:
"Train in the equality of self and others, Firmly establishing the bodhicitta.
When the self is confronted by the other, They are seen to be successively devoid of reality.
It is just as when one stands on the opposite shore; From this, they are perceived as counterparts."
Since that [suffering] is fundamentally non-existent, what nature of self could there be?
If one does not guard against suffering, one will be ensnared by it;
how then can one who practices the Dharma fail to protect themselves?
Arising from false and delusive discrimination, one clings to a self as being permanent.
If the self were originally thus [permanent], how could there be present birth and cessation?
If that [self] were something distinct from birth, for whose sake would one cultivate meritorious deeds?
Seeking wealth and profit, and experiencing various pleasures?
Yet one sees the body grow old and decay; before long it perishes, and is born again as an infant, then a child, and then a youth.
In the span of a single kṣaṇa, it rapidly decays and disintegrates;
where, then, can one speak of a "body"?
Fingernails and hair are all scattered apart.
Initial consciousness entrusts itself to the mother’s womb; having been born, one becomes an infant;
then comes the stage of youth, followed by the signs of aging; finally, one becomes ashes.
This clarifies that the self-nature of the body is merely a provisional arrangement of its various states.
Ultimately there is not even a single speck of dust; how could form and appearance endure for long?
Furthermore, regarding this body, do not speak of it but know it for yourself:
it is carried away by shifting characteristics; when one contemplates this, what "self" could there possibly be?
Through the combination of various states, they manifest conventionally;
within the Buddha’s correct principle, they are to be abandoned according to their correspondence.
If that consciousness did not exist, then [these states] could not be established.
Furthermore, there is no greed, hatred, or delusion; how then could there be merit?
As for the other nine types of worldly things, each has three kinds;
since they lack consciousness and are like clothing and such, how could they produce that bliss?
Clothing cannot produce happiness; one should know that it arises from causes.
If happiness were produced by clothing, how could its characteristic ever exist?
Therefore, according to the correct teaching and reasoning, all conditioned phenomena are said to be impermanent.
Through direct perception and reflection, one sees that things arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
seeing one’s own kin thus, how can one say they are permanent?
When sought within space and location, not even a single atom is to be found.
Just as when an oil lamp is burning and the oil is exhausted, where does that oil go?
Having observed it in this way, one sees that not even a single moment can endure.
Gathering all their kinsmen, they array themselves in solemn procession.
One falsely conceives of a self and its existence; yet others can recognize one's pleasure.
To understand those sentient beings, there is not a single thing that can be accumulated;
since self and other are distinct, even suffering cannot be acquired [by another].
Since such [a self] does not exist in association [with these aggregates],
where could "self" and "other" possibly be? Or, according to their own capacity,
they repeatedly demonstrate that the sentient beings of the world are constantly and intensely oppressed by manifold sufferings.
One should give rise to great compassion, out of pity for them;
having made such an observation skillfully, one should deliver them with equanimity.
Even if one enters the Avīci Hell, it will be like a swan gliding upon a lotus pond.
To cause all sentient beings to always dwell in the ocean of joy;
not seeking liberation for oneself, one rescues others with never-tiring perseverance.
Having performed such benefit, one does not give rise to self-reliance.
There is likewise no weariness, nor does one hope for karmic retribution.
If there were a mass of merit in the ten directions, one would certainly obtain it oneself and another;
without giving rise to a jealous mind, one regards the happiness of others as one's own.
Furthermore, if both oneself and others together practice repentance,
entreat the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and rejoice in meritorious deeds,
making such a dedication that is equal and without distinction, [then one shall attain supreme enlightenment].
According to the merit bestowed by their giving, throughout the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings,
the Bodhisattva practices this conduct; thus they bring great benefit to many,
increase the mind of great compassion, and attain the most supreme peace and security.
Vajrapāṇi and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly provide protection for them; all the hordes of māras tremble with fear.
They are the sons of the Dharma King, whom all the devas praise and extol.
Mounted upon the chariot of the bodhicitta, One skillfully traverses the supreme path.
When sentient beings practice well, They pacify and eliminate the suffering of both self and others;
therefore, I have no attachment, and shall relinquish everything.
If a person is bound by craving, suffering will be without end;
afflictions arise from this, and one suffers in vain regret for the harm already done.
If fire were to burn sentient beings, its fierce flames would pervade them all.
Even down to the size of a fingernail, there is no pleasure to be found even in oneself.
All forms of self-love are said to be the primary root of suffering;
having incinerated them without remainder, one acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.
One who delights in wife, children, and kin must ultimately abandon them all;
contemplating that they arise from causes and conditions, one feels no attachment even to one's own body.
Those wise people who possess true knowledge relinquish both of these.
Knowing that body and mind arise with momentary differentiation—
neither permanent nor impermanent, neither defiled nor originally pure—
one attains enlightenment for oneself; such a person also achieves perfect awakening.
Without thinking in terms of worldly dharmas, I shall benefit sentient beings;
I shall bestow the medicine of the Dharma and images of the Buddha.
Having chosen this through wisdom, my actions shall be in accord with what is to be done.
Guarding one's own wealth and, having accumulated it, being able to distribute it;
whether for oneself or for others, whether in times of little suffering or great suffering—
may all such beings obtain every kind of supreme and exquisite happiness.
When sentient beings encounter objects of desire, they give rise to obstacles and afflictions;
like a snake dwelling in its burrow, one must ultimately bring them to complete purity.
Just as a clean and fertile field brings all crops to maturity, so too does this discipline.
It can remove the afflictions of hunger and heat, and fulfill one’s karmic rewards.
If a person does not distance themselves from fame, profit, and the five desires, their words will lack sincerity; one need not be angry with such a person.
Since he has already lost his own self-interest, what room is there for anger?
Thus, one does not give rise to hatred, and the benefit of others remains uninterrupted.
One practices true patience in wholesome conduct, just as one observes the musk deer possessing its fragrance.
When one's own property is encroached upon by others, one instead suffers harm at the hands of hunters.
Through skillful reflection, one realizes there is no sovereign master;
since there is no personal enjoyment, why would there not be instruction for others?
In this way, those sons of the Buddha eliminate afflictions moment by moment and understand the spheres of the sensory faculties as being like great sores.
Toward those who harbor anger and resentment, they provide benefit and guide them with skillful means.
Intrinsic nature is free from conditioning; how could suffering or pleasure exist therein?
Furthermore, those five great elements are designated by forceful names;
even while abiding within sentient beings, they all accomplish what is beneficial.
If one is untiring in benefiting sentient beings, Then one will not commit any evils;
Therefore, I diligently practice, So that the six elements may be free from decay and affliction.
Reaching to the ultimate limit of space, And to the very boundaries of the world.
I abide for the benefit of sentient beings, bringing their wisdom and minds to maturity.
Acting as an ācārya, I have skillfully studied to transcend all suffering;
regardless of my own capacity, what is there that I do not protect?
If one inflicts suffering and distress upon oneself, for what reason would fear arise?
Following the Teacher’s realization, one understands the various faults of ego-clinging (*māna*).
Abiding in the realm of great compassion, one does not crave the karmic fruits of retribution.
Constantly attending to and practicing what one has learned, how could there be a self in this state of equality?
Seeing those who are deluded, insane, and blind, their steps often falter and they fall into perilous paths,
bringing constant anxiety and distress to both themselves and others.
Seeking after him, we shared his hardships and protected him;
practicing in such accordance, one perceives great merit.
My own faults are not few, being as deep as the vast ocean.
If both oneself and others continue to create [karma], by what means can liberation be attained?
If one follows those wholesome instructions, feels shame for all transgressions,
and always receives the words of others upon the crown of the head, then one should learn everything.
Hearing of those enemies, one feels fear; be careful not to speak of them to others.
My mind and my life are as one; if one rejoices [in harming them], there is no shame.
I alone am able to wage war against the enemies that are the various afflictions.
If this [affliction] dwells within the mind, it causes ruin and brings no peace.
I take refuge in Avalokiteśvara, whose great compassion is peerless,
whose dark-blue hair is gathered in spiraling curls, and which further hangs down like a garland.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, milk-seas flow from the tips of his fingers,
rescuing those in the hells and the realm of hungry ghosts from all the extreme sufferings of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, for virtuous sentient beings as well, he seeks them out by their voices to provide protection.
The Asura Vemacitrin was liberated from that hostile harm.
With a most supreme adornment such as the world had never before beheld,
all sentient beings, both foolish and wise, gazed upon him with universal joy and celebration.
Furthermore, with devout faith, I pay homage to the Great Being Mañjuśrī,
who compiled the treasury of the sublime Dharma that brings benefit and happiness to the world.
He is the peerless Great King of Physicians, who skillfully dispels all poisons and hardships.
Because you bestow happiness and life, I now bow my head to you.
You manifest a vast, clear spring amidst boundless suffering and feverish affliction,
causing all beings to rejoice in their hearts and ensuring that all thirst and craving shall be eliminated.
In all worlds of the ten directions, each manifests as a kalpa-protector;
fulfilling the needs of sentient beings, they universally manifest eyes like blue lotuses.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas praise them, their body hairs standing on end.
I take refuge in the Honored Mañjuśrī, The most supreme and unsurpassed.
All the rare bodhisattva practices And all the accumulated merits—
May self and others obtain inexhaustible blessings therefrom, And all become true sons of Mañjuśrī Buddha.
By transcribing this sublime Dharma, may whatever slight merit I possess, through compassion for sentient beings, cause their excellent wisdom to increase.
All phenomena arise from conditions; when conditions cease, phenomena are extinguished.
My teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, always speaks in this way.
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārabodhisattvaśikṣāsaṃgraha*, Fascicle Twenty-Five.
